Prediction Through a Fixed Generator.
Although the DiT is frozen, gradients still pass through it to the connector and MLLM. Under text-only observation, the MLLM pathway must produce representations that let the fixed generator reconstruct the target video’s semantic, motion, and temporal content from limited evidence. Under complete-video observation, the MLLM has direct visual evidence but must express it through the same connector and generation interface. Training both modes toward a shared video target therefore adapts the MLLM pathway without changing the DiT.
3.5
Inference and Cinematic Control
At inference, FAPL supports three cinematic applications within one architecture.
(i) Generation from Scripts and References.
Given a script and optional character or scene references, the MLLM produces latents that condition the DiT through the trained connector and original interface, followed by flow-based sampling and VAE decoding. No complete target video is needed. The DiT can use MLLM latents alone or together with the original text and VAE reference conditions as separate inference configurations.
(ii) Factor-Aware Control.
We modify only the target factor’s field in the structured prompt and re-encode the edited prompt through the MLLM and connector. We then replace the corresponding span in the original projected latents with the edited field’s span, keeping all other spans unchanged, and condition the DiT on the resulting sequence. We evaluate both the requested change and non-target preservation.
(iii) Multi-Shot Generation.
Shots are generated independently from their descriptions and available references. Shared character and scene references promote consistency, while action and camera instructions vary by shot.

Conclusion
This work studies how MLLM representations can support temporal inference and factor-aware control in cinematic video generation. FAPL makes these representations actionable by grounding the DiT in MLLM latents, supervising factor-specific changes and preservation, and learning prediction from limited inputs. FAPL demonstrates that targeting the right bottleneck delivers substantial gains without added architectural complexity. Our findings further offer insights into how multimodal reasoning and generation can reinforce each other: reasoning guides controllable synthesis, while generation provides grounded supervision for learning to infer missing content from limited observations.
Limitations and Future Work.
Although FAPL addresses a fundamental weakness of existing MLLM-conditioned DiTs by making MLLM latents more actionable, its performance remains bounded by the underlying models. Current MLLMs struggle to interpret 3D blockouts or reason about complex camera motion for DiT control, while the pretrained DiT limits visual fidelity and complex factor realization, such as realistic acting. Future work may incorporate stronger MLLMs and more capable video generators.

article.headline: 让MLLM潜变量真正驱动电影级视频生成
article.lede: FAPL用三阶段训练把MLLM潜变量变成唯一内容条件，在稀疏到视频、因子编辑、多镜头三项任务上均超过UniVideo与O
article.problem: 现有MLLM-conditioned视频DiT虽然接入了MLLM隐状态，但原生文本编码器与VAE参考通路可以让DiT在不依赖MLLM潜变量的情况下降低生成损失，特征接入不等于特征生效。同时，普通视频级监督并不指明某个因子对应的MLLM片段被改动后输出该变什么、该保留什么；而冻结MLLM、只调connector和DiT的做法，也没有训练MLLM本身从稀疏输入产出对生成有用的时序表示。
article.method: 作者提出Factor-Aware Predictive Learning（FAPL），三个阶段都只把MLLM潜变量作为内容条件。Stage I冻结MLLM与connector、只训DiT，用text-only和text+完整视频两种观测做潜变量接地；Stage II保持MLLM冻结，把结构化提示中character、scene、action、camera四个字段对应的投影潜变量span在成对样本间互换，让目标视频监督被替换因子的改变与非目标内容的保持；Stage III冻结训好的DiT，用共享同一视频目标的两种观测联合优化MLLM与connector，使梯度穿过固定生成器回传到理解分支。
article.results: 在13B DiT的UniVideo上搭建FAPL，与Omni-Video 2（1.3B、14B）和UniVideo（13B）对比：Motion Order为61%对UniVideo的48%，Translation Error 0.0586对0.0763，Rotation Error 1.02 rad对1.54 rad，因子编辑∩-Acc为58%对42%，Subject Consistency 0.516对0.462，Scene Consistency 0.471对0.427，多镜头FaceSim-Arc为0.523，而Omni-Video 2（1.3B）为0.412、（14B）为0.468，UniVideo为0.451。消融显示Stage II使用因子span替换时∩-Acc为57%，同数据同预算下不做替换为48%，但Motion Order与相机误差未随之改善；Stage III改用混合观测后Motion Order由57%升至61%，平移与旋转误差分别从0.0629降到0.0586、从1.26降到1.02 rad，编辑精度由57%微升至58%。训练数据为10万条质量过滤的源–目标视频对（每个因子2.5万），推理用50步采样、CFG 5.0。
article.why_it_matters: 论文把问题定位在「MLLM潜变量被旁路」而非架构缺失，并给出不改结构、用固定生成器反向塑造理解模型表示的训练路径，这为理解–生成联合建模提供了一个可复用的监督范式。Stage I的增益在图7中也出现在Omni-Video 2的1.3B与14B上，提示该接地策略并非只对单一backbone有效。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认性能仍受底层模型限制：当前MLLM难以理解3D blockout或推理复杂相机运动，预训练DiT也限制了视觉保真度与真实表演等复杂因子的实现。此外评测主要基于作者构建的CineFactor-10K与ShotVerse-Bench，因子干预依赖把caption改写成四字段结构化提示，这一假设在自由文本场景下的适用性文中未给出验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: FAPL框架总览：Stage I冻结MLLM与connector、用MLLM潜变量训练DiT；Stage II保持该配置并在成对样本间交换因子专属输出span以监督因子相关变化；Stage III冻结已训好的DiT，通过视频重建联合更新MLLM与connector，且纯文本输入与文本加完整视频输入共享同一生成目标。

figure.caption: {Overview of Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL).} Stage I freezes the MLLM and its original connector and trains the DiT using MLLM latents. Stage II retains this configuration and swaps factor-specific output spans between paired examples to supervise factor-aware changes. Stage III freezes the trained DiT and jointly updates the MLLM and connector through video reconstruction, and text-only and text-plus-complete-video inputs share the same generation target.

email_papers.title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
email_papers.abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires 32times fewer retrieval queries and 2048times fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.

Abstract
Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires
32
×
32\times
fewer retrieval queries and
2048
×
2048\times
fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
The code will be released soon.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs)
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2025
;
Bai et al., 2026
)
have advanced rapidly in language understanding, generation, and reasoning. Their growing capabilities support knowledge-intensive applications, but reliable answers require facts that can be missing, poorly retained, or outdated in pretrained parameters
(
Lewis et al., 2020
)
. Knowledge injection addresses this gap by incorporating information from an external corpus. A central challenge is to incorporate this knowledge effectively while preserving existing capabilities and keeping knowledge acquisition and inference costs manageable.
Existing approaches face different trade-offs in addressing this challenge. Continued pretraining (CPT)
(
Gururangan et al., 2020
)
learns from an additional corpus through language modeling, while LoRA
(
Hu et al., 2021
)
offers a parameter-efficient way to adapt the model. These approaches keep inference self-contained, but adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired capabilities
(
Biderman et al., 2024
)
. Non-parametric retrieval instead provides external evidence during generation. RAG
(
Lewis et al., 2020
)
conditions on retrieved passages, and RETRO
(
Borgeaud et al., 2022
)
incorporates retrieved chunks within the decoder. These methods provide access to corpus knowledge without first learning it in model parameters, but datastore search and evidence processing can add substantial inference latency
(
Cao et al., 2026
)
.
Parametric memory learns from retrieved knowledge offline, enabling inference without explicit retrieval. MLP Memory
(
Wei et al., 2026a
)
and Memory Decoder
(
Cao et al., 2026
)
learn to predict retrieval-derived next-token distributions. However, this inference advantage comes with substantial offline costs. Constructing token-level training targets requires retrieval at individual token positions across the corpus, resulting in substantial data construction costs
(
Wei et al., 2026b
)
. Training memory modules on these targets further incurs significant computational cost. Moreover, these methods rely on shallow fusion through output-probability interpolation, without incorporating memory into the decoder’s hidden states. Intuitively, integrating memory into intermediate hidden states allows subsequent layers to further process and combine it with the evolving context. The broader challenge is to enable language models to acquire external knowledge efficiently and use it effectively.
In this work, we introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that combines efficient knowledge acquisition with deep fusion within the decoder (Figure
1
). At a high level, DFM shares memory supervision across multiple token predictions while allowing each token to use the learned memory according to its context. We jointly train a memory predictor and a memory fusion module, using retrieved target memory to supervise the predictor and the standard language modeling objective to train both modules. In this way, external knowledge is not only stored in the predictor’s parameters, but also injected into intermediate hidden states through the fusion module, allowing subsequent decoder layers to utilize the memory during generation. The LLM backbone remains frozen throughout, and memory prediction is performed at the chunk level.
Our experiments demonstrate improvements in both efficiency and downstream performance. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches that construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires
32
×
32\times
fewer retrieval queries and
2048
×
2048\times
fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. DFM achieves the highest average score across six QA tasks on both backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, adaptation across code, mathematics, and law yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively. Ablations further highlight the importance of fusion placement and gate initialization, while showing comparatively small changes in average QA performance across the tested chunk sizes and numbers of memory slots.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We introduce
DFM, a parametric memory architecture with deep fusion
, which integrates learned corpus knowledge into intermediate hidden states so that subsequent decoder layers can process memory together with the evolving context. Inference requires no explicit retrieval.
•
We reduce
the overhead of supervision construction and memory training
through chunk-level supervision and end-to-end training with a frozen backbone. For training data construction, DFM requires
32
×
32\times
fewer retrieval queries and
2048
×
2048\times
fewer retrieved items than existing parametric memory approaches based on token-level targets.
•
We demonstrate
improved QA performance and domain adaptation
. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Across code, mathematics, and law, average gains over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base reach 6.51 and 4.38 points, respectively.
2
Related Work
Model Adaptation.
Continued pretraining adapts language models to additional corpora through further language modeling
(
Gururangan et al., 2020
)
, while LoRA
(
Hu et al., 2021
)
offers a parameter-efficient way to adapt the model.
Such adaptation can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired capabilities
(
Biderman et al., 2024
)
.
Deep Fusion Memory keeps the backbone frozen and learns an added memory module from retrieval-derived targets, jointly training memory prediction and fusion.
Retrieval-Augmented Language Models.
Non-parametric memory exposes corpus information through several interfaces.
k
k
NN-LM retrieves context–token pairs and interpolates a neighbor-derived next-token distribution with the language model output
(
Khandelwal et al., 2019
)
, whereas RAG conditions generation on retrieved passages
(
Lewis et al., 2020
)
.
RETRO combines chunk retrieval with cross-attention inside the Transformer
(
Borgeaud et al., 2022
)
.
xRAG projects a retrieved document embedding into a single token representation prepended to the query, reducing the context passed to the generator
(
Cheng et al., 2024
)
.
These methods retain an external retrieval dependency at inference.
Deep Fusion Memory predicts continuous memory parametrically and uses it inside the decoder without online search.
Parametric Memory.
MLP Memory trains an MLP to predict
k
k
NN token distributions from language model representations
(
Wei et al., 2026a
)
.
Memory Decoder learns a similar distributional target with a standalone decoder
(
Cao et al., 2026
)
.
Memory Decoder at Scale extends this approach to large-scale general and domain memory pretraining
(
Wei et al., 2026b
)
.
MemSFT specializes frozen backbones through a domain memory and a learned token-wise router over the backbone and memory output distributions
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches avoid explicit retrieval at inference, but token-level retrieval incurs substantial data construction costs, and output-probability interpolation provides only shallow fusion.
Deep Fusion Memory reduces the cost of supervision construction by sharing target memory across tokens within each chunk and fuses predicted memory into hidden states through gated cross-attention.
3
Deep Fusion Memory
Deep Fusion Memory consists of a causal chunk-level memory predictor and memory cross-attention modules inserted into selected decoder layers (Figure
1
). We construct target memory offline, then jointly train the added modules with language-modeling and memory-prediction objectives while keeping the backbone frozen. At inference, the predictor supplies memory directly from the input sequence.
Figure 1:
Overview of Deep Fusion Memory.
(a) Memory Prediction.
The memory predictor maps pooled chunk embeddings to predicted memory, supervised by offline target memory. A shared projector maps predicted memory to the decoder’s hidden space.
(b) LLM Backbone.
Selected decoder layers incorporate memory for next-token prediction.
(c) Memory Fusion.
Memory predicted from the preceding context supports token predictions in the next chunk. Per-head gates control the memory cross-attention contribution alongside self-attention. Inference requires no retrieval.

Inference
At inference, the language model uses the same predictor and fusion modules without constructing target memory. Chunk queries are formed from backbone input embeddings, and the memory predictor supplies predicted memory to the selected decoder layers. No datastore search, retrieved text, or external embedding encoder is required. For QA evaluation, predicted memory is computed from the visible prompt and remains fixed during answer generation. Selected decoder layers attend to the predicted memory only at positions associated with the prompt chunks. As defined in Eq.

4.2
Question Answering Performance
Overall Performance.
Table
1
compares DFM with non-parametric and parametric methods across six QA benchmarks. DFM achieves the highest average on both backbones without online retrieval. On Mistral, it raises the six-task mean from xRAG’s 24.14 to 27.21, a
12.71% relative improvement
over the strongest baseline. On Qwen3-8B-Base, it improves from MLP Memory’s 23.80 to 26.46, a
11.19% relative improvement
. These correspond to absolute gains of 3.07 and 2.66 points, showing comparable relative benefits across the two backbone families. Relative to Base, DFM gains 13.59 and 3.75 points, improving all six tasks on Mistral and five on Qwen3. It also outperforms CPT and LoRA on every Mistral task and five Qwen3 tasks.
Single-Hop Question Answering.
On Mistral, DFM reaches 33.57 on NQ and 42.47 on WebQA, improving over Base by 13.27 and 13.19 points. These scores exceed the strongest baseline on each task by 6.18 and 2.26 points, showing gains beyond those obtained through either explicit retrieval or parameter adaptation alone. On Qwen3, NQ improves from 17.60 to 27.46, exceeding RAG by 3.04 points. WebQA instead decreases from 41.78 to 39.47, while MLP Memory achieves 43.26. The contrasting WebQA outcomes show that memory adaptation is not uniformly beneficial across backbones, even when the original weights remain frozen.
Multi-Hop Question Answering.
DFM improves over Base on all four multi-hop benchmarks for both backbones. On Mistral, it leads on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, with Bamboogle increasing from 3.91 to 22.65. Its 2Wiki score rises from 5.87 to 25.00, although RAG remains stronger at 31.02. On Qwen3, DFM achieves the best results on 2Wiki, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, including a 7.55-point gain over Base on 2Wiki. It also improves HotpotQA to 26.46, below xRAG’s 27.74. These results indicate that predicted memory can support tasks requiring multiple pieces of evidence, while explicit retrieval retains an advantage on some benchmarks.

Conclusion
We presented Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that combines efficient supervision construction with deep fusion within the decoder. Sharing target memory across tokens in each chunk reduces retrieval work, while gated cross-attention allows subsequent decoder layers to process predicted memory together with the evolving context. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. DFM improves the six-task QA average over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, DFM improves performance over the base models across code, mathematics, and law. These results demonstrate that shared supervision and learned internal fusion can support efficient knowledge acquisition and effective memory use.

Appendix A
Experimental Details
A.1
Question Answering
Data construction.
We use section and infobox text from Wikipedia December 2018. Records are grouped by normalized article titles and assigned to training, validation, and test splits in proportions of 99.8/0.1/0.1% using seed 42. We remove exact text duplicates across splits, append EOS to each record, and pack records within each split into 2,048-token sequences. Incomplete final sequences are discarded. Tokenization yields 4.70B, 4.29B, and 4.08B training tokens for Mistral, Qwen3, and OLMo3, respectively. Each sequence is divided into non-overlapping 32-token chunks. We encode training chunks with the frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B encoder, using last-token pooling and L2 normalization to obtain 1,024-dimensional representations. A FAISS IVF-PQ index supports offline neighbor retrieval. Following Section
3.1
, each preceding chunk retrieves target memory for the next chunk. We retain the top-16 full chunk embeddings in retrieval-rank order, including the nearest neighbor, and mask the first chunk from memory supervision. The datastore contains training chunks only.

The predictor has 28 layers, hidden width 1,024, FFN width 3,072, 16 query heads, and eight KV heads. Its 16 output heads predict the continuous memory slots. Evaluation.
Table
4
summarizes the six QA benchmarks. DFM uses zero-shot greedy decoding without online retrieval, gold documents, or chain-of-thought demonstrations. Questions are formatted with task-specific question–answer templates. Generation stops at a newline or the token limit, with period and comma as additional stop strings for WebQA. Evaluation batches contain one example per GPU, except WebQA, which uses four. For QA, each memory query is formed from the current visible prompt chunk rather than the preceding chunk used during training. The queries and predicted memory remain fixed during generation. For newly added chunk positions, the adapter pads queries and query-validity masks with zeros, so these positions receive no direct memory update. Generated answer chunks do not refresh the queries, and incremental predictor caching is not used in the reported implementation. F1 measures normalized token overlap and takes the maximum over accepted answers. Substring match checks whether a normalized reference answer occurs in the generated response. Scores are reported on a 0–100 scale, and Avg. is the unweighted mean across the six tasks.

RAG.
RAG uses the frozen Base backbone without additional training. It retrieves the top-1 document from the corresponding domain’s training corpus using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Retrieved Code is prefixed as comments, while Math and Law use a background prefix. The original task prompt is preserved in full; only retrieved background is truncated when the input budget is exceeded. Few-shot examples, sample counts, generation settings, and scorers are identical to Base.
Evaluation.
HumanEval uses three demonstrations and four samples per problem, while HumanEval+ uses zero demonstrations and one sample. Code reports sample-average execution correctness, estimating pass@1. GSM8K uses eight demonstrations and one sample. LawBench evaluates 500 examples for each of its 20 tasks in the zero-shot setting. All methods use a common

article.headline: 块级参数记忆DFM：免检索注入解码器隐状态
article.lede: 上海交大等提出DFM，用块级监督训练参数化记忆，并在解码器中间层融合；推理不需检索。
article.problem: 大模型需要外部知识，但继续预训练可能灾难性遗忘，推理时检索又带来额外开销。已有参数化记忆免在线检索，却依赖昂贵的token级检索监督，且多在输出概率层做浅融合。
article.method: DFM把文本切成块，用因果记忆预测器从先前上下文生成块级记忆，并以离线检索到的块嵌入作为监督。预测记忆经共享投影后，通过带门控的交叉注意力注入选定解码器层，与自注意力并行。骨干网络冻结，记忆预测与融合用语言建模损失和MSE联合端到端训练，推理不做检索。
article.results: 在六个QA任务上，DFM平均分在Mistral-7B-v0.3上从最强基线24.14升至27.21，相对提升12.71%；在Qwen3-8B-Base上从23.80升至26.46，提升11.19%。域适应中，Qwen3-4B-Base和Qwen3-8B-Base平均分别提升6.51和4.38分。相比token级方案，构建数据所需检索查询少32倍、检索条目少2048倍；新增参数0.75B（约少50%），训练约24小时对64小时，降62.5%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把外部知识写进可预测的参数记忆并注入中间隐状态，推理无需检索，有望降低知识更新与领域适配的在线成本。
article.limitations: 但Qwen3-8B上WebQA从41.78降至39.47，Mistral上2Wiki也低于RAG（25.00对31.02）；消融多为单次运行，未测目标构建的实际耗时，代码尚未发布。
article.figure_caption_zh: DFM总览：记忆预测器由离线目标记忆监督，共享投影器把预测记忆送入选定解码器层，经逐头门控交叉注意力与自注意力并行融合，推理无需检索。

A shared projector maps predicted memory to the decoder's hidden space. {(b) LLM Backbone.} Selected decoder layers incorporate memory for next-token prediction. {(c) Memory Fusion.} Memory predicted from the preceding context supports token predictions in the next chunk. Per-head gates control the memory cross-attention contribution alongside self-attention. Inference requires no retrieval.

article.headline: 可微世界模型训练人形控制器，省逾千GPU小时
article.lede: 论文用一个可学习的可微世界模型来训练人形机器人全身控制器，称相比集群规模的无模型强化学习可节省逾1000个GPU小时。
article.problem: 人形机器人全身控制器的无模型强化学习通常需要集群级算力：图注给出的对照工作SONIC（luo2025sonic）用128块L40 GPU训练168小时。这种算力门槛让复现和迭代代价很高。论文要问的是，能否用学到的世界模型把大部分训练搬到「想象」里完成。
article.method: 论文训练一个可微的世界模型，让策略在世界模型的想象rollout中改进，而不是在真实或仿真环境中做大规模无模型试错。图注称整套训练在单块H100上只需3小时。世界模型的结构、训练数据与策略优化细节，论文材料未给出。
article.results: 图注给出的对照是：SONIC用128块L40 GPU训练168小时，本工作在单块H100上训练3小时；作者据此称相比集群规模的无模型强化学习减少超过1000个GPU小时。除此之外，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 如果世界模型能撑起全身控制这类高维连续控制任务，人形机器人策略训练的门槛会从「集群」降到「单卡」，更多实验室就能参与迭代。这也为把可微模型用作策略学习的替代环境提供了算力层面的证据。
article.limitations: 这一对比涉及硬件类型不同（L40与H100）且只针对SONIC一个基线，GPU小时之差不能直接等同于方法效率之差。本次提供的材料只有图注、没有正文，真机迁移效果、任务泛化范围与世界模型误差累积等问题论文未给出具体数字，结论仍需核实。

page_papers.title: Deep Search in Real-World Web Environments
page_papers.abstract: Despite substantial progress in Deep Search agents, their ability to conduct end-to-end research in real-world open Web environments remains insufficiently evaluated. Unlike static retrieval settings, information on the real-world Web is distributed across diverse sources, modalities, and heterogeneous formats, often involving complex interaction mechanisms that require agents to autonomously search for, access, and integrate relevant evidence during execution. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenDS task, designed to evaluate agents' ability to perform multi-step deep search in the live, open Web. This task requires agents to autonomously explore the real Web, discover and connect relevant evidence from multiple independent sources through Web search, browser interaction, and evidence processing, and ultimately determine a unique factual answer. Building on this task formulation, we construct OpenDS-World, a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks spanning diverse information modalities, heterogeneous file formats, and interactive access requirements, with independent human verification to ensure evidence validity and answer uniqueness. We evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol. The best-performing model achieves 39.0% accuracy, while human evaluation across 1,000 independent attempts yields 21.1% accuracy. Further analyses of tool usage, search cost, termination behavior, and failure recovery reveal substantial differences in research strategies across models, as well as persistent challenges in tool coordination and long-horizon search management. OpenDS-World provides a unified evaluation platform for systematically assessing and advancing agents' autonomous deep search capabilities in real-world open Web environments.

Abstract
Despite substantial progress in Deep Search agents, their ability to conduct end-to-end research in real-world open Web environments remains insufficiently evaluated. Unlike static retrieval settings, information on the real-world Web is distributed across diverse sources, modalities, and heterogeneous formats, often involving complex interaction mechanisms that require agents to autonomously search for, access, and integrate relevant evidence during execution. To address this gap, we introduce the
OpenDS
task, designed to evaluate agents’ ability to perform multi-step deep search in the live, open Web. This task requires agents to autonomously explore the real Web, discover and connect relevant evidence from multiple independent sources through Web search, browser interaction, and evidence processing, and ultimately determine a unique factual answer. Building on this task formulation, we construct
OpenDS-World
, a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks spanning diverse information modalities, heterogeneous file formats, and interactive access requirements, with independent human verification to ensure evidence validity and answer uniqueness. We evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol. The best-performing model achieves 39.0% accuracy, while human evaluation across 1,000 independent attempts yields 21.1% accuracy. Further analyses of tool usage, search cost, termination behavior, and failure recovery reveal substantial differences in research strategies across models, as well as persistent challenges in tool coordination and long-horizon search management. Contents
1. Introduction
A central objective of Deep Search is to enable AI agents to autonomously acquire, analyze, and integrate information to solve complex information-seeking and research tasks
(
Xi et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025b
;
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
. Recent advances in large language models and tool-augmented agents have substantially improved their capabilities in multi-round search, Web browsing, and cross-source reasoning
(
Jin et al., 2025b
;
Qiao et al., 2025
)
, enabling them to address increasingly complex information needs
(
Zheng et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2025a
;
Li et al., 2026c
)
. Meanwhile, reliably evaluating these agents’ research capabilities in practical environments has become an increasingly important issue. Existing studies have explored various aspects of agent capabilities, including general tool use, complex information retrieval, persistent Web search, and interactive Web navigation, providing an important foundation for understanding their search, reasoning, and tool-use capabilities
(
Wei et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2025a
;
Xue et al., 2025
)
.
Despite substantial progress in open Web search, multi-round information retrieval, and cross-source reasoning, existing Deep Search evaluations remain insufficient for systematically assessing the complex evidence acquisition requirements of real-world Web environments. The complexity of the real-world Web is primarily reflected in three aspects: Diverse Modalities, where information is presented in various forms, including text, images, audio, and video
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Liu et al., 2026b
)
; Heterogeneous Formats, where information is distributed across resources with different structures and processing requirements
(
Jin et al., 2025b
)
, such as HTML, PDF, XML, and Parquet; and Interactive Access Requirements, where certain evidence cannot be obtained through direct retrieval but requires interactive operations such as Web navigation, interface manipulation, parameter updates, or artifact transfer
(
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
. Together, these attributes constitute the complex evidence acquisition process in real-world Web environments, requiring agents to coordinate information discovery, interactive access, resource processing, and cross-source reasoning throughout multi-step research. However, existing benchmarks
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Java et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
have not sufficiently covered these interconnected challenges, limiting the systematic analysis of agents’ deep search capabilities in real-world environments.
Figure 2
:
An example of deep search in OpenDS-World.
The example connects audiovisual identification, virtual-tour navigation, document inspection, and structured-data retrieval across multiple Web sources.
To address this gap, we introduce the
OpenDS (Open-Web Deep Search) task
, designed to systematically evaluate agents’ ability to conduct deep search across heterogeneous information sources in real-world Web environments. This task requires agents to autonomously search, access, and connect evidence across Web sources with diverse information modalities, resource formats, and interactive access requirements to complete complex multi-step searches. Building upon the OpenDS task, we construct
OpenDS-World
, a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks designed around real-world Web information sources, spanning eight domains: culture, daily life, science, economy, history, nature, society, and technology. Each task requires agents to start from a video containing real-world information and independently discover evidence from multiple sources across the open Web to support the answer. As illustrated in Figure
2
, solving a task may involve accessing online videos, interactive virtual tours, research papers, and structured datasets, and acquiring and connecting relevant evidence through different access mechanisms. To systematically characterize the challenges of evidence acquisition in real-world Web environments, OpenDS-World covers diverse information modalities, heterogeneous file formats, and seven types of access requirements. We employ independent human verification and task filtering to ensure evidence validity, factual accuracy, and answer uniqueness, and further conduct human testing to assess practical research difficulty.
We systematically evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol. The results reveal that current agents still face substantial challenges when conducting deep search in real-world Web environments. The best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra
(
OpenAI, 2026b
)
, achieves only 39.0% accuracy across all 200 tasks. By comparison, human participants achieve an overall accuracy of 21.1% in independent solving attempts (Figure
1
), with 42.5% of tasks remaining unsolved by all assigned human participants. Further analysis reveals substantial differences across models in tool usage, search cost, termination behavior, and failure recovery. More tool calls and longer execution times do not necessarily lead to higher accuracy, reflecting limitations in current agents’ information-source selection, tool coordination, search strategy adjustment, and long-horizon execution management.
By covering diverse information modalities, heterogeneous resource formats, interactive access requirements, and multi-step evidence dependencies, OpenDS-World provides a unified platform for systematically evaluating agents’ ability to conduct deep search across heterogeneous information sources in real-world Web environments. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
Deep Search Task in Real-World Web Environments (OpenDS Task).
We introduce the OpenDS task to systematically evaluate agents’ ability to conduct deep search across heterogeneous information sources in real-world Web environments. The task requires agents to autonomously search, access, process, and connect evidence across information sources with diverse modalities, resource formats, and interactive access requirements, determining a unique factual answer through multi-step research.
•
The OpenDS-World Benchmark.
Building upon the OpenDS task, we construct a benchmark comprising 200 challenging tasks across eight domains, covering diverse information modalities, heterogeneous resource formats, and seven types of access requirements.
•
Systematic Model Evaluation.
We evaluate 12 frontier models under a unified tool environment and execution protocol, systematically analyzing task accuracy, search cost, tool usage, termination behavior, and failure recovery. Our analysis reveals differences in search strategies and execution behaviors across models, as well as key challenges faced by current agents when conducting deep search in complex real-world Web environments.
Figure 3
:
Three complementary properties of a real-world Web source.
An Our World in Data page illustrates how a single source combines (A) diverse modalities, including text and visual charts; (B) heterogeneous formats, including HTML, CSV, JSON, and downloadable ZIP bundles; and (C) interactive access, including region selection, temporal indexing, and declarative API queries. Obtaining relevant evidence requires navigating these connected representations and source states.
2. OpenDS-World
We introduce
OpenDS-World
, a benchmark for systematically evaluating AI agents’ ability to conduct deep search across heterogeneous information sources in real-world Web environments. The benchmark comprises 200 challenging tasks constructed from real-world Web information sources, spanning eight domains: culture, daily life, science, economy, history, nature, society, and technology (Figure
10
(a)). OpenDS-World focuses on the complex process of evidence acquisition in real-world Web environments, evaluating agents’ ability to autonomously discover, acquire, and connect evidence across different information sources involving diverse information modalities, heterogeneous resource formats, and interactive access requirements.
2.1. Open-Web Deep Search
2.1.1. Task Definition
We define
Open-Web Deep Search (OpenDS)
as a factual question-answering task that involves multi-step evidence search and reasoning across heterogeneous information sources in real-world open Web environments. Given a factual question and available initial clues, an agent must autonomously explore the open Web, continuously search for, access, process, and connect relevant evidence across information sources with diverse modalities, resource formats, and interactive access requirements, ultimately determining a unique and verifiable factual answer. In OpenDS, the evidence required to complete a task may be distributed across different websites, documents, multimedia resources, and online applications, while its specific locations and access methods are not provided to the agent in advance. The agent must determine subsequent search targets based on the information currently available, select appropriate information access and processing methods, and progressively establish connections among evidence through cross-source reasoning. Because different information sources vary in content representation, data organization, and access mechanisms, the agent must flexibly coordinate search, interaction, and information processing operations throughout multi-step research, enabling evidence from different sources to be connected and collectively support the final answer. Beyond information discovery and cross-source reasoning
(
Li et al., 2025c
;
Li et al., 2026c
)
, OpenDS emphasizes the continuous process of evidence acquisition and integration across different information modalities, resource formats, and access mechanisms in real-world Web environments. These interconnected requirements collectively constitute the core task characteristics of OpenDS.
2.1.2. Main Attributes
OpenDS is organized around three main attributes of real-world Web information environments:
Diverse Modalities
,
Heterogeneous Formats
, and
Interactive Access Requirements
. These attributes characterize the complexity of the real-world Web in terms of information representation, organizational structure, and access methods, respectively. They jointly influence how agents discover, acquire, and connect evidence across different information sources throughout the search process. Figure
3
illustrates how these three attributes coexist within a single Web source.
Diverse Modalities.
Information on the real-world Web is represented across multiple modalities, including text, images, audio, and video. Relevant evidence may appear in Web text, visual content, spoken information, or multimedia resources, and different stages of the same research task may depend on information from different modalities. Therefore, agents need to continuously search across information sources of different modalities, interpret the clues provided by various types of content, and establish cross-modal evidence connections
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Tian et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026b
)
. OpenDS-World evaluates agents’ capabilities in cross-modal search and evidence integration through evidence paths involving multiple information modalities.
Heterogeneous Formats.
Information on the real-world Web is organized in different file and data formats, such as HTML pages, PDF documents, WebP images, MP3 audio, MP4 video, RSS/XML data sources, and structured data formats such as Parquet. Different formats have distinct content structures, parsing methods, and processing requirements
(
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Jin et al., 2025b
;
Yuan et al., 2026
)
. Even when information belongs to the same modality, its acquisition and processing methods may differ substantially. During cross-source search, agents need to select appropriate access and processing methods according to resource formats, extract relevant evidence from heterogeneous data, and use the acquired information for subsequent search and reasoning. OpenDS-World evaluates agents’ ability to conduct continuous search and evidence integration across heterogeneous resources through combinations of information sources with different formats.
Interactive Access Requirements.
Some information on the real-world Web cannot be obtained through direct observation or simple retrieval. Instead, obtaining it requires specific access operations to reveal or extract the relevant evidence
(
Liu et al., 2026a
;
Xue et al., 2025
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
. These operations may include page navigation, parameter input, temporal indexing, graphical interface manipulation, structured queries, and resource downloads. For example, locating a particular exhibit in an interactive museum virtual tour may require an agent to autonomously explore the interface, switch viewpoints, and identify relevant visual evidence. Access requirements may vary substantially across different information sources. Therefore, agents need to dynamically select operations according to the location and access mechanisms of the target evidence, and establish connections between the acquired information and evidence from other sources. OpenDS-World incorporates different access requirements into task evidence paths to evaluate agents’ ability to continuously acquire and connect information under complex interactive conditions.
2.2. OpenDS-World Construction
2.2.1. Task Construction
Stage 1. Real-World Anchor.
Each evidence path begins with a publicly accessible video. Expert annotators select videos spanning eight domains: culture, daily life, science, economy, history, nature, society, and technology. In total, 500 candidate videos are selected for task construction. They jointly analyze consecutive visual frames and audio content to identify a verifiable initial anchor. The anchor corresponds to an entity whose identification must rely on the audiovisual content of the video.
This constraint prevents anchor identification from degenerating into page-level textual search
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Liu et al., 2026b
)
. To ensure stable access and reproducibility, the videos used during task construction are archived and distributed with the benchmark as part of the task input, with each video matched to its corresponding task by ID.
To ensure an unambiguous semantic reference, the core entity associated with the anchor must uniquely correspond to a valid Wikidata entry. The video, initial anchor, and corresponding Wikidata entry serve as the starting point for subsequent evidence expansion.
Stage 2. Open-Web Evidence Expansion.
At each expansion step along the evidence path, expert annotators first construct a search query based on the current node, and then use Google Search to obtain a candidate set of Web information sources. Annotators inspect the candidate results one by one and select sources while ensuring that each source has a clear semantic relation to the current node and that the evidence is verifiable
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
. During candidate source selection, annotators also consider the modality, format, and access-type attributes to increase the diversity of the final dataset across different forms of Web information. Annotators then extract a new entity from the selected source and designate it as the next node. Although each new node is initially identified from a selected source, its validity is not tied to that source alone. Each node along the evidence path must be independently corroborated by multiple Web sources, ensuring multi-source support throughout the entire evidence chain. This process is recursively applied along the evidence path
(
Tao et al., 2026
)
until reaching a unique and stable terminal node suitable as the reference answer. In this way, the evidence path is dynamically constructed through iterative search, access, and verification over real Web information sources.
Stage 3. Question Inversion.
Once the evidence path reaches a unique terminal node, we designate it as the reference answer and construct the textual question by inverting the complete evidence path into a set of interdependent constraints
(
Wei et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. The intermediate nodes are not explicitly revealed. Instead, each node is transformed into an indirect referring description derived from the evidence accumulated along the preceding path
(
Lu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
.
These descriptions are composed so that no individual clue directly exposes the target entity, while their combination progressively constrains the candidate space and uniquely determines the reference answer. As a result, directly retrieving the answer from an explicit clue cannot solve the question. It requires recovering the latent correspondences among intermediate entities and following the underlying evidence chain.
2.2.2. Human Verification
We conduct independent human verification for each candidate task, involving a total of ten independent reviewers. Reviewers revisit the complete evidence path using the source links preserved during annotation, including the initial anchor, intermediate entities, inter-entity relations, and the final reference answer. The verification process consists of two main aspects: evidence validity and task validity.
Evidence Validity.
Reviewers examine the entities along the evidence path, their semantic relations, and the final reference answer to ensure factual accuracy and support from authentic, accessible, and independently verifiable Web evidence
(
Chen et al., 2025b
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
. To avoid over-reliance on the original source, reviewers treat it as just one reference among several and cross-check the information against multiple additional independent Web sources.
They further verify that each transition between adjacent nodes is explicitly supported by evidence, ensuring factual and logical consistency throughout the evidence path. For the initial Real-world Anchor, reviewers additionally confirm that it can be uniquely identified from the visual and audio content of the video, that its core entity is correctly and uniquely mapped to a valid Wikidata entry, and that the relevant information cannot be directly obtained from the textual content on the same video page.
Task Validity.
Reviewers further examine whether each candidate task satisfies the construction principles, focusing on question clarity, constraint consistency, and answer uniqueness. Specifically, reviewers verify that the key clues in the question accurately correspond to the relevant information along the evidence path, that each constraint is supported by verifiable evidence
(
Java et al., 2026
)
, and that no factual or logical conflicts exist among the constraints. Reviewers also confirm that these constraints collectively determine a unique factual answer, avoiding ambiguity arising from insufficient clues, unclear entity references, or multiple plausible answers
(
Wei et al., 2025
;
Li et al., 2025b
)
. Any candidate task containing factual errors, insufficient evidence, inconsistent relations, ambiguous questions, non-unique reference answers, or violations of the construction principles is directly excluded.
Following the above filtering procedures, we construct the final OpenDS-World benchmark comprising 200 tasks. All tasks have a clearly defined reference answer and a verifiable evidence path.
2.3. Human Testing
After completing human filtering, we further conduct an independent human evaluation to assess the practical difficulty of solving the questions in a real Web environment. This evaluation is to measure how difficult it is for independent solvers to discover the evidence path and to provide human performance data for subsequent difficulty calibration.

2.3.1. Independent Human Solving
We divide the 200 questions into 10 disjoint sets of 20 questions, with each set independently attempted by a group of five human solvers, for a total of 50 participants. Each solver completes only one question set to control individual workload and reduce potential fatigue effects. None of the solvers participated in constructing or filtering the questions they answered, and communication among solvers was not allowed during testing. Human solvers are given only the complete original input, including the video, audio, and textual question. They are not provided with the reference answer or the evidence path constructed during annotation. Solvers may use standard Web browsers such as Google Chrome for conventional Web browsing and search, but they are not allowed to use any LLM-based systems or tools. No uniform time limit is imposed for individual questions. The solving time for each question is measured from the moment a solver begins viewing the task input until the solver voluntarily terminates the attempt. When a solver considers that no further effective progress can be made, the solver may terminate the current question. Each human solver is required to submit a final answer, the total time spent solving the question, and a six-point subjective difficulty rating from 0 to 5, where 0 indicates the easiest and 5 indicates the most difficult. All final answers submitted by the solvers are manually checked to determine whether they are correct. During human testing, if any issue that affects normal solving is identified, the corresponding instance is recorded and jointly reviewed and revised after the testing is completed.
2.3.2. Human Performance Analysis
Human Solvability.
The results of independent human solving indicate that OpenDS-World is highly challenging for human solvers. Across all 1,000 independent attempts, 211 resulted in correct answers, corresponding to an overall human accuracy of 21.10%. At the task level, 115 (57.50%) of the 200 tasks were successfully solved by at least one of the five independent solvers, while the remaining 85 (42.50%) were not solved by any solver. Examining the number of successful solvers per task further shows that only 1 task (0.50%) was successfully solved by all five solvers, while 61 (30.50%), 25 (12.50%), 17 (8.50%), and 11 (5.50%) tasks were successfully solved by one, two, three, and four solvers, respectively. In other words, only 29 tasks (14.50%) were successfully completed by a majority of the solvers (at least three) (Figure
4
(a)). This distribution shows that a substantial portion of OpenDS-World remains highly challenging even for human solvers with unrestricted access to conventional Web browsers, while more than half of the tasks can still be successfully solved by at least one independent solver through actual Web research.
Human Solving Effort.
This difficulty is also reflected in the research effort required to complete the tasks. As shown in Figure
4
(b), the 50 participants spent an average of 12.92 hours completing their assigned sets of 20 tasks, with a median of 9.44 hours and a combined total of approximately 646 hours. Across all 1,000 independent attempts, participants spent approximately 38.8 minutes per attempt on average. Meanwhile, across all 1,000 subjective difficulty ratings, the mean rating was 3.884/5, with a median of 4/5. Among these ratings, 43.00% of the attempts received the highest difficulty rating of 5, another 22.50% received a rating of 4, and no attempt received a rating of 0. Overall, 65.50% of the human attempts were rated as difficulty level 4 or 5 (Figure
4
(c)). The human testing results show that OpenDS-World involves substantial practical research difficulty.

2.4. Task Statistics
OpenDS-World contains 200 tasks, with 787 annotated entries for Web pages and other online resources along their evidence chains. These entries average 3.94 per task, and their task-level count distribution is shown in Figure
10
(c). Each entry is characterized by three attributes: the modality in which evidence is presented, the format of the resource carrying it, and the access type used to obtain it. Together, these annotations cover four modalities, 42 formats, and seven access types, describing both the information encountered during deep search and the interactions required to reach it. At the task level, text appears in 99.5% of tasks, yet the evidence extends well beyond textual content. Images and video occur in 44.5% and 35.5% of tasks, respectively, while audio appears in 16.0% (Figure
5
(a)). Within individual tasks, 82.5% involve at least two evidence modalities (Figure
11
(a)). This diversity is also reflected in resource formats. At the task level, HTML covers 98% of tasks, while MP4 and PDF account for 35% and 31% (Figure
5
(b)), respectively. At the task level, 96.0% involve at least two resource formats
(Figure
11
(b)). At the annotated-entry level, HTML accounts for 56.5% of entries, and MP4 and PDF together contribute 19.3%. The remaining entries span audio, images, structured data, archives, and a long tail of less common formats (Table
2
). Access requirements further reveal the interactive nature of the evidence chains. Although every task includes directly observable evidence, 67.0% also involve navigating links, pages, or nested content, and 60.0% involve transferring artifacts for further inspection. Temporal indexing occurs in 47.5% of tasks, reflecting the need to locate evidence within time-based media, while 42.0% involve parameterized state updates (Figure
5
(c)), such as applying filters or selecting a year or region. Graphical manipulation and declarative queries extend this coverage to visual interfaces and structured information access. Multiple access types occur in 95.5% of tasks (Figure
11
(c)). These complementary statistics show how deep search unfolds across heterogeneous online resources, requiring evidence discovery through multiple forms of content and interaction.

3.2. Main Results
Table
1
presents the main results on OpenDS-World. Overall, current frontier models remain limited in performing Deep Search in real-world Web environments. GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest overall accuracy of 39.00% over 200 tasks, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 at 38.00%, Gemini 3.8 Flash at 36.50%, and Claude Fable 5.1 at 33.50%. GPT-5.6 Sol and Qwen3.8-Max achieve 28.00% and 25.50%, respectively, while GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reach 23.50% and 20.50%. The remaining four models score below 20%. Even the strongest model fails on 122 of the 200 tasks, corresponding to a failure rate of 61.00%. These results highlight the persistent difficulty of finding and integrating information through deep search in real-world Web environments.
Performance declines substantially with task difficulty at the aggregate level. Averaged equally across the 12 models, accuracy drops from 39.66% on Low to 23.50% on Medium and 16.76% on High. GPT-6 Astra declines from 59.26% to 40.98% and 24.71%, while Claude Opus 5.5 achieves 53.70%, 40.98%, and 25.88%, respectively. Model rankings also vary across difficulty levels: GPT-6 Astra leads on Low and ties with Claude Opus 5.5 on Medium, whereas Gemini 3.8 Flash performs best on High at 28.24%. Qwen3.8-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro achieve only 4.71% and 3.53% on High. Although individual models do not always exhibit a monotonic decline across levels, the aggregate decrease indicates that the harder tasks pose a substantial challenge across the evaluated models.
Higher recorded resource consumption does not consistently correspond to higher accuracy. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol consume nearly identical total numbers of tokens, yet their overall accuracies differ by 11.00 percentage points. Gemini 3.8 Flash consumes approximately 5.22 times as many tokens as GPT-6 Astra but achieves a lower accuracy of 36.50%. Similarly, DeepSeek-V4-Pro accumulates approximately 2.39 times the total wall-clock time of GPT-6 Astra while achieving only 12.50% accuracy. These comparisons show that greater time or token consumption alone does not guarantee successful deep search. They motivate further investigation into how models navigate real-world Web sources, locate relevant information, and combine evidence to answer complex questions. Appendix
D
reports detailed performance breakdowns by task domain, evidence attributes, and anchor-video duration.

natural termination and answer correctness remain distinct
: GPT-6 Astra achieves 39.0% accuracy despite its 69.0% natural termination rate. Tool failures impose a disproportionate time cost, accounting for only 2.83%–9.42% of recorded calls but consuming 19.27%–61.90% of recorded tool execution time. For GPT-6 Astra, these proportions are 6.34% and 42.57%, respectively. Switching tools is the most common post-failure decision across the evaluated models, accounting for approximately 83% of cases for Claude Opus 5.5, 81% for Gemini 3.8 Flash, and 79% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 devote larger shares to same-tool retries with modified arguments, at approximately 38% and 37%. Together, these results identify budget exhaustion, incorrect answers at termination, and costly tool failures as key challenges for deep search in real-world Web environments.

(
Tao et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
.
Assessing these capabilities requires considering both discovery difficulty and evidence completeness: benchmarks evaluate persistent fact finding and relational complexity
(
Wei et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
, and extend assessment to the depth and breadth of evidence collection
(
Gupta et al., 2026
;
Lan et al., 2025
)
.
Representing findings as claims makes the information established by a search explicit
(

)
, while controlled corpora help examine retrieval and reasoning under shared evidence conditions

.

)
examine the coordination of navigation, perception, and dependent subtasks.
Assessing whether these interactions complete the task also draws on intermediate visual evidence and action histories from live websites
(
Xue et al., 2025
)
.
These efforts make access operations part of deep search, since a relevant source may require additional navigation, interface manipulation, or artifact processing before its evidence becomes usable.
5. Conclusion
We introduce OpenDS-World, a benchmark for deep search in real-world Web environments. Its 200 tasks originate from audiovisual anchors and require discovering and connecting evidence across heterogeneous online resources. The annotated evidence chains cover four modalities, 42 formats, and seven access types, capturing the diversity of both Web information and the interactions needed to obtain it. Evaluations of 12 frontier models reveal substantial challenges: the strongest model achieves only 39.00% accuracy, and compact evidence chains expand into lengthy execution trajectories as agents resolve uncertain clues and explore candidate sources. Further analyses reveal costly tool failures, frequent budget exhaustion for several models, and a persistent gap between natural termination and answer correctness. OpenDS-World provides a concrete foundation for studying long-horizon search and recursive self-improvement, with the goal of developing agents that can reliably discover, access, and integrate evidence in real-world Web environments.

Appendix B
OpenDS-World Construction Details
B.1. Benchmark Composition
Figure
10
presents the task composition and annotated evidence structure of OpenDS-World, covering domain distribution, anchor-video duration, and evidence-chain size. As shown in Figure
10
(a), the benchmark comprises 200 tasks spanning eight domains, each accounting for 9.0% to 16.5% of the dataset. Science and Society contribute 33 tasks each, followed by Daily Life (30), Culture (27), Nature (22), History (19), Economy (18), and Technology (18). This distribution provides broad coverage across specialized knowledge and everyday information needs, without any single domain dominating the benchmark.
Figure
10
(b) illustrates the distribution of anchor-video durations. The videos range from short clips to extended recordings, with 18.0% of tasks featuring videos shorter than two minutes, 12.0% between two and five minutes, 14.0% between five and ten minutes, 21.5% between ten and twenty minutes, and 34.5% lasting at least twenty minutes. Notably, 56.0% of tasks begin with videos of at least ten minutes, requiring agents to identify relevant clues within potentially extensive temporal content.
Figure
10
(c) shows the distribution of annotated evidence-chain sizes. The 200 tasks contain a total of 787 verified source entries, averaging 3.94 entries per task. Specifically, 44.5% of tasks contain three source entries, 28.0% contain four, 20.0% contain five, and 7.5% contain six or more. Thus, 55.5% of tasks require at least four annotated source entries. These entries constitute the verified evidence supporting the reference answers, while agents must independently discover the relevant sources and establish their connections during execution.

B.2. Evidence Attribute Diversity
Beyond the overall evidence-chain size, OpenDS-World exhibits substantial diversity in information modalities, resource formats, and access requirements. Figure
11
characterizes this diversity by counting the number of distinct attributes within each task. Each attribute is counted at most once per task, regardless of how many annotated source entries exhibit it. All statistics are based on annotated evidence sources and exclude the separately supplied anchor video.
Multimodal Evidence.
As shown in Figure
11
(a), 17.5% of tasks involve a single information modality, while 70.5% involve two modalities, 11.0% involve three, and 1.0% involve all four modalities. Consequently, 82.5% of tasks require evidence spanning at least two modalities, with bimodal evidence being the most common configuration. This distribution highlights the prevalence of multimodal evidence integration, where agents must establish connections across information presented in textual, visual, audio, and video forms.
Format Diversity.
Figure
11
(b) presents the number of distinct resource formats involved in each task. Only 4.0% of tasks involve a single format, whereas 55.0% involve two formats, 27.0% involve three, and 12.5% involve four. The remaining 1.5% involve five or six formats. Overall, 96.0% of tasks require at least two resource formats, and 41.0% involve three or more. Unlike modality diversity, format diversity reflects differences in resource representation and processing requirements. For instance, HTML, PDF, and CSV may all contain textual information but require different access and parsing mechanisms. The observed distribution therefore emphasizes the heterogeneity of resource handling in real-world Web research.
Access Diversity.
Figure
11
(c) illustrates the number of distinct access requirement types associated with each task. The most common configuration involves four access types, accounting for 30.0% of tasks, followed by two types (26.0%), three types (22.0%), and five types (13.0%). Overall, 95.5% of tasks involve at least two access types, 69.5% involve at least three, and 47.5% involve four or more. Two tasks require all seven access types. These results demonstrate that evidence acquisition frequently involves combinations of heterogeneous operations.

B.3. Long-Tail File Formats

B.4. Access Requirement Taxonomy
To characterize the diversity of evidence access mechanisms in real-world Web environments, we classify access requirements into seven types according to the operations needed to obtain the target evidence, as summarized in Table
3
. These types cover immediate observation, hypermedia transitions, parameterized state updates, temporal indexing, graphical state manipulation, declarative queries, and artifact transfer. Together, they describe the principal operations involved in accessing evidence across heterogeneous Web sources.
Table 3
:
Taxonomy of access requirements.
The seven access types characterize distinct operations
involved in obtaining annotated evidence.
Multiple labels may apply to the same source entry.
Code
Access type
Definition
O
Immediate Observation
Observe the target evidence directly in the current state,
without changing the source state.
N
Hypermedia Transition
Change location through discrete navigation within
or across pages and documents.
P
Parameterized State Update
Change the source state by entering or selecting
explicit parameters.
T
Temporal Indexing
Locate content along the temporal dimension
of a source.
G
Graphical State Manipulation
Expose information through interaction with
a graphical or spatial representation.
Q

X
Artifact Transfer
Transfer an information-bearing artifact from a remote

The access labels are not mutually exclusive and can be combined to describe multi-operation evidence acquisition. For example, retrieving evidence from a downloadable report may involve following a link (N), transferring the file (X), and inspecting its contents (O). Similarly, locating and examining a specific video segment may require both temporal indexing (T) and immediate observation (O). For task-level statistics, we take the union of the access labels assigned to all annotated source entries within each task, counting each type at most once per task. Consequently, coverage percentages across access types may sum to more than 100%.
Importantly, this taxonomy is defined at the level of access operations, independent of the specific tools used to perform them. For instance, parameterized state updates modify explicit input values or selections, whereas graphical state manipulation changes the spatial or visual representation through interaction. Declarative queries specify target records or retrieval conditions through structured interfaces. A single tool may support multiple access types, while a particular access operation may require multiple tool calls.
These annotations describe task-side access requirements along the verified evidence paths and form the basis for the coverage statistics and difficulty-conditioned analysis presented below. Agent actions are derived separately from execution trajectories.
B.5. Source Requirements Across Difficulty Groups
Figure
12
compares the distributions of information modalities, resource formats, and access requirements across human-calibrated difficulty groups. Based on the independent human evaluation, the 200 tasks are divided into three groups: Low comprises 54 tasks solved by at least two human participants, Medium comprises 61 tasks solved by exactly one participant, and High comprises 85 tasks that none of the five participants solved. These groups are defined by observed human solving success as the sole difficulty criterion. Coverage percentages are calculated separately within each group to account for differences in group size.
The distributions reveal several differences in evidence composition across difficulty groups. As shown in Figure
12
(a), audio coverage increases from 7.4% in Low to 22.4% in High, whereas image coverage decreases from 48.1% to 38.8% and video coverage decreases from 40.7% to 30.6%. The resource format distributions in Figure
12
(b) also vary across groups. For example, ZIP coverage increases from 1.9% in Low to 12.9% in High, while the coverage of formats grouped as Other increases from 31.5% to 48.2%.
Differences are also observed in access requirements. As illustrated in Figure
12
(c), hypermedia transition (N) coverage increases from 61.1% in Low to 72.9% in High, while artifact transfer (X) coverage rises from 53.7% to 67.1%. In contrast, temporal indexing (T) remains relatively stable at approximately 47%–48% across all three groups. Other access types exhibit non-monotonic patterns, indicating that their prevalence does not consistently increase with task difficulty.
Overall, the results show that difficulty groups differ in their combinations of evidence modalities, resource formats, and access requirements. Compared with the Low group, the High group shows higher coverage of audio, ZIP archives, hypermedia transitions, and artifact transfers, and lower coverage of image and video evidence.

C.1. Setting
C.1.1. Tool Setting
Table
4
summarizes the 16 tools available in the OpenDS-World evaluation environment, including their input parameters and supported operations. Browser interactions are conducted within a persistent session, where agents identify interaction targets using element indices returned from the current page state. For non-Web resources, the environment supports access to downloaded artifacts through task-local file paths, as well as video frame sampling and subtitle extraction within specified temporal intervals.
C.1.2. Input Videos Process
To ensure consistency and reproducibility of task inputs, OpenDS-World preserves the initial videos as read-only files and makes them accessible to models through the predefined identifier
input_video
, avoiding dependence on the availability of the original YouTube videos during evaluation. Models can inspect either the entire video or specific temporal intervals through a unified video-reading interface, while external videos are accessed via URLs or video identifiers. The video reader samples 10 frames by default and supports 1 to 100 frames per call, sampling at the midpoints of equally spaced temporal intervals. The same sampling strategy applies to inspection within a specified time range. Additionally, a separate subtitle-reading interface supports the extraction of timestamped subtitles from the entire video or a specified temporal interval.

C.2.1. Budget Management

C.2.2. Context Management
To control context growth during long search trajectories, the harness applies deterministic compaction to older observations before each model request, without relying on an additional summarization model. As shown in Table

C.2.3. Termination Mechanism
Research Termination.
The research phase terminates naturally when the model
produces a complete, nonempty answer without requesting
additional tool calls. It may also terminate due to budget
exhaustion, incomplete output, context overflow, or
execution errors. The harness records the research
termination reason and answer-generation status separately,
while answer correctness is determined by the independent
evaluation procedure.
Final Answer Generation.
If the research phase ends without a complete answer,
the harness enters a separate finalization stage using
the evidence collected during research. No tools are
available during this stage, preventing further searches
or access to external resources.
As shown in Table
5
,
the default configuration permits at most two model
requests sharing a 5,000-token output budget, with
4,000 tokens allocated to the first request.
Only nonempty, complete responses without tool calls
are accepted, and the finalization outcome is recorded.

GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest accuracy in six categories, including Artifact Transfer (X) and Declarative Query (Q), with accuracies of 46.67% and 61.54%, respectively. Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 achieve 43.33% and 40.00% accuracy in Artifact Transfer, respectively, while GPT-5.6 Sol reaches 32.14% in Parameterized State Update (P). Qwen3.8-Max, GLM-5.3-Flash, and Kimi K3 achieve 32.63%, 29.47%, and 28.42% accuracy, respectively, all exceeding their corresponding overall accuracies. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash also achieves relatively high accuracy in Temporal Indexing (24.21%) and Declarative Query (30.77%). In contrast, Qwen3.8-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro (T), and GLM-5.3 (T) exhibit relatively low accuracy across most access requirement categories. ) minutes, containing 36, 24, 28, 43, and 69 tasks, respectively. These groups are shared by all 12 evaluated models. The analysis considers the duration of the provided anchor video.
