page_papers.title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
page_papers.abstract: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged Local Expert in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared Meta Expert hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

Abstract
As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged
Local Expert
in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared
Meta Expert
hold greater potential.
To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed,
our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70–80% of the experts
, substantially improving the model’s scaling potential.
Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

Introduction
Figure 1:
Comparison between Vanilla and Meta-Expert models. All models are
trained under the optimal setting of the Vanilla model, at varying depths
and scales. Models with Meta Experts achieve comparable loss to the Vanilla
baselines with only 70–80% as many experts, or 75–90% as many
parameters, and the savings in both experts and parameters grow as the
models get deeper and larger, indicating the favorable scalability of Meta
Experts.
In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have gradually approached or even surpassed human-level ability in general text, mathematics, and code
(
Brown et al., 2020
;
OpenAI et al., 2024
)
. This progress owes much to the increasing scale of model parameters and training data: intelligence has been improved substantially as both factors grow
(
Kaplan et al., 2020
;
Hoffmann et al., 2022b
)
.
To enable ever-larger models, parameter sparsification has become an important approach
(
Shazeer et al., 2017
;
Fedus et al., 2022
;
Muennighoff et al., 2025
)
. As the module that accounts for the vast majority of model parameters, the feed-forward network was originally a densely computed block.
(
Vaswani et al., 2017a
)
. However, as model size grows, such dense computation gradually becomes prohibitively expensive, creating efficiency bottlenecks for both training and inference
(
Lepikhin et al., 2021
;
Fedus et al., 2022
)
. Meanwhile, although feed-forward networks are densely computed, only a sparse subset of parameters is actually activated for a given token during its forward pass
(
Li et al., 2023
;
Mirzadeh et al., 2024
)
; the remaining inactive parameters still participate in the computation, leading to substantial waste.
To address this, researchers have proposed designing feed-forward networks with a natively sparse-activation structure, most notably the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)
(
Shazeer et al., 2017
;
Fedus et al., 2022
)
. MoE splits the feed-forward network into multiple sub-networks along the intermediate dimension and routes each token to only a limited number of them before computation. This design endows the model with a large total parameter count while ensuring that each token’s forward pass computation uses only a small fraction of parameters, reconciling scale with efficiency.
With the advent of increasingly sparse MoE models, parameter efficiency along the width dimension has been steadily improved
(
Dai et al., 2024
)
. In this work, however, we ask how parameter efficiency can be improved along the depth dimension
(
Raposo et al., 2024
)
. On the one hand, interpretability studies suggest that feed-forward networks store relatively static knowledge
(
Geva et al., 2021
;
Dai et al., 2022
)
, and that different layers may store similar knowledge, suggesting nontrivial redundancy across layers
(
Meng et al., 2022
;
Takase and Kiyono, 2023
;
Fan et al., 2019
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Men et al., 2025
)
. On the other hand,
Looped Transformers reuse the same parameters across recurrent applications
of a block
(
Dehghani et al., 2018
;
Giannou et al., 2023
;
Bai et al., 2019
;
Csordás et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2026a
)
,and recent work
shows that this design can attain the reasoning performance of much larger
models with far fewer parameters
(
Bae et al., 2025
;
Saunshi et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
. This benefit, however, comes with
additional recursions and greater serial depth, incurring higher computational
and latency costs.
To balance parameter storage efficiency and computational cost, this work explores the potential of another Parameter Loop scheme — Cross-Layer Expert Sharing. Unlike Looped Transformers, which keep the total parameters of each layer unchanged but increase the number of recursions, we aim to keep the number of recursions unchanged while increasing the candidate experts of each layer, and use the sparse activation of MoE to keep both the activated parameters and the computation per layer unchanged. We refer to the experts shared across layers as
Meta Experts
, and the layer-private experts in the conventional design as
Local Experts
.
Our experiments show that, compared with the Local Expert of hierarchical architectures, Meta Experts reduce parameter redundancy and achieve lower cross-entropy loss together with higher downstream task accuracy. At a fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, our model achieves comparable performance to Vanilla MoE with only 70% as many experts, indicating a substantially higher effective capacity per parameter.
Further analysis reveals another reason why cross-layer expert sharing is effective: Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible paths for storage and retrieval. Compared with hierarchical architectures, cross-layer expert sharing implicitly provides more flexible residual connections: beyond the forward residual connections, it introduces a backward residual connection at the activation level—one that operates within a single forward pass and is therefore absent from existing models.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) A systematic analysis of the effect of Meta Experts on model
performance, covering their activation and total-number ratios among all
experts, their presence in every layer, and their partial hierarchical
organization. Although these configurations moderately affect performance,
Meta Experts consistently bring significant improvements.
(2) An explanation of why Meta Experts are effective from the perspective
of residual connections. By comparing the forward hidden-state updates and
the backward parameter updates of models with and without Meta Experts, we
show that this design grants shallow and deep layers bidirectional access
to representations across depth, enabling more flexible information
retrieval.

3
Empirical Comparison between Meta and Local Experts
To systematically analyze the effect of Meta Experts on model performance,
we start from a model with only Local Experts and incorporate Meta Experts
in various forms, comparing model capabilities with and without them.
3.1
Setups
Core Variables.
We consider two types of relationship between Meta Experts and Local Experts:
(1) the quantitative relationship
: the ratio of their total numbers within the whole model and their activated numbers within each layer (See Fig
3
.(a));
(2) the topological relationship
: whether every layer contains both Meta and Local Experts (See Fig
3
.(b)), and whether the Meta Experts are also hierarchically organized (See Fig
3
.(c)).
Common Settings.
During the experiments, we first sweep all the variables on a 2B-A0.5B
model, and then select the relatively better-performing configurations for
the scaling ladder experiments.
Throughout the experiments, we keep the total number of experts and the
total activation count fixed, which indirectly ensures that different
models have similar FLOPs, enabling a fairer comparison. When comparing
models at different FLOPs, all models adopt the training-optimal
configuration of the Vanilla MoE structure, rather than a configuration
tuned specifically for our design. Detailed experimental setups can be found in
A.3
Metrics.
In addition to cross-entropy loss and downstream task accuracy, we introduce
an expert-redundancy metric as a complementary perspective for analyzing
expert specialization under different architectural settings. It allows us to
examine how expert topology affects the overlap among learned expert
functions. The exact training configurations and the definition of the
redundancy metric are deferred to Appendix
A.2
.
Figure 3:
The Quantitative and Topological Comparison between Meta and Local Experts.
3.2
Meta/Local Experts’ ratio
We first study the effect of the ratio between the total numbers of Meta
Experts and Local Experts, and of their activation ratio within each layer,
on model performance.
Settings.
For the total-number ratio, we consider Meta Expert proportions of
0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%; for the activation ratio, we consider proportions
of 25%, 50%, or 75%. For concreteness, consider a two-layer model with 256
experts in total and 8 experts activated per layer. A Meta/Local number
ratio of 75% then corresponds to 192 Meta Experts, shared across all
layers, and 32 Local Experts per layer; an activation ratio of 75%
corresponds to activating 6 Meta Experts and 2 Local Experts per layer.

The results show that, at any activation ratio, a higher total-parameter
proportion of Meta Experts consistently leads to lower loss and redundancy;
meanwhile, allocating a higher activation ratio to Meta Experts also helps
reduce the loss. Taken together, these observations attest to the
effectiveness of Meta Experts. On the other hand, while assigning a higher
activation ratio to Local Experts is detrimental to the loss, it does help
reduce the redundancy among experts. This suggests that, compared with Meta
Experts, Local Experts—each of which is activated in only one layer under
the traditional architecture—may be harder to train sufficiently, and
this under-training may give rise to redundancy.

3.3
Meta/Local Experts’ topology
We next investigate the effect of the topology of Meta/Local Experts on
model performance. On the one hand, we explore whether every layer should
include Meta Experts; on the other hand, we explore whether the Meta
Experts should themselves be partially hierarchically organized.
Settings.
On the one hand, we consider variants in which Local Experts are used
exclusively, with no Meta Experts introduced at all: either in only the
first 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers of the model, in only the last 1, 2, 4, or 8
layers, or in both the first and the last 1, 2, or 4 layers. On the other
hand, we consider partitioning the Meta Experts into 2, 4, or 8 sub-pools,
which are then accessed in a looped manner—either in a chunked or an
interleaved fashion.

Pilot Experiments
(Fig

It can be observed that both operations—introducing Local-Experts-only
layers, and organizing the Meta Experts hierarchically so as to mimic the
topology of Local Experts—generally incur a loss degradation, which
further demonstrates the positive role of Meta Experts in model
performance. Notably, under a lighter degree of intervention, the loss
slightly improves: for example, when only the first two and the last two
layers are restricted to Local Experts, or when the Meta Experts are looped
only twice. This suggests, on the one hand, that experts in the shallowest
and deepest layers serve more differentiated functions, with essentially
no mutual redundancy between these layers—a conclusion also supported by
the expert redundancy measurements. On the other hand, mildly hierarchical
Meta Experts help improve the model capability slightly; hierarchy,
however, introduces a certain amount of expert redundancy, and why this
redundancy does not translate into a higher loss remains an open question
for further investigation.

hand, that the proportion of specialized shallow and deep layers relative
to the total number of layers may remain roughly constant as model depth
changes; on the other hand, deeper models also call for a larger hierarchical
expert topology; the Local Experts of the Vanilla model, however, are
overly hierarchical, and can therefore only achieve suboptimal results.

Downstream Performance of Meta Experts-based Model
For a more comprehensive comparison, beyond cross-entropy loss, we further
compare the downstream task capabilities of different configurations
through training at a larger scale.

Conclusion
In this work, we present an empirical and theoretical analysis of
cross-layer expert sharing in MoE models, contrasting the hierarchically
arranged
Local Experts
of standard architectures with inter-layer
shared
Meta Experts
. Our systematic comparisons—over the
Meta/Local ratio, the activation ratio, and the topology of the shared
pool—show that Meta Experts consistently reduce expert redundancy and
cross-entropy loss while improving downstream task accuracy: at a fixed
number of activated experts and expert granularity, models built on shared
experts match the performance of Vanilla MoE with only 70–80% of the
expert budget, substantially improving scaling potential. Beyond these
empirical observations, our analysis shows that a shared expert block is
not merely a parameter-saving device: it widens the forward residual
connections and grants hidden states bidirectional access to expert content
across depth, improving both the storage and the retrieval of information.
Taken together, our results suggest that inter-layer redundancy, long
treated as an intrinsic cost of deep MoE models, can instead be converted
into effective capacity. Future directions include extending this analysis
to larger models and broader architectures, and understanding why mildly
hierarchical shared experts introduce redundancy without degrading
performance.

Reproducibility statement
We have taken several steps to make the results in this paper reproducible, and
we reference here the parts of the paper that support them. The complete
experimental configuration for the scaling ladder is given in
Appendix
A.3
: the per-depth architecture is listed in
Table
2
and the per-depth training schedule—global batch
size, optimizer steps, warmup and decay, learning rate, token budget, and
training FLOPs—in Table
3
. Every rung, and every
architectural variant at a given rung, shares the same backbone, optimizer, and
parallelism policy; only the depth-dependent knobs in those tables change, so a
single set of hyperparameters fully specifies each run. The evaluation protocol
used for the compute-versus-loss analysis is described in the same appendix: for
each run we report the language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten
training steps. Our models are implemented on top of Megatron-LM, a widely used open-source framework, which helps ensure reproducibility.

Appendix A
Appendix
A.1
Related Work
Weight Tying
was originally introduced to share
parameters between the embedding layer and the language model
head
(
Press and Wolf, 2017
;
Inan et al., 2016
)
: since the two matrices map tokens
to and from the hidden space, tying them nearly halves the corresponding
parameters while often improving perplexity, and the practice has become
standard in modern language models
(
Vaswani et al., 2017b
;
Raffel et al., 2020
)
.
Beyond tying modules at the same depth, weight tying can be pushed further,
to reusing parameters
across
depth
(
Dehghani et al., 2018
;
Lan et al., 2019
)
.
Looped Transformer
pushes weight tying to extreme:
the same block is applied multiple times per token, unrolling a small set
of weights into arbitrary depth
(
Dehghani et al., 2018
;
Giannou et al., 2023
;
Hua et al., 2025
)
. This line of work shows that weight reuse
across depth can substitute for parameter growth, and that a compact
recurrent model can match the reasoning performance of much larger ones
(
Bae et al., 2025
;
Saunshi et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
, at
the cost of additional recursions and a higher degree of serialization.
Meta Experts share the same motivation—extracting more effective capacity
from a fixed parameter budget—but apply tying at a finer granularity and
within a single feed-forward pass: only the expert block is reused across
layers, without extra recursions, so training and inference retain the
parallelism of standard Transformers, while attention may remain
layer-specific. Depending on
what
is reused across depth, this
paradigm subsumes several lines of work.
Attn Weight Sharing
reuses the attention projections (or
entire attention blocks) of different layers, yielding moderate parameter
savings at little accuracy cost
(
Xiao et al., 2019
;
Lan et al., 2019
;
Mu et al., 2026
)
. These results suggest that the per-layer
parameter budget of Transformers is partially redundant—but leave open
where
the redundancy concentrates and whether the same principle
applies to the rest of the block.
Attn KV-Cache Sharing
reuses not
parameters but activations: in long-context or serving scenarios, multiple
layers attend to a common KV cache, trading representational independence
for inference memory and throughput
(
Sun et al., 2024
;
Brandon et al., 2024
;
Zuhri et al., 2025
;
Wu and Tu, 2024
;
Wu et al., 2025
)
. Such sharing is typically applied at deployment
time, affects the cache rather than the learned weights, and is often found
to be nearly lossless—suggesting that layers can tolerate
reading
the same content, but not that they should
store
the same content.
Meta Experts operate on the storage side: the shared expert pool is written
by every layer during training, so cross-layer sharing reshapes what the
model stores and how hidden states retrieve it, rather than merely reusing
cached activations at inference.
FFN Weight Sharing
is the closest line to our work: it
reuses feed-forward parameters across layers, either by tying the FFN of
all layers or by sharing it among a subset
(
Lan et al., 2019
;
Pires et al., 2023
;
Thawakar et al., 2024
)
. Existing
studies, however, focus on dense FFNs and report mixed results, and sharing
is typically applied uniformly to every layer.
MoE Weight Sharing
has been explored in
several recent works: experts are shared across layers, but almost always
under an every-layer sharing topology, whose communication and memory
overhead is difficult to scale
(
Li et al., 2025
;
Tan et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026a
;
Huang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026b
;
Jiao et al., 2026
)
. Meta Experts
generalize this idea to a more flexible regime: a shared
pool
of
experts is accessed through several topology that is more friendly for
communication and memory (reserving boundary layers for local experts,
sub-pool partitioning with chunked or interleaved access), allows the model
to decide which content is worth sharing across depth—and, as our analysis
shows, implicitly turns the shared experts into bidirectional residual
pathways between layers.

article.headline: 跨层共享专家让 MoE 少用两三成专家
article.lede: 清华与上海 AI Lab 提出 Meta Expert：让各层共用同一专家池，在激活量固定时用 70–80% 的专家追平
article.problem: 主流 MoE 模型按层各自配置私有专家（Local Expert），但已有可解释性研究表明不同层存储的知识高度相似，层间存在明显冗余。现有做法多沿宽度方向提升参数效率，也就是增加专家数；深度方向的参数复用则主要靠 Looped Transformer，需要额外递归并增加串行深度，因而带来计算与延迟代价。
article.method: 作者把专家池从「每层私有」改为「跨层共享」：所有层共用一套路由器和专家池（Meta Expert），每层仍按 top-k 稀疏激活，激活参数与计算量不变，只减少总存储。作者在 2B-A0.5B 模型上扫描 Meta/Local 的数量比（25%/50%/75%/100%）、激活比（25%/50%/75%）与拓扑（边界层是否保留 Local、共享池是否再切成 2/4/8 个子池循环使用），再沿 12/16/20/24 层的算力阶梯验证。作者还提出用 CKA 核谱的 Gini 系数作为专家冗余度指标，并从残差通路角度做了理论分析：共享块让各层在激活层面获得路径长度为 O(1)、与层距无关的双向读写通道。
article.results: 在激活专家数与专家粒度固定的条件下，「只用 70–80% 的专家」即可匹配 Vanilla MoE 的性能；按摘要给出的口径，参数量只需 75–90%，但正文第 3.4 节又写成省下约 20–30% 的专家（15–25% 的参数），两处数字口径不一致。6B-A1.6B 模型训练 200B token 后，MMLU 上 Vanilla 为 0.4087，MR75 为 0.4120，MR75+Loop2 为 0.4175；C-Eval 上从 0.4354 升到 0.4487；OpenBookQA 上从 0.3500 升到 0.3640；TriviaQA 上最佳为 MR75+F2L2+Loop2 的 0.2042，Vanilla 为 0.1924。消融显示，把首尾各两层限制为 Local Expert 并叠加 2 个子池（F2L2+Loop2）时，损失与冗余度相对 Vanilla 的比值随算力增长而持续改善。
article.why_it_matters: 该结果说明，深 MoE 长期被当作固有成本的层间专家冗余可以被转化为有效容量，而且共享只发生在 FFN 专家块上，不引入递归，训练与推理仍保持标准 Transformer 的并行性，是一条与宽度扩展正交的扩容路径。
article.limitations: 下游验证只做了 6B-A1.6B、200B token 这一档，作者自己承认预算有限，导致不同 Meta 变体在不同数据集上各有胜负，而且 MR75+F2L2 在 MMLU 上（0.3928）反而低于 Vanilla（0.4087）。纯 Meta（100%）配置被认为可能训练不稳定；理论部分只刻画了读写通路与路径长度，并未保证信号不衰减；轻度分层共享专家带来的冗余为何不转化为更高损失，作者也明确留作未解问题。

page_papers.title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
page_papers.abstract:
AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact.
  Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners.
  AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input.
  It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame.
  We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses sim10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection.
  To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.

AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
Ruicong Liu*

October 22, 2026
Abstract
AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing intact.
Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners.
AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input.
It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame.
We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses
∼
\sim
10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection.
To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
1
Introduction
Coding agents and tools, such as GEAR
[
1
]
game-creation system, can now turn a one-paragraph prompt into a playable game in minutes, complete with game logic, physics, camera, win conditions, and working HUD
[
7
]
. What they cannot produce is good art. The output usually contains gray boxes, colored cylinders, and cones on flat-shaded ground. Human studios spend months replacing this kind of “programmer art” through modeling, texturing, and lighting.
Splitting a game into an engine that manages state and a generative model that renders pixels has quickly become a common idea. Concurrent systems such as CWM
[
8
]
, PWM
[
15
]
, Matrix-Game 4.0
[
32
]
, StreamRender-H3
[
29
]
, Marionette
[
26
]
, and SolarRenderer
[
33
]
all adopt it in some form. We do not argue for this setting. Instead, we build a rendering layer that is more
general
in what it accepts and more
faithful
in what it keeps.
Figure 1
:
AnyGameRenderer turns crude gameplay into polished game visuals.
Top:
one checkpoint handles diverse genres and input types, and renders one input in many styles. Insets show the crude input.
Bottom:
an agent writes the game and the engine outputs a blockout, which AnyGameRenderer renders into the final visuals. This allows style switching and skips modeling, texturing and animation.
As shown in
Figure
1
, AnyGameRenderer takes a crude gameplay recording and a text prompt (optionally with a style anchor image), and outputs the same gameplay re-rendered in the prompted style, frame-aligned with the input. It adds characters, motion detail, and effects, while keeping the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing. This brings two practical benefits. A game can easily switch to a new visual style by changing only the prompt. It also makes vibe gaming faster, since a game only needs code and a blockout, without modeling, texturing or animation.
There are three properties that set AnyGameRenderer apart.
(1) It generalizes across genres.
Prior and concurrent works are demonstrated mainly on third-person, first-person, or driving footage, with limited coverage of the genres that agents actually produce. As illustrated in
Figure
1
, AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters. In addition, it accepts diverse input types, including gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, wireframes, and coarse mockup.
(2) It keeps entity correspondence.
The hard part of game rendering is bookkeeping: twelve enemies become nine when three die; a reinforcement wave walks in at
t
=
4.2
t{=}4.2
s; a tiny far-away mob must not dissolve into fog. AnyGameRenderer substantially improves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, entities appear and disappear on the right frame, and fewer small entities are lost. The zero-shot base model often fails here: entities never appear, colored blocks stay unrendered, and characters appear even when they are not in the input.
(3) Its input is plain video.
Many concurrent systems rely on costly or complex representations, such as per-object class labels (StreamRender-H3, CWM), state-augmented 3D boxes (PWM), or low-poly engine proxies (Matrix-Game 4.0). AnyGameRenderer instead accepts whatever a crude game looks like, including gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic-colored maps, wireframes, and coarse clay figures, at different granularities and with one checkpoint.
To achieve these properties, we build paired (crude video, styled video) data from three sources. (i) GEAR’s multi-stream rendering data covers 38 agent-made games, helping the model generalize across genres and input types. (ii) Two-stream rendering in Unreal Engine uses scenes scripted with same-color groups that change count mid-clip, entity sizes from 20 to 600 px, and frame-aligned appearance and disappearance, teaching the model to keep entity correspondence. (iii) Real gameplay recordings, converted into crude inputs by 3D-box detection, help the model render realistic scenes. Together they yield 10,330 training clips.
Existing renderers are evaluated at the frame level, with edge agreement, point tracks, or pairwise judges, which cannot tell whether each entity is rendered correctly. We therefore design an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, each annotated with ground-truth boxes, and evaluate it with four metrics.
Temporal match
measures whether each entity appears and disappears on time;
position match
measures whether it stays at the right place;
unrendered rate
measures how often crude input blocks are left unrendered; and
hallucination rate
measures how often the output contains entities that do not exist in the input. Compared with the zero-shot base, AnyGameRenderer raises temporal match from 50.9% to 62.9% and position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, and lowers the unrendered rate from 4.1% to 2.9% and the hallucination rate from 52.1% to 46.0%.
Contributions.
•
We propose a video-to-video generative renderer for games. A single checkpoint handles a wide range of genres and input types, renders them in diverse prompted styles, and preserves entity correspondence with the input.
•
We build a paired dataset with three sources: multi-stream rendering data from GEAR, two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine with scenarios designed for correspondence, and detection-based reconstruction from real gameplay recordings. Together they yield 10,330 training clips.
•
We propose an entity-level benchmark and metrics for entity correspondence. The metrics measure whether each entity appears on time, stays in place, and is neither unrendered nor hallucinated. On this benchmark, AnyGameRenderer improves temporal match from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% over the zero-shot base.
2
Related Work
2.1
AI-driven game creation
Early work uses large language models to generate game content such as levels and rules. MarioGPT
[
34
]
generates Super Mario Bros. levels from text, Word2World
[
28
]
turns stories into playable 2D tile worlds, and LLMGG

Generative rendering for games
A growing body of work keeps the engine in charge of game state and uses a generative model only to render pixels. Neural forward rendering from G-buffers

CWM

AnyGameRenderer differs from these systems in three ways. First, they are demonstrated mainly on realistic third-person, driving, or a few self-built 3D scenes; our method generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters. Second, many of them rely on a fixed intermediate representation, while we take plain video. Third, none of them measures entity-level correspondence. Frame-level metrics barely change when a small entity is missing or a group arrives late, and edge agreement even rewards leaving crude blocks unrendered. We make correspondence, including the count, timing and position of every entity, the main target of both training data and evaluation.

3.2
Caption schema: the correspondence contract
We keep the base model’s six-segment format (
subject_definitions
,
summary
,
retention_analysis
,

,
overall_soundscape
,
non_diegetic_music
) and follow four rules, which we call the correspondence contract.
Subjects are entities; crude shapes are their representation.
Each subject is defined as the real entity, and the crude input is named as its representation, e.g., “
every blue ellipsoid in
<Video 1>
is one raccoon-like orchard raider, and the whole blue group is a group of identical ones
.” The color-to-identity mapping is set per clip, groups are described at class level with explicit statements that they exist.
Retention analysis fixes what follows the input.
This segment declares position, apparent size, timing, and head count as preserved exactly, and leaves appearance to the prompt. It also describes empty space positively: “areas empty in
<Video 1>
stay empty; no character is added that has no primitive in
<Video 1>
.”
Positive assertions only.
The base model has no negative prompt, and negative phrasing tends to produce what it names (“no HUD” reliably produces a HUD). All captions are therefore written as positive statements.
Programmatic captions with deliberate noise.
Captions are generated automatically from engine metadata and detection results, not written by hand. Each caption lists every character that may appear in the game, even if some never show up in the clip. We keep this noise on purpose: it teaches the model to decide what exists from the video, not from the text. As a result, the model rarely adds characters that are named in the caption but missing from the input.

4
Data
We build (crude video, styled video) pairs from three sources: multi-stream rendering data from GEAR covers different genres and input types; two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine targets entity correspondence; and real gameplay recordings add realistic layouts, cameras, and motion. In every pair, the crude and styled videos share the same camera and layout and are frame-aligned by construction.
4.1
GEAR games
GEAR
[
1
]
is a game-creation system that builds small games end-to-end from a prompt and can export different render passes from a running game. Our multi-stream rendering data uses 38 agent-made games, covering shooters, survivors, tower defense, kart racing, arena, and co-op designs. This source contributes
3,221
clips. Each clip has five aligned passes: the target render; a primitive pass, where the scene is a gray blockout and characters are simple geometric shapes; a coarse pass, with a more detailed blockout and low-poly clay figures; a 12-class semantic map; and depth. Each clip also comes with an anchor image, a caption, and 3D boxes.
We train on the pair of primitive and target.
4.2
Unreal Engine
Each Unreal Engine scene uses two-stream rendering: it is rendered from the same simulation and camera as a gray blockout with colored blocks for characters and as a full render. The protagonist is always blue, and other characters use a six-color set.
Rather than collecting generic gameplay, we script scenes around the zero-shot failures (see examples in
Figure
3
) to ensure entity correspondence:
•
Count changes in same-color groups.
Groups of 2 to 20 characters walk in, spawn, walk out, or despawn during the clip, in dense clusters, columns, or scattered formations. This targets crowds left as unrendered blocks and entities that appear late or never.
•
Characters of different colors entering and leaving.
This targets wrong entry and exit timing when several character types share a scene.
•
Entity sizes from 20 to 600 pixels
, including boss-sized characters and characters moving toward or away from the camera. This targets small, distant entities that dissolve into the background.
•
Mixed camera views
: 35% follow, 30% top-down, 20% isometric, and 15% side. This keeps the model from relying on a single viewpoint.
We keep clips where the protagonist is visible in at least 95% of frames. Each clip carries metadata on the scene, characters, colors, and events, from which its caption is generated. This source contributes
3,910
clips.

5.1

Benchmark.
The benchmark contains 59 cases with 753 annotated entities: 11 held-out two-stream rendering cases from Unreal Engine (gray blockouts), 14 real recordings with detected solid boxes, and 34 multi-stream rendering cases from GEAR across 6 held-out games. 5.2
Entity correspondence
Quantitative results.
Table
2
reports results on all 59 cases and on each source. Over all cases, our method improves all four main metrics: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, the unrendered rate falls from 4.1% to 2.9%, and the hallucination rate falls from 52.1% to 46.0%. The secondary statistics show the same trend. On-time appearance rises from 55.9% to 67.6%, entities that never appear fall from 26.0% to 20.2%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%.
Gains differ by source. On GEAR’s multi-stream rendering cases, temporal match rises by 13 points and missed count changes nearly halve. On Unreal Engine’s two-stream rendering cases, temporal match reaches 96.6%, close to the GT floor of 98.5%, and no entity is missed. Real recordings improve the least: temporal match rises from 46.5% to 51.1%, the unrendered rate is similar, and missed count changes stay at 20.0%.
Qualitative comparison.
Figure
4
shows seven held-out cases. The zero-shot model works well on sparse scenes with clean captions, but on game footage it fails in three ways. First, it leaves crude shapes in the output: blue cubes in an orchard, cyan cylinders in an arena, and a blue cylinder in the grass where an elk should be. Second, it drops the input viewpoint when the style is far from typical game footage, turning a top-down blockout into a frontal anime group shot or a first-person Minecraft-like scene. Third, it adds characters named in the caption that have no block in the input. AnyGameRenderer fixes all three in these cases while keeping the prompted style.

5.3
Generalization across genres
A single checkpoint handles all five genres in our benchmark: first-person shooters, top-down, third-person, crowd, and vehicle games (
Figure
5
). AnyGameRenderer improves temporal match over the zero-shot model in every genre, with the largest gains on crowd and third-person games. It also lowers the unrendered rate in every genre except crowd games, where both models are already near zero, and improves position match most on vehicle games. The hallucination rate falls on crowd games but rises slightly on top-down and third-person games. Top-down games remain the hardest, with low temporal match for both models.

6
Conclusion
We presented AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns the programmer art of agent-made games into high-quality visuals. We train a single LoRA on MiniMax-H3, using paired data from GEAR’s multi-stream rendering, Unreal Engine’s two-stream rendering, and real gameplay recordings. The resulting checkpoint handles a wide range of genres. It takes plain video as input, from gray blockouts and colored primitives to semantic maps and wireframes. It also keeps entities in sync with the input. On a held-out benchmark, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%. As coding agents build more and more games, we believe a general renderer that keeps every entity in place will help these games look as good as they play.

article.headline: 一个LoRA把方块游戏渲染成成品画面
article.lede: Alaya Lab 用 LoRA 微调 MiniMax-H3，把灰色方块游戏视频渲染成成品画面，同时保住每个实体的位置与
article.problem: AI 编码智能体已能在几分钟内生成可玩的游戏，但画面往往是「程序员美术」：灰色方块、彩色几何体和纯色语义块。现有生成式渲染器大多依赖 G-buffer、逐物体类别标签或低模代理这类昂贵表示，且只在帧级别评测，无法判断每一个实体是否被正确渲染。
article.method: 作者把游戏渲染当成参考视频编辑任务：以粗糙游戏录像作为参考视频、六段式 caption 说明每个粗糙形状代表哪个实体，用 rank-128 LoRA 微调冻结的 33B MiniMax-H3 ref2va，只训练自注意力与前馈层。训练数据共 10,330 段 124 帧、1344×768 的配对片段，来自三处：GEAR 的 38 款智能体自制游戏（3,221 段）、Unreal Engine 双流渲染（3,910 段，脚本化设计同色群体数量变化与 20–600 像素的实体尺度）、以及经 3D 框检测重建的真实游戏录像（3,199 段）。caption 由引擎元数据程序化生成，并刻意保留「列出但未出场角色」的噪声，迫使模型从视频而非文本判断实体是否存在。
article.results: 在自建的 59 个留出案例、753 个实体的基准上，相比零样本基模型，时间匹配率从 50.9% 升至 62.9%，位置匹配率从 57.1% 升至 61.9%，未渲染率从 4.1% 降至 2.9%，幻觉率从 52.1% 降至 46.0%；按时出现率从 55.9% 升至 67.6%，从未出现的实体比例从 26.0% 降至 20.2%，漏检的数量变化从 34.7% 降至 21.3%。分数据源看，Unreal Engine 双流案例的时间匹配率达 96.6%，接近真值管线上限 98.5%；真实录像提升最小，时间匹配仅从 46.5% 到 51.1%。
article.why_it_matters: 若渲染层能从纯视频出发并保持实体一致，游戏只需代码和 blockout 就能更换美术风格，跳过建模、贴图与动画；论文同时补上了以往缺失的实体级评测口径。
article.limitations: 真实录像子集提升有限，未渲染率反而从 2.6% 微升至 2.9%，漏检数量变化停在 20.0%；幻觉率仍有 46.0%，而真值管线上限本身就有 34.1% 的幻觉率，说明基于 SAM3 开放词表分割与匈牙利匹配的评测流程本身误差不小。俯视视角仍是最难的类别，幻觉率在俯视和第三人称类别上还有上升，且所有结论只覆盖 5.17 秒、24fps、768p 的短片段。
article.figure_caption_zh: AnyGameRenderer 总览：(a) 来自 GEAR 多流渲染、Unreal Engine 双流渲染与真实录像 3D 框重建的三类配对数据；(b) 一个训练样本，由粗糙视频、目标首帧锚点和六段式 caption 组成；(c) 冻结的 MiniMax-H3 DiT 只训练自注意力与前馈层上的 LoRA。

figure.caption: {Overview of AnyGameRenderer.} (a)~Paired data from three sources. GEAR games use multi-stream rendering, which pairs each game render with several aligned crude streams such as blockouts and semantic maps. Unreal Engine scenes use two-stream rendering, which pairs a full render with blockouts. Real gameplay recordings are converted into blockouts by detecting 3D bounding boxes. (b)~One training sample: the crude clip is the input video {<Video 1>}, the target's first frame serves as an optional anchor, and a six-segment caption defines which real entity each crude shape represents and what must be preserved. (c)~Text, {<Video 1>}, anchor, and noisy target tokens form one sequence for the frozen MiniMax-H3 DiT. Only the LoRA adapters on self-attention and feed-forward layers are trained, and the model renders the input gameplay in the prompted style.

page_papers.title: F2G-Pose: Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting for Direct RGB-D Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
page_papers.abstract: This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/.

Abstract
This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object’s 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction.
To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs.
The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at
https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/
.
1
Introduction
Category-level 6D object pose estimation recovers an object’s 3D rotation and translation without requiring an instance-specific CAD model or reference views at test time. In practical RGB-D perception, this estimate is often coupled with metric size and usable object geometry for benchmark evaluation
[
42
,
50
,
9
]
, physical interaction
[
37
,
38
,
6
]
, and robotic control
[
45
,
23
,
44
,
15
,
14
,
25
]
.
This setting is inherently challenging because partial observations from a single crop or segmented point cloud provide incomplete evidence: symmetries induce rotational ambiguity, occlusions hide discriminative geometry, and intra-class variations alter shape, size, and appearance.
Consequently, category-level perception must produce reliable metric predictions from ambiguous, incomplete, and noisy observations.
Previous work has addressed this problem from two complementary directions. Deterministic category-level methods estimate pose and size through canonical coordinates
[
42
]
, correspondences
[
2
]
, shape priors
[
16
]
, deformation models
[
39
]
, alignment procedures
[
24
]
, or direct regression
[
26
,
43
,
17
]
.
While these methods enable efficient inference, reliance on intermediate structures can lead to compounding errors.
Under occlusion, missing depth, intra-class variation, and domain shift, the final metric estimate can become sensitive to the reliability of these intermediate structures. Direct regression can avoid some post-hoc alignment steps, but reliable direct prediction still requires representations that preserve local geometric cues and global object structure under partial observations.
A complementary line of work models pose ambiguity explicitly. GenPose
[
51
]
and GenPose++
[
50
]
formulate category-level pose estimation as conditional pose distribution modeling, sampling multiple hypotheses and converting them into a prediction through scoring, filtering, clustering, or aggregation. This is principled for uncertainty representation, but it introduces a candidate-to-decision gap: deployed accuracy depends not only on the sampled hypotheses, but also on whether post-hoc extraction can select or aggregate a reliable representative. Moreover, this conversion must operate under a practical inference budget as in Fig.
3
, so sampling quality, candidate extraction, and computational cost become coupled. Joint-RegDiff
[
20
]
and RFMPose
[
32
]
improve generative pose inference through joint regression–diffusion learning with score-scaling sampling and Riemannian flow-matching trajectories, respectively, but both still rely on iterative generative inference to produce the prediction, so prediction quality remains coupled with
sampling dynamics, candidate extraction, and inference cost.
We introduce F2G-Pose, a direct RGB-D framework that jointly estimates category-level pose, size, and camera-frame completed geometry in a single feed-forward pass. By leveraging geometry-aware foundation feature lifting and dense geometric supervision, it bypasses intermediate canonical shape alignment and avoids the sampling and candidate extraction used by sampling-based pose estimators.
Specifically, we lift dense visual foundation features
[
13
]
to the partial point cloud for semantic cues, encode local geometry via DGCNN tokenization, and integrate object-level structure using a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer that provides conditional capacity across diverse shape regimes.
Then, the pose-size head predicts the final metric estimate, while the shape head reconstructs camera-frame geometry as both auxiliary supervision and a usable output. This joint design encourages the shared representation to encode visible local evidence, object extent, and visible-to-complete geometric structure for consistent direct prediction under partial observations.
To evaluate the effectiveness of this design, we train the task-specific network only on pose-annotated synthetic data from 149 SOPE categories
[
50
]
and test on SOPE
[
50
]
, ROPE
[
50
]
, HANDAL
[
10
]
, and HouseCat6D
[
17
]
. These benchmarks cover synthetic benchmark accuracy, synthetic-to-real transfer, additional real-object evaluation, and camera-frame shape reconstruction. F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while running at 28 FPS for pose inference. Beyond benchmark accuracy, we evaluate latency, robustness to perturbations and occlusion, shape reconstruction, GenPose++ candidate behavior, and real-world robotic manipulation.
These results demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of direct feed-forward prediction, while robotic experiments demonstrate deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs.
Contributions.
Our contributions are threefold:
(1)
We present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct RGB-D framework that predicts category-level 6D pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape in a single feed-forward pass, sharing its representation across pose, size, and shape learning.
(2)
We introduce geometry-aware foundation feature lifting to map dense visual features onto partial point clouds. DGCNN encodes local geometry, a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer integrates object-level structure, and camera-frame shape completion provides dense geometric supervision for metric prediction.
(3)
Extensive evaluations across synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets demonstrate that F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, real-time inference, and high-quality shape completion. Furthermore, physical manipulation experiments demonstrate pick-and-place success, timely decision readiness, and deployment feasibility under segmented RGB-D inputs.
2
Related work
Category-Level 6D Pose Estimation.
Category-level methods aim to generalize pose estimation across unseen object instances within a category
[
42
,
43

17

[
42

introduced the notion of canonical space to enable pose alignment without requiring CAD models. Follow-up approaches
[
24
,
26
,

,

[
39
,
16

to jointly predict object size and shape.
While these methods remove the need for object-specific models, many rely on intermediate canonical coordinates, correspondences, deformation fields, or shape priors whose reliability can degrade under occlusion, missing depth, and strong intra-category variation. Recent works have attempted to scale category-level 6D learning using larger and more diverse datasets
[
53
,
18

Diffusion-based methods such as GenPose
[
51
]
and GenPose++
[
50

model pose and size as multi-modal distributions, but often rely on auxiliary scoring networks to filter outlier samples.
Joint-RegDiff
[
20

eliminates the need for such scoring networks through time-dependent score scaling, and RFMPose
[
32

SecondPose
[
3

also combines foundation-model features with geometry for direct category-level pose and size estimation through an SE(3)-consistent representation. F2G-Pose additionally predicts complete camera-frame shape to provide dense supervision for the shared pose-size representation, and uses MoE encoding to provide conditional capacity across diverse categories.
Instance-Level Novel Object Pose Estimation.
Another line of work estimates pose for novel object instances using CAD models
[
19

29

[
21

Recent foundation reconstruction models such as SAM 3D
[
35

Together, these methods broaden object-centric 3D perception, but generally target instance-specific reconstruction or reference-conditioned alignment rather than category-level pose-size estimation under a fixed taxonomy.
F2G-Pose targets this complementary category-level setting: it uses category-level canonical supervision during training, but requires only a segmented RGB-D observation at inference time for the evaluated taxonomy.

MoE-Based Object Encoding
The DGCNN tokens encode local surface neighborhoods and point-wise visual cues. We process these tokens with a stack of Transformer blocks with multi-head self-attention

To increase representation capacity with conditional expert aggregation, we replace the standard feed-forward layers in each Transformer block with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers

3.3
Direct Pose-Size and Shape Decoding
F2G-Pose uses two lightweight decoding branches on top of the shared object representation. The pose-size branch predicts the metric state directly, while the shape branch predicts complete geometry in the camera frame. Both branches are trained jointly, so dense geometric supervision can regularize the representation used for direct pose and size prediction without adding any test-time optimization or candidate extraction.

Representation analysis.
Table
6
studies how different RGB-D representations affect direct pose-size prediction.
All variants are trained with the same pose-size losses, while varying the feature aggregation strategy, contextual encoder, foundation backbone, and the use of auxiliary shape supervision.
Replacing global feature pooling with DGCNN tokens improves both IoU and rotation-sensitive VUS, showing that local surface neighborhoods provide important geometric cues for direct pose estimation.
Adding Transformer context further improves performance by integrating local RGB-D evidence into an object-level representation.
The full model achieves the best results, indicating that local geometric tokenization, object-level context, and camera-frame geometry supervision are complementary.
Finally, replacing RADIO with DINOv2 or CLIP causes only modest degradation in IoU50, suggesting that the improvement is driven primarily by the architecture and supervision rather than by a specific foundation backbone.

Compared with the overall ROPE performance, F2G-Pose shows moderate degradation on these material subsets, with reflective objects being more difficult than transparent ones, especially in VUS and Chamfer distance.

Robot manipulation.
We validate the final pose-size decision in a real pick-and-place setup using an ARX robotic arm, a parallel-jaw gripper, and an external RealSense RGB-D camera.
All methods receive the same object masks and RGB-D crops, and the evaluated objects include bottles, bowls, cans, mugs, cups, hammers, pans, and wrench-like tools.
The predicted pose and metric size determine the grasp approach and placement target; the completed camera-frame shape is used only for collision checking.
Each trial randomizes object placement within a tabletop start region, and success requires grasping, transporting, and placing the object at the target without dropping or collision. The full model achieves 74/80 successful picks and 68/80 successful placements.

GenPose++ is effective when run with its full sampling and clustering pipeline, but the full pipeline is too slow for the 50 ms control budget; reducing candidates improves responsiveness at the cost of lower pick-and-place success.

Conclusion
We present F2G-Pose, a direct RGB-D framework that estimates category-level 6D pose, metric size, and camera-frame shape from a single observation.
By lifting dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds and encoding local-global geometry with a MoE Transformer, F2G-Pose predicts the deployed pose-size state in one feed-forward pass.
Experiments on SOPE, ROPE, HouseCat6D, HANDAL, and ARX manipulation show a favorable balance of accuracy, inference latency, and manipulation success, while the shape branch provides dense geometric supervision and approximate planning geometry.
Limitations.
F2G-Pose assumes a segmented RGB-D crop at inference time, so mask failures and severe depth corruption can propagate to pose, size, and shape.
The method remains sensitive to thin or asymmetric parts, severe occlusion, and symmetric low-texture objects that admit multiple plausible rotations.
High-precision metric alignment remains weak under cross-dataset domain shift, which may require downstream refinement for tasks with tight geometric tolerances. Symmetry-aware supervision does not eliminate ambiguity under severe occlusion or near-symmetry, and the model provides no calibrated uncertainty or abstention mechanism.
Future work will address mask-free operation, broader real-object coverage, articulated or deformable categories, and active perception for heavy occlusion.
Broader Impact.
F2G-Pose advances category-level object perception for robotics and augmented reality. While improved pose estimation can benefit assistive manipulation and human–robot collaboration, it could also be applied in surveillance or autonomous systems without adequate safety oversight. We encourage responsible deployment with appropriate human supervision.

The fused RGB-D point set is tokenized by a DGCNN encoder with two downsampling stages, reducing 1024 input points to 128 object tokens. The pose-size branch directly regresses rotation, translation, and metric size. The shape branch predicts 512 initial points, concatenates 256 farthest-point-sampled observed points, scores the 768 candidates and retains 512, then predicts four local offsets per retained point for a 2048-point completed shape. The qualitative failure cases are drawn from ROPE and are consistent with the limitations stated in the paper: corrupted depth on thin or reflective structures, heavy occlusion, and ambiguous rotations for symmetric or weakly textured objects.

B.5
Reference-Free and Single-Reference Evaluation Protocols
Any6D (zero reference).
“Zero reference” means that no additional reference view is supplied beyond the test RGB-D observation. We use the official repository’s reference-free image-to-3D pathway, which reconstructs a coarse shape from the test observation and subsequently estimates pose using that reconstructed shape.
Any6D (one reference).
We randomly sample one additional view of the same object from its ROPE multi-view sequence as the reference image and apply the standard reference-query inference protocol.
FoundationPose (one reference).
We evaluate the model-free pathway under the same one-reference constraint. One additional real view of the same object is randomly sampled from its ROPE sequence; an object mesh is reconstructed from that view and used for pose estimation.

article.headline: 单次前向直出类别级位姿、尺寸与相机系形状
article.lede: F2G-Pose 把冻结 RADIO 的密集视觉特征逐点提升到部分点云，单次前向回归类别级 6D 位姿、尺寸与相机系形状
article.problem: 类别级 RGB-D 位姿估计要在没有实例 CAD 模型或参考视图的情况下恢复物体的旋转与平移，而类内差异、对称性和单视角部分观测让该任务高度歧义。已有方法难以兼顾可靠性与效率：依赖规范化坐标、对应关系或形状先验的中间结构类方法容易误差累积，扩散类方法则需要迭代采样并配合事后候选筛选或聚类，推理延迟高。
article.method: 模型取冻结 RADIOv2.5 第 8/16/23 层特征加权融合，按投影关系把逐点视觉特征贴到分割后的部分点云上，再用 DGCNN 把 1024 个点令牌化为 128 个 512 维 token。随后由 8 个 Transformer 块（前馈层换成 8 专家、top-2 路由的 MoE，并加负载均衡损失）编码全局物体表示，两个并行解码头分别直接回归 6D 旋转（连续 6D 表示）、平移与度量尺寸，以及相机坐标系下的补全形状。形状分支先预测 512 个粗点，与最远点采样的观测点拼接打分后融合，再为每点预测 4 个局部偏移，输出 2048 点稠密形状，用 Chamfer-L1 与位姿/尺寸的 Smooth L1 联合训练。
article.results: 仅用 SOPE 的 149 类合成数据训练：SOPE 上 IoU50 AUC 为 43.7（GenPose++ 为 31.9），IoU75 为 16.5（GenPose++ 为 6.4），平均旋转误差 15.7°、平移误差 0.88 cm（GenPose++ 为 19.9°/1.14 cm）；ROPE 上 IoU25/50/75 分别为 46.5/27.8/5.8，5°2cm VUS 为 11.3。位姿单模推理 28 FPS，含形状补全的完整模型 23.7 FPS，而 GenPose++ 为 4 FPS。相机系形状补全的 Chamfer-L1 在 SOPE 为 5.42×10⁻³、HouseCat6D 为 7.1×10⁻³，对比 AdaPoinTr 的 24.41 与 32.3。HANDAL 上零参考迁移 IoU25/50/75 为 35.0/11.7/0.3。ARX 真机抓放 80 次试验中成功抓取 74 次、放置 68 次，平均感知延迟 36 ms。消融中去除 RGB 基础特征后 ROPE IoU25 从 46.5 降到 34.5，去除 MoE 降到 41.0，去除形状监督降到 39.5。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「采样候选—打分筛选」的生成式流程换成一次前向的确定性预测，在保持实时性的同时把精度推到 SOPE/ROPE 的当前最好水平，并在真机抓放中满足 50 ms 控制预算。相机系形状补全既作为稠密几何监督提升位姿精度，也可直接供下游规划与碰撞检查使用。
article.limitations: 方法假定推理时已有分割好的 RGB-D 裁剪，掩码失败或深度严重损坏会传导到位姿、尺寸与形状；作者也承认对细长/非对称部件、严重遮挡和低纹理对称物体敏感，跨数据集高精度对齐仍弱（HANDAL IoU75 仅 0.3），且不提供校准不确定度或拒识机制。评测只在 SOPE 训练，ROPE 与 HANDAL 属已见类别、未见实例的迁移，并非未见过类别的泛化。
article.figure_caption_zh: F2G-Pose 流程：裁剪 RGB 图与分割部分点云经 RADIOv2.5 特征提取并按投影逐点提升，DGCNN 令牌化后由 MoE Transformer 编码全局表示，两个并行解码分支在一次前向中分别输出 6D 位姿与度量尺寸、以及由粗到细的相机系补全形状。

figure.caption: {F2G-Pose Overview.} Given a cropped RGB image and segmented partial point cloud, F2G-Pose extracts dense RADIOv2.5 features~ {heinrich2025radiov2} and lifts them onto 3D points by projection. DGCNN tokenization produces fused RGB-D object tokens, and a MoE Transformer encodes a global object representation. Two parallel decoder branches directly predict (i) 6D pose and metric size and (ii) camera-frame completed shape through coarse-to-fine refinement. The pipeline produces a pose-size-shape estimate in one feed-forward pass.

page_papers.title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
page_papers.abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.

Abstract
Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.
1
Introduction
The rapid proliferation of Agentic AI has positioned text-to-speech (TTS) systems as foundational voice interfaces for autonomous, multimodal agents. As these agents scale to global deployments, the ability to rapidly adapt to new languages particularly low-resource and under-documented ones has become a critical bottleneck. Extending conditional TTS models to novel linguistic settings is fundamentally constrained by
vocabulary expansion
: every unseen phonetic or graphemic unit requires a corresponding embedding in the model’s conditioning space. In practice, these tokens are initialized randomly and fine-tuned with extensive paired audio, a requirement that is infeasible when target-language data is scarce or costly to collect. This initialization bottleneck severely limits cross-lingual generalization and perpetuates a stark accessibility gap in speech technology.
We address this gap with
SEAM
(Spectral Embedding Alignment & Merging), a principled, self-calibrating initialization method. SEAM treats subtoken embeddings as a discrete signal, applies spectral low-pass filtering to preserve low-frequency phonetic compositionality, and projects the result onto the pretrained embedding manifold via closed-form ridge regression. Grounded in the Lipschitz continuity of conditional generation, our approach is designed to promote acoustic stability and compositional faithfulness from the initialization stage. Our contributions are:
1) A spectrally grounded merging operator that preserves temporal phonetic structure and suppresses boundary artifacts;
2) A closed-form, self-calibration protocol that requires no gradient-based optimization or target-language audio;
3) Data-efficiency gains over standard initialization heuristics, enabling rapid vocabulary expansion for low-resource TTS.
2
Related Work
Recent cross-lingual and low-resource TTS research has focused on model-level adaptation strategies, including zero-shot multi-speaker transfer via external speaker encoders
Casanova et al. (2022)
, cross-lingual phoneme sharing
Huang et al. (2022b)
, and meta-learning for rapid speaker alignment
Huang et al. (2022a)
. While these methods improve transferability, they typically assume access to substantial target-language data for embedding alignment or rely on gradient-based optimization that becomes unstable when data is extremely scarce. Consequently, the foundational step of vocabulary expansion remains underexplored. Current practice adapts heuristics from language modeling, most notably decomposing unseen tokens into known subtokens and averaging their embeddings
Tikhomirov and Chernyshev (2024)
. Although computationally trivial, this permutation-invariant pooling discards the strict temporal order and articulatory dynamics essential to speech synthesis, forcing the model to relearn sequential structure from scratch during fine-tuning and inflating sample complexity. Our method provides an order-preserving, spectrally grounded initialization that aligns novel embeddings with the pretrained manifold, thereby stabilizing optimization and drastically reducing the target-language data required for subsequent adaptation.
To our knowledge, no prior work proposes an audio-guided initialization specifically for vocabulary expansion in autoregressive transformer-based TTS, making the zero-audio property of SEAM particularly important.

Continuity Principle

5
Conclusion
We presented SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method for low-resource TTS vocabulary expansion. By spectrally merging subtoken embeddings and aligning them via closed-form regression, SEAM preserves phonetic order and reduces sample complexity by up to 4× across languages and architectures. While dependent on subtoken decomposability and IPA transliteration, SEAM offers a lightweight, reproducible pathway to stabilize early-stage TTS adaptation.

6
Limitations
Despite its data efficiency, SEAM operates within three primary constraints:
•
Subtoken & IPA Dependency:
Initialization requires reliable decomposition into known subtokens. For non-Latin scripts or languages lacking robust IPA transliteration tables, mapping errors may propagate to the conditioning space.
•
Fine-Tuning Requirement:
SEAM addresses the initialization bottleneck but does not replace downstream adaptation; acoustic alignment still requires paired target-language audio but much less than other initialization methods.
•
Evaluation Variance in Extreme Low-Resource Regimes
: At very small budgets, word-level overlap between training and test splits can inflate metrics non-monotonically, as observed for Kazakh.
7
Ethical Considerations
SEAM aims to reduce barriers for low-resource language TTS, promoting equitable access to speech technology. However, like all voice synthesis methods, it carries dual-use risks: malicious actors could exploit improved initialization for unauthorized voice cloning or disinformation. We mitigate this by releasing only embedding initialization code not full model weights and requiring explicit consent for any deployment involving human voices. All experiments use publicly available, ethically sourced corpora. We encourage adopters to follow local regulations and community guidelines, particularly when working with under-documented languages.

B.7
Ablation: Audio-Guided Initialization
To assess whether incorporating target-language audio during initialization improves upon SEAM’s zero-audio design, we conduct an ablation comparing zero-audio SEAM against an audio-guided variant. We note that, to the best of our knowledge, no prior published work proposes an independent audio-guided initialization method specifically for vocabulary expansion in autoregressive transformer-based TTS. We therefore position this experiment as an ablation validating the zero-audio property, rather than a comparison against an existing baseline.
The
Audio-Guided
variant proceeds in two stages: (1) SEAM initialization is applied identically to the zero-audio setting; (2) the newly initialized embeddings and the LM head are further refined via AdamW optimization on 1 hour of calibration audio from the target language before the main fine-tuning phase begins.

The refinement step causes embedding norms to inflate to atypical values, distorting the geometric alignment established by SEAM’s closed-form calibration. The closed-form ridge regression produces embeddings that are geometrically well-calibrated to the pretrained manifold; subsequent audio-guided refinement disrupts this calibration, causing the model to fall into a poor local minimum that requires significantly more data to escape. The absence of any independent audio-based initialization baseline in the literature further underscores that SEAM’s zero-audio property fills a genuine methodological gap.
Appendix C
Side-by-Side (SBS) Human Evaluation Guidelines
Annotators evaluated synthesized audio samples using a Side-by-Side (SBS) preference framework, focusing on two orthogonal dimensions:
Realism
(acoustic naturalness) and
Linguistic Correctness
(fidelity to orthographic and phonological norms of the target language). Below are the standardized criteria and decision protocols provided to annotators.
C.1
Dimension 1: Realism (Naturalness)
Annotators rated each sample on a 5-point scale. The following anchors guided the assessment:
•
5 (Excellent):
Indistinguishable from professional human speech. Prosody is fluid, timbre is natural, and paralinguistic cues (e.g., breath, micro-pauses) are appropriately integrated.
•
4 (Good):
Largely natural but exhibits minor artifacts, such as slight pitch irregularities, mild robotic timbre, or subtle prosodic mismatches (e.g., flattened intonation on interrogatives). Comprehension remains effortless.
•
3 (Fair):
Noticeable synthesis artifacts or pacing irregularities (e.g., unnatural pauses, fragmented rhythm), but speech remains fully intelligible. Pronunciation may occasionally mismatch syntactic context.
•
2 (Poor):
Severe articulation errors, phoneme hallucinations, or repetitive stuttering. Speech is strained or partially unintelligible, significantly impeding comprehension.
•
1 (Bad):
Highly robotic, garbled, or completely unintelligible. Contains nonsensical syllable sequences or arbitrary breaks that destroy syntactic coherence.
C.2
Dimension 2: Linguistic Correctness
Linguistic correctness measures adherence to the phonological, morphological, and orthographic conventions of the target language (French, Kazakh, or Russian). Annotators identified and penalized the following error categories:
•
Phoneme & Stress Accuracy:
–
Russian/Kazakh:
Correct realization of vowel reduction (
akanye
), palatalization (soft vs. hard consonants), and lexical stress placement. Misplaced stress that changes word meaning is a critical error.
–
French:
Correct liaison, elision, and nasal vowel production. Failure to apply obligatory liaison (e.g.,
les_amis
) or incorrect nasalization (e.g.,
bon
vs.
bonne
) is penalized.
–
Kazakh:
Accurate pronunciation of vowel harmony and consonant assimilation rules. Errors in front/back vowel alignment within a word constitute a linguistic error.
•
Lexical & Orthographic Fidelity:
–
Any substitution, omission, or addition of words compared to the reference text is penalized.
–
Numbers, abbreviations, and proper nouns must be pronounced according to target-language conventions (e.g., Russian: “1995”
→
\rightarrow
tysyacha devyatsot devyanosto pyat’
; French: “M. Dupont”
→

monsieur Dupont
; Kazakh: “2024”
→

).
–
For Cyrillic scripts (Russian/Kazakh), the model must distinguish visually similar letters with distinct phonemes.
•
Prosody & Intonation:
–
Intonation contours must match sentence type (e.g., rising pitch for questions in French/Russian; declarative fall for statements).
–
Sentence-level stress and phrasing should reflect syntactic boundaries. Arbitrary pauses within phrases or unnatural emphasis on function words are penalized.

Scoring and Preference Decision
For each side-by-side trial, annotators assessed both Model A and Model B against the above criteria. The final preference was determined as follows:
•
If one model demonstrated significantly higher realism
and/or
fewer linguistic errors, it was selected as preferred.
•

•
Each linguistic error (phoneme, stress, lexical, or prosodic) resulted in a proportional downgrade in the overall quality assessment for that sample.
•
