Appendix D
Extended Related Work
Cross-Lingual and Zero-Shot TTS Adaptation.
Recent advances in zero-shot and cross-lingual TTS have dramatically expanded speaker and language coverage. Models such as VALL-E, VoiceCraft, and CosyVoice leverage discrete acoustic tokenizers and autoregressive or diffusion-based decoding to synthesize speech from short prompts
Wang et al. (2023)
;
Peng et al. (2024)
;
Du et al. (2024)
. While highly effective for well-resourced languages, their adaptation to under-documented languages remains constrained by the need for paired text-speech data or language-specific phoneme inventories . Cross-lingual transfer methods typically rely on shared phoneme spaces, speaker-invariant conditioning, or meta-learning for rapid alignment
Casanova et al. (2022)
. However, these approaches still require substantial target-language fine-tuning to stabilize novel token embeddings, leaving the foundational step of vocabulary expansion underexplored.
Vocabulary Expansion and Subtoken Initialization.
The standard pipeline for handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) tokens decomposes unseen units into known subtokens via byte-pair encoding (BPE) or phoneme-grapheme mappings, then initializes embeddings using random draws or arithmetic mean pooling
Tikhomirov and Chernyshev (2024)
. While computationally trivial, mean pooling is permutation-invariant and discards the sequential articulatory structure essential to speech synthesis.
Positioning.
SEAM bridges these research threads by introducing a unified, zero-audio pipeline that combines spectral low-pass filtering with closed-form ridge regression. Unlike iterative alignment methods, SEAM computes the optimal projection analytically, ensuring geometric stability from step zero. By explicitly retaining DFT phase information, it overcomes the permutation invariance of mean pooling while avoiding the data dependencies of contrastive alignment. This positions SEAM as a lightweight, theoretically grounded complement to modern zero-shot and cross-lingual TTS frameworks, specifically targeting the sample-efficiency bottleneck in vocabulary expansion.

article.headline: 频谱合并子词嵌入：零音频扩展TTS词表
article.lede: SEAM 不需要目标语言音频，只用子词嵌入的频谱合并与闭式岭回归为新词元初始化，在三种语言上以最多四分之一的数据逼近基线
article.problem: 条件式 TTS 模型扩展词表时，新音素或字素单元通常随机初始化，再用大量配对音频微调，这在低资源语言上几乎不可行。现有做法是把未见词元拆成已知子词再取平均，但平均池化对顺序不敏感，丢掉了语音合成所需的时序结构与发音动态。
article.method: SEAM 把子词嵌入序列的每一维当作离散信号，做 DFT 后用高斯低通滤波（默认 K=4、σ=2.0）保留低频分量，再把实部与虚部拼成特征向量。随后用闭式岭回归（λ=1e-6）把特征投影到预训练条件流形上，训练对来自旧词表自身的 BPE 分解，因此完全不需要目标语言音频，也不需要梯度优化。对非拉丁文字，先转写成英语 IPA 再做子词分解。
article.results: 在 Chatterbox 上，俄语 5 小时预算下 SEAM 的 CER 为 14.88%，随机初始化为 20.80%、平均池化为 17.53%；25 小时预算下，SEAM 比平均池化分别低 2.22（俄语）、10.63（哈萨克语）、0.87（法语）个 CER 点，比随机初始化低 9.16、27.34、3.77 点。哈萨克语 100 小时 SEAM 的 CER 为 4.39%。作者称这相当于最多 4 倍的数据节省，但 100 小时预算下各方法已收敛：俄语 SEAM 为 7.68%，略高于随机初始化的 7.62%；法语 SEAM 为 9.26%，略高于平均池化的 9.06%。人评用 25 小时训练的 SEAM 对比 100 小时训练的平均池化，非平局偏好率俄语 61.4%（p=0.041）、哈萨克语 65.1%（p=0.002）、法语 70.6%（p<0.001）；在 VibeVoice 上，俄语 5 小时的 CER 为 6.14%，低于平均池化的 8.34% 和随机初始化的 9.26%。
article.why_it_matters: 词表扩展是低资源语言接入 TTS 的第一道门槛；SEAM 把这一步变成一次无需音频、无需梯度优化的线性求解，轻量且可复现，便于快速跨语言部署。
article.limitations: 方法依赖可靠的子词分解与 IPA 转写，转写错误会直接传进条件空间，而且它只解决初始化，后续仍需目标语言音频微调；人评每种语言只有 5 名母语者、25 条语句，极低资源下训练集与测试集的词级重叠还会让指标非单调（哈萨克语随机初始化从 5 小时到 25 小时由 11.62% 升到 32.60%）。
article.figure_caption_zh: 子词嵌入序列的频谱能量衰减：累计能量在 k=3 时已超过 99%，σ=2.0 的高斯滤波保留 k∈{0,1,2,3} 四个频点并压制高频边界噪声。

figure.caption: Spectral energy decay in subtoken embedding sequences. Cumulative energy (blue) exceeds 99\% by $k=3$, confirming bandlimited compositionality. The Gaussian filter $ =2.0$ (green) suppresses high-frequency noise while retaining bins $k \{0,1,2,3\}$ (red dashed line). This empirically validates $(K=4, =2.0)$ without hyperparameter tuning.

page_papers.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
page_papers.abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
Jiatong Li & Yatao BianNational University of Singapore
Affiliation:
Corresponding to:
ybian@nus.edu.sg
https://github.com/phenixace/Open-MolLean
Abstract
Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state.
A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements.
We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.
1
Introduction
Chain-of-thought prompting makes a model’s intermediate reasoning visible
(
Wei et al., 2022
)
. In chemistry, this is appealing as chemists could examine the intermediate reasoning steps to improve the explainability of the final answer
(
Wang et al., 2026
;
Narayanan et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Zhao et al., 2025
)
. However, a model can invoke a functional group absent from a molecule, lose track of a bond, or claim a property improvement without establishing it. Analyses of chemical reasoning find fabricated structural claims even alongside correct answers
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
, and broader evaluations reveal uneven chemical competence and overconfidence
(
Mirza et al., 2025
)
. These errors concern the stated chemistry itself, a failure mode complementary to causal unfaithfulness, where an explanation misrepresents how the answer was produced
(
Turpin et al., 2023
)
.
We therefore ask
what must a chemical reasoning language represent for its steps to be verifiable?
Lean offers a precedent: a model proposes a derivation and a proof assistant checks its formal obligations
(
Moura and Ullrich, 2021
;
Jiang et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2023
)
. Chemical reasoning combines graph transformations, structural observations, empirical estimates, and choices among plausible candidates. Chemistry tools already support capable agents
(
M. Bran et al., 2024
;
Boiko et al., 2023
)
; the key step is to give successive operations and claims a shared molecular referent and an explicit acceptance condition.
We introduce
MolLean
, a process-verifiable language grounded in a maintained molecular state (Figure
1
). A
transition
constructs, modifies, or reorganizes represented molecules. A
readout
obtains information without changing them, and an assertion tests a claim against that information. The model selects actions and obligations; a Lean-based kernel checks admissible transitions and native structural predicates. Descriptor- and knowledge-dependent assertions obtain typed witnesses from external providers. These distinctions let construction, transformation, and observation share one language while each keeps its own form of evidence.
The state does more than record the output: it determines which atoms a later edit addresses, which molecule a property readout measures, and whether an accepted prefix remains usable after a failed proposal. MolLean supports primitive edits, construction macros, joint transformations, and candidate introduction at different granularities. An accepted edit supplies the referent for subsequent checks, and a rejected edit leaves the maintained state intact. Verification thus applies directly to the model’s declared commitments.
We expose the same language through whole-trace and interactive interfaces.
MolLean One-pass
submits a complete trace;
MolLean Refinement
revises a rejected trace from the initial state.
MolLean-MCP
lets the model inspect the current state, attempt an operation, and use immediate feedback to choose its next action. External feedback is central to revision: tool-grounded criticism guides reasoning more reliably than intrinsic self-correction
(
Huang et al., 2024
;
Gou et al., 2024
)
. MolLean specifies what that feedback refers to and when it commits a change.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
A state-grounded chemical reasoning language and verification contract.
MolLean unifies molecular transitions, readouts, and assertions, with explicit boundaries between native structural checks and externally witnessed claims.
•
Two feedback regimes over shared execution semantics.
Whole-trace refinement revises complete traces from the input; MolLean-MCP interacts with the maintained state and commits only accepted edits.
•
An evaluation on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks.
With Qwen3.6-27B, refinement improves over direct chain-of-thought on every task, and MCP reaches the highest reaction accuracy. On ChEBI-20, refined traces reach 79.0% soundness and 33.1% answer accuracy, identifying task fidelity as the next challenge beyond repairing rejected steps. Qwen3-4B gains substantially on structural tasks.
2
MolLean
MolLean is a reasoning language built around a simple contract: an operation refers to the current molecular state, verification decides whether it is admissible, and only an accepted transition commits a new state. Readouts and assertions observe that same state without editing it. Lean implements the chemical core, while Python handles parsing, state transport, reference resolution, and inference control (Figure
1
).

and stopping once accepted. Thus the model can replace its entire plan after a failure.
MolLean-MCP
exposes transitions, checks, and readouts as stateful tools, supplied to the model as function-calling schemas within the inference loop. The model can inspect the state before choosing its next operation; rejected proposals leave it unchanged.
finish
invokes closing gates. MCP uses the language interactively; One-pass and Refinement submit complete programs.
Verification compares only against the input or a self-proposed candidate; dataset references enter only the independent scorer (Section
3
). Each task declares its initialization, allowed operations, closing obligations, and scorer.
3
Experiments
We ask whether MolLean improves task performance, how accepted traces relate to correct answers, and when interactive verification is useful. The main comparison uses Qwen3.6-27B; an additional Qwen3-4B evaluation examines whole-trace inference with a smaller model.

Whole-Trace Refinement Improves Task Performance
Refinement improves over Direct CoT on all 12 task types (Table
1
), with gains of 12.0–48.2 percentage points under each task’s binary success criterion. For optimization, this range uses direction-only success, and similarity-weighted scores show the same gains. Atom and bond counts improve by 46.8 and 48.2 points, and component addition by 44.2. Paired bootstrap intervals for the primary Refine-minus-CoT score exclude zero in every task (Table
2
).
One-pass already improves over CoT on 11 tasks. On forward reactions, One-pass (23.6%) trails CoT (35.0%), and refinement raises accuracy to 62.8%, showing that feedback is most valuable when the initial plan misses the verifier’s obligations. Improvements extend to reference-based tasks, with ChEBI-20 accuracy increasing from 18.1% to 33.1% and retrosynthesis from 3.0% to 20.8%. These results identify two complementary benefits: expressing a candidate as an executable trace, and using a failed check to revise that candidate.

At the final refinement budget, retrosynthesis reaches 88.2% trace soundness and 20.8% exact set-match accuracy; ChEBI-20 reaches 79.0% soundness and 33.1% accuracy; and functional-group generation reaches 97.6% acceptance and 41.8% benchmark success. In these tasks, the declared obligations capture part of the instruction, and native functional-group patterns follow MolLean’s own definitions.
For ChEBI-20, 1,075 outputs are both sound and correct, 1,533 are sound but incorrect, 17 are correct without certification, and 675 satisfy neither criterion. These exhaustive outcomes distinguish process acceptance from task success (Appendix
E.4
). Atom-count generation shows the opposite profile: 444 of 467 accepted traces meet its task criterion, compared with 1,075 of 2,608 on ChEBI-20. A count maps directly to a predicate, whereas a textual description requires the model to select and combine the right structural obligations. Instruction-to-constraint grounding is therefore the main lever for further gains, as the salt example in Section
4
illustrates.
3.4
Interactive Verification Strengthens Reaction Prediction
Figure
2
c shows the signed differences between the two interfaces. MCP achieves the best reaction results, with 66.4% forward-reaction and 27.4% retrosynthesis accuracy against 62.8% and 20.8% for Refinement. Refinement leads on atom counts (88.8% versus 82.6%), bond counts (69.0% versus 56.2%), QED optimization (59.0 versus 49.4 weighted-score points), and ChEBI-20 (33.1% versus 23.5%), and both protocols reach 100.0% on component addition and 97.0% on component deletion.
Whole-trace refinement can revise an entire plan, and MCP conditions each action on the maintained state and immediate feedback. Immediate feedback helps the model maintain references across a sequence of dependent edits, as in multi-step reactions, while restarting permits larger changes of plan. The two interfaces are therefore complementary. Appendix
E.2
reports the interaction-length distributions.

4
Case Studies: Repairs and Specification Gaps
Figure
4
pairs molecular structures with verification feedback in six cases, illustrating how rejected commitments are repaired and how an accepted revision can still miss the intended task.
Figure 4:
Molecular cases of repair and incomplete specification.
(a,c) Refinement changes action granularity or the attachment site. (b,e) A property or count assertion rejects an otherwise valid candidate. (d) MCP repairs an edit within the same maintained state. (f) A revised salt description drops a required component, giving an accepted but incorrect answer. Molecular drawings use the saved structures; numbers in (c,d) denote input atom indices. Refinement restarts from the task input, whereas MCP continues within its episode.
Valence and attachment sites.
In the forward-reaction example (a), forming a bond to an acyl carbon before breaking its bond to chlorine would give carbon valence five. The one-pass trace is rejected. Refinement replaces the sequential edits with a joint bond-formation and bond-cleavage operation, removes the detached chlorine, and obtains the correct carbonate product. The aldehyde-addition example (c) instead needs a different attachment site: the same
AttachGroup
macro fails at substituted aromatic carbon 10 and succeeds at carbon 11. The revised trace then passes the functional-group-change and input-relative similarity checks. The carbonate requires suitable action granularity, whereas the aldehyde requires a suitable molecular referent.
Measured properties and explicit counts.
In (b), the one-pass edits lower QED
(
Bickerton et al., 2012
)
from 0.674 to 0.573 despite an instruction to increase it. The graph edits pass, and the property assertion fails. Refinement reaches QED 0.767, with success-weighted similarity 0.743. RDKit supplies the measurement and Lean checks the requested direction. In (e), a valid 27-carbon chain fails
AtomCount
because the instruction requests 25. Refinement proposes a 25-carbon chain and passes that count. Both cases separate candidate validity from the requested property, with different evidence sources: atom count is native to the graph, and QED is an externally computed descriptor checked through a witness.
Interactive recovery and incomplete specifications.
In (d), MCP’s phenyl attachment at carbon 5 is refused without changing the state. The next edit attaches it to nitrogen 1, followed by two checks. The episode finishes correctly after four counted calls, including the refusal. In (f), one-pass proposes the correct salt and fails the disconnected-proposal check. Refinement omits chloride and its count obligation, producing an accepted cation that misses the target salt. Effective revision therefore requires both accurate execution and a specification that continues to express what the user asked for.
5
Related Work
Chemical language research connects molecular representations with natural-language descriptions and instructions. Text2Mol introduced text-based molecular retrieval and ChEBI-20
(
Edwards et al., 2021
)
; MolT5 studied translation between molecular and natural-language representations
(
Edwards et al., 2022
)
; and Speak-to-Structure evaluates instruction-driven generation, editing, and optimization
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
. SELFIES addresses molecular-string validity
(
Krenn et al., 2020
)
, whereas structural reasoning targets molecular understanding
(
Jang et al., 2025
)
. ChemBench evaluates chemical knowledge and reasoning more broadly
(
Mirza et al., 2025
)
. These perspectives complement evidence that fluent chemical reasoning can contain unreliable structural claims
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Among executable chemical languages, XDL expresses synthesis procedures for compilation into laboratory instructions
(
Mehr et al., 2020
)
.
Formal and executable reasoning make different parts of a derivation checkable. Lean separates proof construction from proof checking
(
Moura and Ullrich, 2021
)
; Draft, Sketch, and Prove links informal planning to formal proofs
(
Jiang et al., 2023
)
, and LeanDojo supports programmatic interaction with Lean
(
Yang et al., 2023
)
. Learned process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning with a trained verifier
(
Lightman et al., 2024
)
. PAL and Program of Thoughts use execution to ground generated computations
(
Gao et al., 2023
;
Chen et al., 2023
)
.
Feedback and tool use turn evaluation into part of generation. Self-Refine uses model-generated feedback
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
, and CRITIC grounds revision in external tools
(
Gou et al., 2024
)
, which is more reliable than intrinsic self-correction on reasoning tasks
(
Huang et al., 2024
)
. ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions
(
Yao et al., 2023
)
. In chemistry, ChemCrow integrates specialized tools
(
M. Bran et al., 2024
)
, Coscientist connects planning with experimental automation
(
Boiko et al., 2023
)
, and ChemReasoner steers catalyst search using computational-chemistry feedback
(
Sprueill et al., 2024
)
.
6
Conclusion
MolLean grounds chemical reasoning in a maintained molecular state, combining Lean-checked obligations with explicit external witnesses. MolLean-MCP makes this feedback available during generation. Whole-trace refinement improves Qwen3.6-27B performance across all 12 tasks, MCP delivers the strongest reaction results, and Qwen3-4B gains substantially on structural tasks. Grounding instructions in explicit constraints is the natural next step toward chemical reasoning that is both verifiable and faithful to the task.

A molecular graph stores indexed atoms, bonds, and stereochemical annotations. Atom fields include element, formal charge, radicals, aromaticity, and virtual hydrogen information; bond fields specify endpoints and order. Virtual hydrogens contribute to element and formula readouts, and the bookkeeping ledger counts graph atoms. The
leaving_pool
is excluded from the predicted answer and remains part of that ledger. Additions, removals, and proposals update the atom-count ledger.
References are pairs
(mol_id, atom_idx)
into the graph state. A cross-molecule bond joins two index spaces, and a fragment split creates a new molecule identifier. In whole-trace execution, Python tracks accepted primitive merges and remaps subsequent step references through that history. Lean separately rebases references inside tracked compound bundles. MCP uses the current atom map returned in feedback for later model calls. Python also exports the maintained graphs to molecular strings.

Evaluation Details
D.1
Task Setup and Scoring
Generation begins from an empty state; editing and optimization begin from the input molecule. Forward prediction begins from reactants and retrosynthesis from the product. Editing requires one active output molecule and disallows whole-molecule replacement, while optimization permits candidate proposals. Generation, ChEBI-20, and reaction tasks use terminal realizability checks. Closing bookkeeping applies throughout.
Non-reaction tasks score the first active molecule; reactions score the full active set. A rejected whole-trace completion can still provide a scored answer from its available state, or a parsed answer when no state is returned. Failed certification can therefore coexist with a correct answer. Missing or invalid answers receive zero. article.headline: 用 Lean 逐步检查化学推理
article.lede: MolLean 把分子状态当作推理锚点，让 Lean 内核逐步校验化学操作与断言，在 12 个任务、8,800 个样例上
article.problem: 化学思维链里经常出现凭空捏造的结构与性质断言：模型会引用分子里并不存在的官能团、跟丢某根键，或声称某性质得到改善却从未验证。这类错误针对的是模型自己陈述的化学内容，与解释不忠实于真实决策过程属于不同的失效模式。论文要回答的是：一种化学推理语言必须表示什么，它的每一步才可被检验。
article.method: MolLean 把推理写成针对一个被维护的分子状态的操作序列：转移（构造、编辑、片段分离等）修改状态，读出与断言只观察状态而不修改它；每一步都送进 Lean 内核检查，只有被接受的转移才会提交新状态，被拒绝的步骤不改变当前状态。结构类断言（原子数、键数、环数、分子式、芳香性、官能团、R/S 立体中心）由 Lean 原生判定；涉及描述符或外部知识的断言则通过类型化的 witness 协议，由 RDKit 等外部提供者返回字段、Lean 在其上检验谓词。系统提供三种推理接口：一次生成完整轨迹的 One-pass、从初始状态重写被拒轨迹的 Refinement，以及带状态工具、可逐步获得反馈的 MolLean-MCP。
article.results: 评测覆盖 12 个任务共 8,800 个匹配样例（S2-Bench 九项各 500 例、USPTO-50k 正向与逆合成各 500 例、ChEBI-20 全部 3,300 例测试集）。Qwen3.6-27B 上，Refinement 相对直接 CoT 在全部 12 个任务上都有提升，按各任务二元成功标准计为 12.0–48.2 个百分点：原子计数从 42.0% 升到 88.8%，键计数从 20.8% 升到 69.0%，组分添加从 55.8% 升到 100.0%，ChEBI-20 从 18.1% 升到 33.1%，逆合成从 3.0% 升到 20.8%。MCP 在反应任务上更好，正向反应 66.4%、逆合成 27.4%，而 Refinement 分别为 62.8% 与 20.8%。但接受率与正确率分离明显：ChEBI-20 上 Refinement 轨迹 soundness 达 79.0%，其中 1,075 条既 sound 又正确、1,533 条 sound 但不正确。Qwen3-4B 上结构类任务增益明显（原子计数 15.8%→56.8%，组分添加 13.4%→91.4%），但逆合成在所有协议下都是 0.0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「可执行的化学承诺」与「自由文本解释」分开：构造、变换、观测共享同一套分子指称，失败的操作会留下可诊断的拒绝理由，从而让修复有明确对象，而不只是模型自我批评。作者也指出，soundness 与答案正确率是两个独立指标，接受一条轨迹并不保证它满足用户的原始指令。
article.limitations: 论文自己把「任务保真度」列为主要短板：ChEBI-20 上 1,533 条轨迹执行完全合规却答案错误，盐酸盐案例中修订版直接删掉氯离子和对应的计数义务后仍被接受，说明自我提出的 OutcomeMatch 无法恢复被丢弃的约束；此外外部 witness 的提供者返回值被信任，描述符质量受 RDKit 制约，小模型在依赖化学知识的参考生成任务上几乎无收益。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图 1：MolLean 的语言、执行契约与推理接口——状态与转移族及只读查询（a）、适配器只提交被 Lean 接受的后继状态并示例乙醇到 1-丙醇的构造（b）、以及 One-pass、Refinement 与 MCP 三种接口（c）。

figure.caption: {MolLean's language, execution contract, and inference interfaces.} (a) The state, transition families, and read-only queries; native predicates are decided in Lean, while witnessed claims apply a Lean predicate to a typed provider response. (b) The adapter holds $S_0= {init}(x)$, sends each operation to the Lean kernel, and commits only accepted successors; witness requests and responses pass through the adapter. In the example, generation starts empty, admits ethanol as $S_1$, and attaches methyl to obtain 1-propanol as $S_2$; a false carbon count is rejected and $S_2$ is unchanged. (c) One-pass executes one trace; refinement rewrites a rejected trace from $S_0$; MCP continues from the current state. Dataset references are used only by an independent scorer.

page_papers.title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
page_papers.abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

Introduction
Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions, supporting policy evaluation and model-based planning
(
Yang et al., 2024
;
Wu et al., 2024
)
.
Accurate simulation requires modeling robot motion and resulting scene changes.
Latent action models encode visual transitions as proxy actions
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Ye et al., 2025
)
, allowing world models to learn dynamics from large-scale videos without explicit action annotations
(
Gao et al., 2026
)
.
These latent actions are learned through future-observation reconstruction, with the current observation providing visual context
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Liang et al., 2026
)
.
For action-conditioned simulation, inferred latent actions serve as supervision for mapping robot controls into the learned latent action space.
Learning this mapping is challenging since reconstruction objectives encourage latent actions to encode robot motion together with object responses and other scene changes
(
Nikulin et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
For example, similar end-effector motions may produce different object responses under different contact states
(
Gu et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
, introducing scene-dependent variation beyond robot motion into the adaptation target.
These interaction outcomes are useful for world modeling, since accurate simulation requires predicting how robot motion affects the surrounding scene.
This motivates a dedicated kinematic component for action adaptation, together with a residual component retaining complementary transition information for dynamics learning.
To this end, we propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling.
Robot skeletons describe robot configuration and motion while abstracting scene appearance.
Related robot world models use skeleton sequences or kinematic renderings as direct conditioning signals for generation
(
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Wu and Gao, 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
.
SkeLAM uses paired RGB and skeleton transitions to learn kinematic and residual components from RGB observations.
Skeleton supervision grounds the kinematic latent in robot motion, while the residual latent supplies complementary information for RGB reconstruction.
Together, the two components jointly support reconstruction, providing a dedicated target for action adaptation while retaining information for dynamics learning.
During representation learning, skeletons supervise the RGB latents, while the deployed interface uses RGB observations and robot actions.
We further introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction, which replaces the RGB kinematic latent with its paired skeleton counterpart while retaining the RGB residual.
Reconstructing the same transition under this substitution encourages compatible motion conditioning in the RGB decoder, extending cross-modal correspondence beyond alignment in latent space.
The world model learns from both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout prepares it for the zero-residual condition used at deployment.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions.
At inference, generation uses the current observation and robot actions.
To assess motion accuracy and visual fidelity, we evaluate SkeLAM on DROID
(
Khazatsky et al., 2024
)
.
Compared with DreamDojo, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1%.
Motion probing shows that the kinematic component approaches the performance of the concatenated representation with half the latent dimensions, while latent interventions and component ablations support its role in generation.
Qualitative results further demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts.
Open-loop policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model that separates the conditioning roles of robot motion and complementary visual dynamics, providing a dedicated kinematic target for robot action adaptation.
•
We introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction to encourage compatible RGB and skeleton motion conditioning during generation.
Combined with branch dropout, this design supports robot action conditioning through the
kinematic pathway learned from visual transitions.
•
Experiments on DROID demonstrate gains in motion accuracy and visual fidelity, supported by representation analyses and component ablations.
We further show zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and agreement between predicted and measured policy success rates.

4
Experiment
We evaluate the effect of the kinematic–residual decomposition on action-conditioned world modeling, and examine motion transfer and rollout evaluation as downstream applications.
Specifically, we investigate the following questions:
•
RQ1 (World modeling):
Does adapting robot actions to a dedicated kinematic component improve motion accuracy while preserving visual fidelity? (Section
4.2
)
•
RQ2 (Motion representation):
Do skeleton-grounded kinematic latents support more accurate linear decoding of robot motion than unstructured latent actions? (Section
4.3
)
•
RQ3 (Motion transfer):
Can a kinematic representation learned from robot interactions transfer human motion to generated robot rollouts in a zero-shot setting? (Section
4.4
)
•
RQ4 (Policy evaluation):
How closely do open-loop world-model rollouts reproduce policy rankings and success rates measured in real robot executions? (Section
4.5
)

4.2
Action-Conditioned World Modeling
Quantitative results.
To assess how accurately SkeLAM simulates the consequences of robot actions, we evaluate motion accuracy and visual fidelity on DROID.
Table
1
shows that SkeLAM ranks first on seven of eight metrics among the reported action-conditioned models, including all four visual fidelity metrics.
Compared with DreamDojo and CD-LAM, SkeLAM reduces ADE by 19.5% and 23.7%, respectively, alongside LPIPS reductions of 11.1% and 17.4%.
These improvements indicate closer agreement with both the target robot trajectories and visual observations.
Ctrl-World and OSCAR achieve higher direction F1, while SkeLAM attains lower trajectory error and stronger visual fidelity.
In particular, compared with Ctrl-World, SkeLAM reduces ADE from 42.96 to 41.15 px and LPIPS from 0.4029 to 0.1310.
The combined improvements in trajectory accuracy and visual fidelity support the generation of robot motion together with the associated scene dynamics.

To evaluate whether generated rollouts reproduce robot motion while preserving scene structure, we compare predictions with ground truth in Figure

The overlaid trajectories reveal deviations from the reference motion in DreamDojo and OSCAR, accompanied by visible arm deformation in later frames.

Ablation studies.
To assess how each component supports action-conditioned generation, we compare variants in Table
2
.
(i) Skeleton supervision
grounds the RGB kinematic latent in robot motion; removing it increases ADE from 41.15 to 64.59 and reduces magnitude correlation from 0.5277 to 0.2009, supporting geometric supervision for learning motion representations suitable for action conditioning.
(ii) Cross-modal swap
couples skeleton supervision to RGB generation beyond latent alignment; removing it increases ADE to 66.74 and reduces magnitude correlation to 0.1897, while LPIPS rises from 0.1310 to 0.1436, supporting reconstruction-level RGB–skeleton alignment for downstream action conditioning.
(iii) Residual latent
retains complementary scene dynamics; zeroing it from world-model pretraining maintains similar visual fidelity (0.1305 vs. 0.1310 LPIPS) while ADE increases to 43.37 and magnitude correlation decreases to 0.4737, suggesting that complementary visual information benefits motion conditioning.
(iv) Action adaptation
supervises the action-to-kinematic mapping; omitting adapter regression increases ADE to 65.84, supporting explicit supervision of the mapping from robot actions to the learned kinematic representation.
Further details and adaptation-budget analysis are provided in Appendix
D
.

To examine whether the learned motion representation transfers across embodiments, we use human demonstration videos from UniSkill
(

The RGB encoder extracts latent actions from these videos to directly condition SkeLAM, with a robot observation specifying the initial scene.
All model parameters remain fixed during transfer.
We compare with the pretrained checkpoint of DreamDojo
(
Gao et al., 2026
)
, which supports latent-action conditioning.
As shown in Figure
5
, SkeLAM generates distinct end-effector motions corresponding to the human demonstrations: a downward reach for the towel-pushing prompt and an upward movement for the tissue-pulling prompt.
DreamDojo exhibits limited end-effector displacement in both examples.
These results provide qualitative evidence that human-derived latent actions can guide robot motion despite differences in embodiment and scene appearance.

5
Conclusion
We presented SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling.
The kinematic component provides a motion-grounded target for robot action adaptation, while the residual retains complementary visual dynamics.
Cross-modal swap reconstruction and branch dropout support reuse of the learned kinematic pathway for action-conditioned generation.
Experiments on DROID show improved motion accuracy and visual fidelity, with representation analyses supporting kinematic specialization.
Qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer, while policy evaluation yields success-rate estimates consistent with real robot executions.
These results support structuring latent actions around robot motion while retaining complementary information for generation.
Future work will extend the current recorded-action replay protocol to closed-loop policy evaluation.
A key question is how prediction errors affect subsequent policy decisions and task outcomes over longer interaction horizons.

article.headline: 骨架引导潜在动作提升机器人世界模型
article.lede: SkeLAM 将视频潜在动作拆成骨架监督的运动学分量与残差分量，在 DROID 上降低末端执行器误差和 LPIPS。
article.problem: 从视频重建学习到的潜在动作会把机器人运动、物体响应和其他场景变化混在一起，因而难以与机器人控制量建立稳定对应。世界模型又需要同时预测机器人运动和场景动态，直接拿这种混合表示做动作适配会增加场景相关变化。
article.method: SkeLAM 用机器人骨架监督把 RGB 迁移潜在动作分解为运动学潜变量和残差潜变量，并通过跨模态交换重建让 RGB 解码器兼容骨架运动条件。世界模型用独立投影分别接入两个分量，训练时做分支 dropout，为部署时残差置零做准备。一个轻量动作适配器把机器人动作映射到运动学空间，再微调世界模型生成未来观测。
article.results: 在 DROID 的 400 个片段上，SkeLAM 的末端执行器 ADE 为 41.15 px，较 DreamDojo 的 51.11 px 降低 19.5%，LPIPS 从 0.1473 降至 0.1310（降低 11.1%）；相比 CD-LAM，ADE 和 LPIPS 分别降低 23.7% 和 17.4%。消融中移除骨架监督使 ADE 从 41.15 升至 64.59，移除跨模态交换重建升至 66.74；线性探针下运动学分量的 EEF MAE 为 5.99×10⁻³、R² 为 0.3200。开环策略评估的成功召回率为 33.33%，平衡准确率 63.02%，成功率 MAE 为 4.76 个百分点。
article.why_it_matters: 把动作适配目标限制在骨架监督的运动学潜空间，可以让世界模型用机器人动作而非未来帧残差来驱动生成，这对策略评估和模型规划更可控。跨模态交换重建也提供了一种在视频潜在动作中注入结构化运动先验的通用思路。
article.limitations: 论文的 DROID 增益没有均匀迁移到 AgiBot：SkeLAM 的 SSIM 为 0.8479，高于 DreamDojo 的 0.8330，但 LPIPS 0.1049 差于 0.0889，ADE 21.10 也高于 19.55。策略评估仍是开环动作回放，成功召回率仅 33.33%，人类到机器人迁移也只有两个定性例子。
article.figure_caption_zh: SkeLAM 总览：骨架监督与跨模态交换重建把 RGB 迁移潜变量分解为运动学与残差分量，世界模型通过独立投影和分支 dropout 接入，动作适配器在推理时预测运动学潜变量而残差置零。

(B) Separate projections condition the world model: keep retains both branches, partial drops one, and null drops both. (C) An action adapter predicts kinematic latents, with the null residual at inference.

page_papers.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
page_papers.abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.

Rethinking Sequence Compression with
Test-time Regression
Sihan Yang   Jie Huang   Hanxuan Li   Yifan Guo   Weigao Sun   Yiran Zhong   Weiyang Liu
The Chinese University of Hong Kong   Independent Researcher   Token Foundry
Alibaba Group
*
Corresponding author
spherelab.ai/ttr-compressor
Abstract
Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming.
We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation.
Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass.
This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression.
We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models.
On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin.
For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
Figure 1:
Overview of TTR-Compressor.
(a) Unlike pooling and projection, which process tokens independently, TTR-Compressor fits all tokens jointly and thereby captures the interplay among them. (b) TTR-Compressor outperforms existing methods on both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.
1
Introduction
Sequence compression is a ubiquitous operation in modern efficient large model architectures
(
Qwen Team, 2026b
;
DeepSeek-AI, 2026
)
, and yet remains surprisingly underexplored. For example, block-wise sparse attention compresses each token block into a summary vector used to score and select relevant blocks
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Yuan et al., 2025
)
, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) merge neighboring visual features into compact tokens before feeding them into the language backbone
(
Wang et al., 2025
;
Bai et al., 2025
;
Team et al., 2026a
)
. In both settings, the compressor acts as a critical information bottleneck. Once information is discarded, it cannot be recovered downstream.
One would expect compression to be a carefully designed architectural component. However, most models rely on simple mechanisms, such as parameter-free pooling, learned projections over concatenated tokens, or at best, attention-weighted pooling.
We argue that these default compressors share a fundamental structural limitation,
i.e.
,
they aggregate tokens using weights that do not account for inter-token relationships
.
Mean pooling uses uniform weights, linear projection uses fixed position-dependent weights, and attention-weighted pooling scores each token independently.
As a result, redundant tokens can reinforce one another, while distinctive information is diluted.
From a statistical perspective, these methods primarily exploit
first-order
token statistics while ignoring
second-order
inter-token correlations, the very structure that reveals which information is redundant and which is distinctive.
We introduce a fundamentally different compression strategy. Rather than asking
which weighted average
best summarizes a set of tokens, we let the tokens define a regression problem
and take its
fitted coefficients
as the summary. Specifically, our proposed TTR-Compressor, constructs a self-supervised ridge-regression problem directly from the input tokens, requiring no external labels, and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation.
This formulation creates a natural division: the outer training loop meta-learns
which
regression problem produces task-useful representations, while the inner closed-form solution determines
how
that problem should be fitted to each input. The key distinction from conventional pooling and projection arises from the Gram matrix in the regression solution.
By explicitly capturing inter-token correlations, TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly, so redundant evidence has diminishing rather than purely additive influence.
This input-adaptive behavior cannot be reproduced by a fixed projection or additive token combination.
Moreover, learning the regularizer removes the need for ridge hyperparameter tuning in large-scale pretraining. Because the compression window is typically smaller than the channel dimension (
i.e.
,

We evaluate TTR-Compressor on two applications that impose fundamentally different requirements on compression. In
block-wise sparse attention
, the compressed summary must act as a faithful
retrieval key
. In this setting, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms traditional baselines on RULER
(
Hsieh et al., 2024
)
retrieval tasks, surpassing sophisticated attention-based compressors
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
by a considerable margin. In
visual token merging
, by contrast, the compressed summary must preserve a faithful
representation
. Here, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the widely used MLP merger across diverse compression ratios, and achieves comparable performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are summarized below:
•
A novel compression framework.
We introduce a test-time regression framework for sequence compression, reframing token summarization as an instance-adaptive optimization problem.
•
A practical operator.
We derive an efficient dual closed-form solution and eliminate hyperparameter tuning, making TTR-Compressor fully practical and scalable for large-scale pretraining.
•
Empirical effectiveness.
As a drop-in component in large models, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms conventional baselines in both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.
2
Related Work
Sequence compression.
Compressing a sequence of tokens into a single vector is a fundamental operation across modern architectures, with applications ranging from multimodal token reduction
(
Bolya et al., 2022
;
Li et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2024
;
Cha et al., 2024
;
Chu et al., 2024
)
to block-wise sparse attention
(
Jiang et al., 2024
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
Gao et al., 2024
;
Lai et al., 2025
)
.
Existing compression operators largely fall into three paradigms:
(1)
parameter-free pooling
, such as mean pooling;
(2)
concatenation followed by learned projection
; and
(3)
attention-based compression
, which summarizes tokens via attention-weighted averaging
(
Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023
;
Yang et al., 2025b
)
.
A fundamental limitation of these families is that they compute token combinations without explicitly accounting for the inter-token correlations.
In contrast, TTR-Compressor derives its representation as the solution to a linear system whose Gram matrix directly encodes these correlations, providing an expressive, drop-in replacement for the operators above.
Test-time regression and test-time training.
The idea of adapting part of a network on each input at inference time dates back to fast-weight programmers
(
Schmidhuber, 1992
;
Schlag et al., 2021
)
and was revived as test-time training (TTT), first for robustness under distribution shift
(
Sun et al., 2020
)
and then as sequence-modeling layers whose hidden states are small models updated by gradient descent on a self-supervised loss
(
Sun et al., 2024
;
Behrouz et al., 2026b
;
Behrouz et al., 2026a
;
Han et al., 2026
)
. In-Place TTT
(
Feng et al., 2026
)
further extends this paradigm by directly adapting the existing MLP projection weights of pretrained Transformers. A parallel line of work reinterprets linear attention and its descendants (
e.g.
, DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2024
)
, Gated DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2025c
)
, Longhorn
(
Liu et al., 2025
)
, Titans
(
Behrouz et al., 2026b
)
) as online regression: each layer maintains a key-to-value regressor that is refined with one gradient or delta-rule step per token and read out by the query. MesaNet
(
von Oswald et al., 2026
)
pushes the inner optimization to convergence, solving the problem at every time step with conjugate gradients, while LaCT
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
updates fast weights over large, unordered chunks to improve hardware utilization.
TTR-Compressor differs from these methods in two fundamental ways. First, because compression operates independently on small, disjoint blocks without cross-block dependencies, the regression admits an efficient,
exact closed-form solution
via a single
T
×
T
T\times T
dual solve. This avoids both iterative gradient-based inner optimization (as in TTT, ViT
3
, In-Place TTT, and MesaNet) and single-step approximations (such as delta-rule updates). Second, rather than using test-time regression to produce input-dependent model weights
(
Bertinetto et al., 2018
;
Sun et al., 2020
)
or a fast-weight memory that is subsequently queried
(
Schlag et al., 2021
;
Yang et al., 2025c
;
Behrouz et al., 2026b
)
, we use regression to directly yield a
representation
of a token block. Specifically, the fitted coefficients themselves serve as the compressed representation (
e.g.
, a visual token or a retrieval key).

5
Applications and Experimental Results
We evaluate TTR-Compressor in two settings: block-wise sparse attention for efficient language modeling, where compressed representations guide context selection, and visual token merging for efficient multimodal understanding, where they serve as the visual input to the language backbone.
5.1
Block-wise Sparse Attention
Architecture and Baselines.
Block-wise sparse attention partitions the context into blocks, scores their compressed representations against each query, and attends to tokens in selected blocks alongside a local window. The compressor therefore determines which distant information remains accessible: an uninformative summary can prevent a relevant block from being selected, regardless of the quality of its individual token representations.
We adopt HiLS-Attention
(
Hu et al., 2026
)
as a base framework and vary only the compressor. HiLS-Attention has three effective architectural components: hierarchical softmax attention, which combines within-block attention with learned block-level weights; low-rank query calibration, which adapts queries for scoring compressed representations; and HoPE, which applies RoPE to only a subset of feature dimensions to support length extrapolation. We compare four compressors: mean pooling, concat & projection, the attention-weighted pooling used in the original HiLS-Attention, and TTR-Compressor. Full attention and sliding-window attention serve as additional references.

We train 345M-parameter language models on the FineWeb dataset
(
Penedo et al., 2024
)
with an 8K context length. Training runs for 30,000 optimization steps with a global batch size of 128 sequences, corresponding to approximately 30B tokens, and uses AdamW with a learning rate of

Results.
As shown in Table
1
, the choice of compressor largely determines retrieval quality. TTR-Compressor outperforms all baselines by a large margin, and its advantage persists when extrapolating to 16K and 32K. We attribute this to its second-order modeling: pooling and projection add up tokens independently, so the redundant context that fills most of a block drowns out the few informative tokens. The Gram matrix in TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly and reduces the influence of redundant evidence, so the resulting key keeps the distinctive content that queries need to find. The convolutional variant brings a further gain, reaching 12.24 points over the strongest baseline, as convolution makes the regression targets more informative and thus improves compression quality. On the benchmarks in Table
2
, the evaluation contexts are too short to activate sparse attention, so these results only reflect the common-sense reasoning ability acquired during pretraining. Concat & Projection has substantially more parameters than the other compressors, which may benefit pretraining. TTR-Compressor performs well and on par with full attention.

Architecture and Baselines.

Concluding Remarks
In this work, we revisit sequence compression, a pervasive yet often overlooked bottleneck in modern architectures, through the lens of test-time regression. Instead of relying on fixed pooling or learned projections, we formulate token compression as an instance-adaptive ridge regression problem, allowing the compressed representation to be solved directly from each input sequence.
By exploiting inter-token correlations through second-order interactions, TTR-Compressor offers a more expressive way to preserve sequence information while remaining lightweight and parameter-efficient. Its dual-form solution further makes this formulation scalable in practice.
Empirically, TTR-Compressor performs strongly across both block-wise sparse attention and multimodal token reduction, improving long-context retrieval while matching standard visual mergers with significantly fewer tokens.
More broadly, our results suggest that sequence compression need not be viewed as static aggregation, but as an input-dependent inference problem that adapts to the structure of each sequence. We expect this perspective establishes test-time regression as a simple, expressive, and scalable primitive for efficient foundation models.

E.1
Scaling Up Model Size and Training Budget
To further verify that the advantage of TTR-Compressor is not merely an artifact of the smaller-scale setting used in the main paper, we scale up both the model size and the training budget. Specifically, we train a 1B-parameter model on 100B tokens and evaluate it on the same RULER subtasks across context lengths ranging from 4K to 32K. For comparison, we also scale up Attention-Weighted Pooling—the strongest baseline among all compression methods evaluated in the main paper’s 345M-parameter experiments—to the same 1B-parameter, 100B-token setting.
As shown in Table
7
, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the Attention-Weighted Pooling baseline across almost all context lengths and subtasks, achieving an average accuracy of 0.7996 compared to 0.735. article.headline: 序列压缩即测试时回归：新压缩器提升长上下文检索
article.lede: 研究者把序列压缩重新表述为测试时岭回归，用对偶 Cholesky 闭式解直接算出压缩表示，每个压缩器仅 2d 个可学习参
article.problem: 现有的序列压缩器——均值池化、拼接后学习投影、注意力加权池化——都用不考虑 token 间关系的权重来聚合 token：均值池化用均匀权重，投影用固定的位置相关权重，注意力池化则对每个 token 独立打分。结果是冗余 token 相互叠加、相互强化，而真正独有的信息被稀释。作者指出，从统计上看，这些方法只用到一阶 token 统计量，忽略了 Gram 矩阵所刻画的二阶 token 间相关性，而后者恰恰能揭示哪些信息冗余、哪些信息独特。
article.method: TTR-Compressor 直接用输入 token 构造一个无需外部标签的岭回归问题：键取归一化后的特征，标量目标由共享的学习投影给出，回归的拟合系数就作为压缩表示。压缩窗口通常小于特征维度，因此内层用 T×T 对偶形式做一次 Cholesky 分解精确求解；外层则把目标投影和可学习对角正则矩阵 D（由 softplus 参数化）通过任务损失端到端反传，形成双层优化。键做归一化、而目标保留原始 token 范数，是这一设计的关键：若目标也归一化，拟合项会退化为让 h* 坍缩到与输入无关的静态向量。
article.results: 在块稀疏注意力设置下（345M 参数模型、8K 上下文、约 30B token 训练），TTR-Compressor 的 RULER 平均分为 0.5092，带卷积的版本为 0.5144，而最强基线注意力加权池化为 0.3920，即领先 12.24 个点；32K 长度的 S-NIAH-1 上，带卷积版本达到 0.988，基线为 0.740。附录把规模扩到 1B 参数、100B token 后，平均分为 0.7996，对照的注意力加权池化为 0.735。视觉 token 合并中，2×2 分组的平均分从 MLP 的 54.93 提到 55.92，带卷积为 56.03；3×3 分组从 52.27 提到 54.85（带卷积），比 MLP 高 2.58 点。文本密集基准上，3×3 卷积变体相对 MLP 在 OCRBench、InfoVQA、ChartQA 上分别提升 4.10、4.54、3.56。摘要称其在 55.6% 更少的视觉 token 下达到 MLP 相当的性能。
article.why_it_matters: 序列压缩是块稀疏注意力和多模态大模型中的关键信息瓶颈，而一个只有 2d 参数、可直接替换池化或投影的算子，意味着不必改动架构就能改善长上下文检索与视觉 token 的利用效率。它把「压缩」从静态聚合重新理解为一个依赖输入的推理问题，这一视角可能迁移到其他需要信息瓶颈的模块。
article.limitations: 主实验的语言模型只有 345M 参数、约 30B token，1B/100B 的扩展结果放在附录且只对比了一个基线；表 2 的零样本常识推理中，评估上下文太短、稀疏注意力未被激活，压缩器实际不参与推理，TTR 平均 48.16 与全注意力持平，ARC-c 的 23.29 还低于多数基线。方法依赖 T≪d 的前提，且对实现细节敏感：去掉键归一化后平均分从 0.5092 崩到 0.2531，固定 λ 时结果在 0.4238 到 0.5023 之间波动，视觉 2×2 的平均提升也只有约 1 个点。
article.figure_caption_zh: TTR-Compressor 总览：(a) 双层学习——内层把序列压缩写成测试时岭回归，用对偶 Cholesky 精确求解得到表示 h*，外层用任务梯度端到端学习回归参数；(b) 通过 Gram 矩阵把 token 联合耦合，相比加性池化，冗余 token 的相对影响被削弱。

figure.caption: {Overview of TTR-Compressor.} (a) Bilevel learning: The inner solve formulates sequence compression as test-time ridge regression with an exact dual Cholesky solve to obtain the representation $ {h}^*$, while the regression parameters are learned end-to-end via task gradients. (b) Input-dependent second-order adaptation: By jointly coupling tokens through the Gram matrix, TTR naturally diminishes the relative influence of redundant tokens compared to additive pooling. For intuitive illustration, we set $ {D}= {I}$ and uniform targets $ {v}= {1}$; as typically learned in practice, a smaller regularizer $ {D}$ further amplifies this deduplication effect, yielding an even higher relative share for distinct tokens.

page_papers.title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V
page_papers.abstract: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.

Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V
Zhenghan Chen
1
,
Zekai Shao
1,
†
\dagger
,

2

1

Siming Chen
1,*

\dagger
Project Lead,
*
Corresponding author
Project Repository:
https://code2video-compass.github.io/
Abstract
Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos.
However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated.
We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings.
Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency.
It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos.
We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text–video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality.
Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases.
We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs)
[
41
,
3
,
18
,
44
,
38
]
are making it increasingly feasible to create complete videos through executable code, a task requiring world knowledge, spatial reasoning, creative judgment, and complex programming.
Compared with direct video generation, code-based approaches explicitly represent visual structures and animation parameters, enabling fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse
[
33
,
12
,
46
]
.
Generating complete videos that follow textual instructions requires models to plan coherent narratives and visuals, reliably generate lengthy code across interdependent files, and coordinate animations and evolving states across scenes and timelines.
Moreover, visual references introduce additional challenges, requiring models to reconstruct the referenced appearance or motion and integrate it into the complete video
[
63
,
29
]
.
Existing benchmarks for direct video generation, including VBench
[
22
]
, EvalCrafter
[
32
]
, and T2V-CompBench
[
51
]
, evaluate visual quality, semantic alignment, and compositional requirements, while LongAV-Compass
[
30
]
extends evaluation to longer sequences and multiple input conditions. Code-based tasks target specialized applications or representations, including Manim educational videos
[
13
]
, data narratives
[
35
]
, SVG animations
[
53
]
, and web animation reconstruction
[
24
]
. Similarly, HeyGen’s Code2Video Benchmark
[
62
]
focuses on short motion graphics clips representing individual beats of product launch videos.
Nevertheless, as shown in Tab.
1
, existing code-based benchmarks remain limited in task coverage and input modalities, and lack comprehensive evaluation combining objective and subjective metrics.
To address these gaps, we introduce
Code2Video-Compass
(Fig.
), a general-purpose benchmark for code-based text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) generation, where models create complete videos following textual instructions and, when provided, reconstruct and integrate visual references at appropriate temporal positions.
Guided by a taxonomy of motion-design practices, we combine independently constructed tasks based on curated textual instructions and visual references with tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos.
This yields 2,104 tasks across 10 categories and 24 subtypes, each annotated along three complexity dimensions: construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency.
We further propose a comprehensive dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics.
Objective evaluation measures execution success, token consumption, technical and aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, text–video alignment, and reference fidelity.
Subjective evaluation employs an MLLM-as-a-judge protocol to evaluate fine-grained instruction following through explicit checklists and evaluate holistic creative quality across content coherence, visual design, motion quality, and viewer engagement.
In summary, our main contributions are as follows:
•
General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation.
We formulate unified T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks that require MLLMs to generate executable code for video generation.
•
Taxonomy-Driven Benchmark Dataset.
We curate 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories and 24 subtypes, annotated along three complexity dimensions, each with three levels.
•
Comprehensive Dual-Level Evaluation Framework.
We integrate 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics to evaluate code-based video generation capabilities.
•
Extensive MLLM Benchmarking and Insights.
We evaluate 15 proprietary and open-weight MLLMs, revealing that video quality and execution reliability do not always align, with performance declining as complexity increases.
