Related Work
2.1
Direct Video Generation
Benchmarks for direct video generation have established diverse evaluation tasks and frameworks for assessing model capabilities. VBench
[
22
]
and EvalCrafter
[
32
]
evaluate perceptual quality, while T2V-CompBench
[
51
]
and TC-Bench
[
16
]
examine compositional and temporal constraints. VBench++
[
23
]
and KeyFrame-Compass
[
52
]
extend evaluation to image conditioning and keyframe adherence. StoryBench
[
9
]
, MSVBench
[
48
]
, and LongAV-Compass
[
30
]
further address narrative progression and long-range consistency, with the latter covering text, image, and video conditioning. T2AV-Compass
[
10
]
combines objective and subjective evaluation.
However, code-based video generation requires evaluating operational performance and the technical, semantic, and creative quality of complete videos.
2.2
Code-Based Video and Animation Generation
Prior work has explored code-based video and animation generation across specialized applications. Code2Video
[
13
]
introduces a Manim-based agent framework and the MMMC benchmark for educational videos, while DataReel
[
35
]
supports animated data storytelling. LogoMotion
[
31
]
generates editable logo animations, and MG-Gen
[
49
]
produces layered HTML animations from images. InternSVG
[
53
]
and LottieGPT
[
12
]
explore structured vector animations.
Evaluation of code-based generation has advanced within specific tasks. MMMC evaluates aesthetics, knowledge transfer, and efficiency, while Animation2Code
[
24
]
evaluates execution, appearance, and motion fidelity. MoVer
[
34
]
verifies motion constraints, and HeyGen’s Code2Video Benchmark
[
62
]
employs subjective evaluation of short promotional motion graphics. However, comprehensive evaluation of complete code-generated videos across diverse creative categories and input conditions remains limited.
Tab.
1
summarizes task sources, generation paradigms, input settings, scale, and evaluation.
3
Code2Video-Compass
3.1
Task Formulation
Code2Video-Compass evaluates general-purpose code-based video generation, where MLLMs translate textual instructions and optional visual references into executable projects. The rendering stack supports HTML/CSS, SVG, Canvas, and Three.js, with Remotion
[
46
]
producing the videos. Generated videos must exhibit coherent progression across events or visual states, with reference content reconstructed through code rather than directly embedded or replayed. We consider three input settings:
Text-to-Video (T2V).
Models interpret a self-contained instruction and generate code
to realize the specified visual content and temporal progression.
Image-to-Video (I2V).
Models interpret the instruction and reference keyframe, understand its visual content, determine where it should appear in the complete video, and generate code to reconstruct and integrate its visual state.
Video-to-Video (V2V).
Models interpret the instruction and reference clip, determine its placement in the complete video, and generate code to reconstruct and integrate its appearance, motion, and event sequence.
3.2
Data Categories and Complexity
We derive 10 categories from professional motion-design websites, award categories, template libraries, and creative portfolios
[
25
,
5
,
7
]
:
(1) Explainer Motion Graphics; (2) Branding & Promotional Motion;
(3) Kinetic Typography; (4) UI & Product Motion;
(5) Data & Infographic Animation; (6) Title Sequences;
(7) Broadcast & Show Graphics; (8) Illustrative & Character Narrative;
(9) Abstract & Experimental Motion; and (10) 3D Motion.
The categories are further refined into 24 subtypes using YouTube
[
61
]
examples, considering communication purpose, visual structure, and temporal organization. This taxonomy supports multiple labels per task and guides data collection and category-level analysis. We further define three complementary complexity dimensions, each with three levels.
Construction Complexity
measures visual construction demands: standard primitives and component compositions (Level 1), custom geometry and detailed structures (Level 2), and procedural or simulation systems (Level 3).
Dynamic Animation Complexity
measures temporal organization: staged sequences (Level 1), coordinated changes across elements and scenes (Level 2), and complex concurrent motion or transformations (Level 3).
State-Dependency Complexity
measures the temporal span over which objects, data, and states must remain consistent: adjacent stages (Level 1), intervening stages (Level 2), and long-range dependencies across multiple changes (Level 3).
3.3
Data Construction
Figure 2
:
Data construction pipeline. (A) Independent tasks are developed from curated text seeds, reference images, and video clips. (B) Paired T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks are derived from shared complete source videos. (C) Both task sets undergo prompt construction, QA checklist development, and annotation of subjects, temporal events, motion types, and three complexity dimensions, yielding 2,104 tasks.
We construct 2,104 tasks through two complementary strategies, as illustrated in Fig.
2
. The Independent Task Set broadens creative coverage using text seeds and visual references, while the Paired Task Set grounds tasks in real-world creative practice by deriving them from complete professional and user-created videos.
Three co-authors conduct manual verification and quality review throughout the data construction process.
Independent Task Set.
For T2V, we source prompts from VidProM
[
54
]
and video descriptions from Shot2Story
[
19
]
. After source-specific cleaning, deterministic sampling yields 54,443 candidates, which we embed using all-MiniLM-L6-v2
[
47
]
. With GPT-6.1 Sol
[
40
]
assistance and human review, taxonomy-guided curation narrows the pool to 720 candidates, from which we select 145 diverse task seeds.
For I2V, we curate reference images from LICA
[
20
]
, SciDraw-6K
[
11
]
, SynthChartNet
[
39
]
, and PD12M
[
36
]
. For V2V, we collect animation videos from YouTube
[
61
]
. For both settings, we curate 15 candidates per subtype and select five through content verification and manual quality review, yielding 120 references from 360 candidates in each setting. We crop a continuous 2–10 s key segment from each selected video to form the V2V reference clip. These seeds and references guide complete-video task construction.
Paired Task Set.
To cover professional and user-created videos across platforms, we collect 197 animation records from YouTube
[
61
]
and 2,473 candidate URLs from Bilibili
[
8
]
, REDnote
[
45
]
, and X
[
58
]
. We screen candidates for video completeness and suitability for code-based generation with assistance from Gemini 3.8 Flash
[
18
]
, retaining 979 videos. We remove exact duplicates using normalized URLs and SHA-256 hashes, and identify near-duplicates across all video sources using SSCD
[
43
]
frame embeddings indexed with FAISS
[
15
]
. Temporal matching distinguishes reposted works from videos with similar visual styles. After deduplication, we score the remaining 915 videos for narrative progression, content, visual design, and motion quality using Gemini 3.8 Flash. Human review retains 573 complete videos, from which we select representative keyframes and crop continuous 2–10 s reference clips with Gemini 3.8 Flash assistance and human verification. Each video yields aligned T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks with shared creative goals and event progression, totaling 1,719 tasks.
Prompt Construction and Annotation.
We develop detailed, self-contained instructions for both task sets with assistance from Gemini 3.8 Flash and human review. Independent instructions specify a new complete video based on each text seed or visual reference. For each paired source, we jointly develop T2V, I2V, and V2V instructions with shared core content requirements and event progression. Instructions specify visual elements, spatial relationships, exact text and data, motion, event sequences, and cross-stage dependencies, including reference content and surrounding events where applicable. We annotate subjects, temporal events, motion types, and three complexity dimensions, and construct fine-grained QA checklists for instruction following, as described in Sec.
3.5.2
.
We iteratively review and refine these checklists with assistance from GPT-6.1 Sol.
3.4
Dataset Statistics
Figure 3
:
Distributions of (a) video categories, (b) motion types, (c) subject types, (d) event counts, and (e) target durations across 958 records (573 paired sources + 385 independent tasks). A record may have multiple video categories, motion types, and subject types.
Figure 4
:
Task complexity and prompt length. C, D, and S denote construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity. (a) Record counts by category and complexity level (1–3), with multi-label records counted in each assigned category. (b) Prompt token distributions across T2V, I2V, and V2V, as in Tab.
1
.
The benchmark combines 1,719 paired tasks from 573 source videos with 385 independent tasks, totaling 2,104 tasks across T2V (718), I2V (693), and V2V (693). For coverage analysis, we count each paired source once, resulting in 958 records comprising 573 paired sources and 385 independent tasks. Figures
3
and
4
characterize coverage across creative categories, subjects, motion types, video duration, prompt length, and the three complexity dimensions, demonstrating the breadth and diversity of the benchmark.
3.5
Dual-Level Evaluation Framework
We introduce a dual-level evaluation framework comprising 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers execution reliability, efficiency, video quality, text–video alignment, and reference fidelity. We employ Gemini 3.8 Flash
[
18
]
to evaluate instruction following and rate four dimensions of holistic video quality.
3.5.1
Objective Evaluation
Operational Performance
.
Practical video creation requires reliable execution and efficient generation. Execution success measures whether the code produces a usable video, while token consumption measures generation effort.
Execution Success (ES).
Usable video projects must execute and render successfully. We report the fraction of sampled tasks producing complete, playable videos without errors under the shared backend and resource limits. Failed outputs receive zero on all non operational metrics to prevent inflated averages from excluding difficult tasks.
Token Consumption (TC).
We measure generation efficiency using mean API-reported output tokens per attempted task, consistent with token-based model comparisons such as Artificial Analysis
[
6
]
.
Video Quality
.
Rendered videos need clear images, appealing visual presentation, and temporally consistent motion. The objective metrics capture these complementary properties through technical quality, aesthetic quality, and motion smoothness.
Technical Quality (TQ).
Technical degradation, including blur, noise, and compression artifacts, affects the clarity of rendered content. The technical branch of DOVER++
[
57
]
provides a score for this aspect of video quality.
Aesthetic Quality (AQ).
The visual appeal of composition, color, and style contributes to effective presentation. Averaging frame-level scores from Aesthetic Predictor V2.5
[
1
]
gives a video-level estimate of aesthetic quality.
Motion Smoothness (MS).
Smooth motion should be temporally predictable from neighboring frames. We resample videos to 24 FPS and use AMT
[
28
]
to predict each intermediate frame from its two neighbors. The score is one minus the mean RGB absolute error normalized by 255, excluding comparisons across hard cuts.
Text–Video Alignment
.
Instructions describe individual events and the overall progression of a complete video. Local TVAlign and Global TVAlign evaluate semantic correspondence at these two scales across T2V, I2V, and V2V.
Local TVAlign (L-TVA).
Local TVAlign measures local semantic correspondence between eight-frame sliding video windows and text chunks derived from global and event-level descriptions. We compute window-level alignment scores using ViCLIP-L
[
55
]
and aggregate them across the video.
Global TVAlign (G-TVA).
Global TVAlign measures semantic alignment between the complete video and the instruction as a whole, complementing local alignment and reference-fidelity metrics. We use Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B
[
27
]
to encode the instruction and frames spanning the video, then compute their embedding cosine similarity.
I2V Reference Fidelity
.
Reference keyframes may appear at any stage, so we search the full generated video for the closest matching frame. Perceptual and structural fidelity measure visual resemblance and image structure.
Perceptual Fidelity (PF).
Recognizable subjects and visual elements are central to reconstructing the reference image. We use DINOv3
[
50
]
features to locate the closest matching frame and measure perceptual resemblance.
Structural Fidelity (SF).
Faithful reconstruction also requires preserving the reference’s local image structure. SSIM
[
56
]
measures luminance, contrast, and structural similarity at the same matching frame.
V2V Reference Fidelity
.
The reference clip must be reconstructed within a complete video, so we first locate its corresponding interval in the output. Sequence alignment, appearance fidelity, and motion fidelity measure visual sequence correspondence, appearance similarity, and motion consistency within this interval.
Sequence Alignment (SA).
To measure whether the reference’s visual progression is preserved despite timing differences, we locate the corresponding interval using subsequence dynamic time warping (DTW) on DINOv3
[
50
]
frame embeddings. The score is the mean cosine similarity along the matched path.
Appearance Fidelity (AF).
The reconstructed interval should preserve the reference’s subjects, colors, and shapes. Within the localized interval, we perform constrained DTW using DreamSim
[
17
]
cosine distances and define AF as one minus the path-averaged distance.
Motion Fidelity (MF).
Similar visual appearance and temporal sequences do not necessarily imply similar motion patterns. We use CoTracker3
[
26
]
to extract point trajectories from the reference clip and the localized generated interval and compare their displacement directions and magnitudes after spatial and temporal normalization. We aggregate trajectory similarities through bidirectional best matching.
3.5.2
Subjective Evaluation
Instruction Following (IF)
.
We derive verifiable QA checklists from each instruction and employ Gemini 3.8 Flash
[
18
]
to check whether the generated video satisfies each requirement. Each checklist contains up to 16 questions, including up to 14 generic questions across six dimensions and two task-specific questions. The six dimensions are (1)
Content
, covering exact text and information, (2)
Attribute
, covering appearance and quantity, (3)
Composition
, covering layout, framing, and color, (4)
Relations
, covering spatial and logical connections, (5)
Dynamics
, covering motion, interaction, transformation, viewport motion, and temporal relations, and (6)
Aesthetics
, covering style. The two task-specific questions cover full-video requirements or reference integration. IF reports the fraction of questions passed.
Holistic Video Quality
.
Creating an effective complete video requires coherent content, purposeful design, expressive motion, and sustained viewer interest. We rate these four aspects using five-point Likert scales.
Content Coherence (CC).
Content coherence is rated based on progression, relationships among stages, state continuity, and consistency of text, data, charts, and interfaces.
Visual Design (VD).
Visual design is rated based on composition, typography, readability, color, visual hierarchy, and purposeful detail within the intended style.
Motion Quality (MQ).
Motion quality is rated based on easing, pacing, continuity, transitions, coordinated elements, temporal hierarchy, and behavioral variety, capturing both smoothness and expressive choreography.
Viewer Engagement (VE).
Viewer engagement is rated by how well emphasis, pacing, and presentation sustain interest in a way that suits the video’s intended use.

Overall Performance.
Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the best average rank across all three settings, with 1.60 on T2V, 1.08 on I2V, and 1.15 on V2V, followed by Claude Sonnet 5.5 in each setting.
Proprietary models occupy the top three positions in every setting.
Among open-weight models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash leads T2V, while MiMo-V2.6-Pro leads I2V and V2V.
Execution success varies considerably across models, ranging from 0.52 to 0.94 on T2V, 0.59 to 0.96 on I2V, and 0.69 to 0.97 on V2V.
T2V.
Claude Opus 5.5 leads IF and CC with scores of 0.91 and 4.05, respectively, along with AQ and both text–video alignment metrics.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 leads MQ and VE with scores of 3.85 and 3.90, while GPT-6.1 Sol leads VD with 3.88 and TQ, highlighting distinct strengths among leading models across evaluation dimensions.
I2V.
Claude Opus 5.5 leads both image-fidelity metrics, with PF of 0.89 and SF of 0.66, as well as all five subjective metrics.
GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna achieve similar image fidelity, with PF scores of 0.83 and 0.82 and SF scores of 0.65 and 0.62, but differ considerably in IF at 0.86 versus 0.70 and MQ at 3.47 versus 2.61, suggesting that faithful keyframe reconstruction does not necessarily ensure strong instruction following or motion quality.
V2V.
Claude Opus 5.5 leads all three clip-fidelity metrics, with SA of 0.88, AF of 0.79, and MF of 0.44, as well as all five subjective metrics.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves comparable clip fidelity, with SA of 0.87, AF of 0.77, and MF of 0.44, but lower IF and CC scores of 0.76 and 3.36, compared with 0.93 and 4.00 for Claude Opus 5.5, highlighting the gap between reference-clip reconstruction and complete-video requirements.
5
Insights and Discussions
5.1
Quality and Reliability Analysis
As shown in Sec.
4.2
, execution success varies substantially across models, motivating a closer examination of how execution failures affect overall quality scores.
We use mean holistic video quality, averaged across four holistic quality metrics, to compare performance over all evaluated tasks and successfully rendered videos.
As shown in Fig.
5
, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol achieve higher mean holistic quality among successfully rendered videos, with scores of 4.19 and 4.15, respectively, compared with 4.04 for Claude Opus 5.5. However, their higher execution failure rates reduce their full-set means to 3.62 and 3.61, while Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest full-set mean of 3.87.
Higher video quality on successful runs can coexist with lower execution reliability, highlighting the need to consider both when evaluating code-based video generation.
Figure 5
:
Mean holistic video quality across all evaluated tasks and successfully rendered videos for 15 MLLMs. Bars indicate the difference between the two averages.
5.2
Failure Analysis
We analyze 2,756 error cases to characterize failure patterns across models. As shown in Fig.
6
, failure types vary considerably across models. Compilation errors and missing APIs or packages account for 83.4% of GPT-6 Astra’s failures, while missing APIs and packages alone dominate Qwen3.8-Max at 59.7%. In contrast, runtime exceptions account for 75.0% of Claude Opus 5.5’s failures and over half of those for GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. These distinct profiles reveal different sources of failure across models, ranging from code compilation and dependency handling to runtime execution.
Reliably generating lengthy code across interdependent files remains a major challenge, with compilation, dependency, and runtime failures varying across models.
Figure 6
:
Distribution of failure types across nine selected models.
5.3
Complexity Analysis
To examine how current MLLMs handle increasing task complexity, we analyze performance across construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity levels. As shown in Fig.
7
, performance generally declines with increasing complexity, with SF particularly affected. SF decreases by 14.38% and 12.82% of its score range from L1 to L2 under construction and dynamic animation complexity, respectively. Across most metrics, these two dimensions exhibit steeper declines from L1 to L2 than from L2 to L3, whereas state-dependency complexity shows larger declines from L2 to L3 across all 15 metrics. These contrasting patterns suggest that even moderate construction and dynamic animation complexity can challenge current MLLMs, whereas lower state-dependency complexity is relatively manageable and long-range dependencies remain challenging.
Figure 7
:
Performance changes between adjacent complexity levels, using the notation in Fig.
4
. Values are normalized by metric scale, with positive values indicating performance declines.
5.4
Generation Effort and Cost
We analyze the relationship between generation effort, API cost, and holistic video quality in Fig.
8
. Higher token consumption does not necessarily yield better quality. GLM-5.3-Flash uses 90.0k output tokens per request, compared with 13.9k for GPT-6 Astra, yet achieves a lower quality score of 2.94 versus 3.62. API costs also vary substantially at comparable quality levels. GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra achieve nearly identical quality scores of 3.61 and 3.62, yet GPT-6 Astra incurs approximately 6.1 times the estimated API cost. Claude Opus 5.5 achieves the highest quality score of 3.87 at a lower estimated cost than GPT-6 Astra.
Greater generation effort and API spending do not necessarily translate into better video quality, revealing substantial differences in efficiency across models.

5.5
MLLM Judge Validation
We further validate the Gemini 3.8 Flash judge on 300 outputs from six models of varying capabilities, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8-27B, and MiniMax M3, each evaluated on the same 50 tasks sampled to balance categories and complexity levels.
Each output is evaluated three times to assess scoring stability.
For human validation, three independent raters evaluate a subset of 200 outputs for instruction following and mean holistic video quality.

Conclusion
We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for complete code-based video generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V, comprising 2,104 diverse tasks and a comprehensive dual-level evaluation framework. Evaluation of 15 MLLMs reveals persistent challenges in execution reliability, instruction following, reference fidelity, and handling increasing task complexity. We believe that Code2Video-Compass provides valuable insights into the limitations of current MLLMs and serves as a diagnostic testbed for advancing reliable, coherent, and high-quality code-based video generation.

article.headline: 代码视频生成基准：15 个 MLLM 同台评测
article.lede: Code2Video-Compass 包含 2,104 个任务，覆盖 T2V、I2V、V2V 三种输入，用 12 项客观
article.problem: 基于代码的视频生成能让模型把视觉与时间要求翻译成可执行程序，从而实现细粒度控制、定向编辑和组件复用。但现有代码类基准多面向 Manim 教学视频、SVG 动画、网页动画重建等专门任务，缺少跨创意类别、跨输入模态的完整视频生成评测。
article.method: 作者从专业动效网站、模板库与创作平台归纳出 10 个类别、24 个子类，并从「结构构建、动态动画、状态依赖」三个维度各分三级标注复杂度。数据由两部分构成：一是依据文本种子与视觉参考独立构建的任务，二是从 573 个完整专业或用户视频派生出的成对 T2V、I2V、V2V 任务，最终合计 2,104 个任务。评测框架含 12 项客观指标（执行成功率、token 消耗、技术质量、美学质量、运动平滑度、局部和全局文本对齐、参考保真度等）与 5 项主观指标（指令遵循加四项整体质量）。
article.results: 论文在 1,054 个固定子集任务（360 个 T2V、347 个 I2V、347 个 V2V）上评测 15 个来自 9 个家族的模型。Claude Opus 5.5 在三种设置下平均排名均为第一，T2V 为 1.60、I2V 为 1.08、V2V 为 1.15；执行成功率区间分别为 T2V 0.52 到 0.94、I2V 0.59 到 0.96、V2V 0.69 到 0.97。T2V 上 Claude Opus 5.5 的指令遵循为 0.91、内容连贯为 4.05；I2V 上其感知保真 PF 为 0.89、结构保真 SF 为 0.66；V2V 上序列对齐 SA 为 0.88、外观保真 AF 为 0.79、运动保真 MF 为 0.44。失败分析覆盖 2,756 个错误样本：编译错误与缺失 API 或依赖占 GPT-6 Astra 失败的 83.4%，缺失 API 单独占 Qwen3.8-Max 失败的 59.7%，运行时异常占 Claude Opus 5.5 失败的 75.0%。复杂度上升时性能普遍下降，SF 在构建复杂度和动态动画复杂度从 L1 到 L2 时分别下降其分数区间的 14.38% 与 12.82%。成本方面，GLM-5.3-Flash 每次请求 90.0k 输出 token 只得到 2.94 的质量分，而 GPT-6 Astra 用 13.9k token 得到 3.62；质量接近的 GPT-6 Astra 与 GPT-6.1 Sol（3.62 对 3.61）中，前者 API 成本约为后者的 6.1 倍。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「代码即视频」从单一专门任务扩展到通用创意场景，并同时衡量执行可靠性与成片质量；结果表明高分模型也可能频繁编译失败，为后续 agent 式修复与长代码生成研究提供了诊断基准。
article.limitations: 评测只取约一半记录构成的 1,054 个固定子集，且每个模型仅单次 API 调用、不给执行反馈或修复机会，可能低估具备调试循环的系统；渲染栈固定为 HTML/CSS、SVG、Canvas、Three.js 配合 Remotion，结论未必迁移到其他渲染环境。此外，技术质量、美学等客观分依赖 DOVER++、Aesthetic Predictor 等外部模型，主观分由 Gemini 3.8 Flash 担任评委，其与人类评分的皮尔逊相关仅 0.796（指令遵循）与 0.783（整体质量），并非完全可靠；V2V 输入上 GPT 与 Claude 收到 4 FPS 帧序列、其余模型收到原生视频，也存在输入形式不一致的隐患。
article.figure_caption_zh: 数据构建流程：独立任务集与成对任务集分别来自文本种子、参考图像和完整源视频，经提示构建、QA 清单与主体、事件、运动类型及三维复杂度标注后，共得到 2,104 个任务。

page_papers.title: Foundation4D: Towards a unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles
page_papers.abstract: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by 13.4% relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.

Introduction
Two central goals in the development of autonomous vehicle systems are understanding the driving environment and reconstructing recorded scenes for simulation. Both require recovering scene geometry, objects, their motion, and the space they occupy. Unified perception models learn these capabilities through shared visual representations, avoiding the repeated processing of the same observations by separate networks. UniAD and PARA-Drive connect perception with prediction and planning
[
1
,
2
]
, while GeoUP jointly predicts depth, 3D objects, and semantic occupancy from driving video
[
3
]
. These outputs capture much of the structure and motion needed for scene reconstruction. Simulation additionally requires recovering scene appearance so that the environment and its moving actors can be rendered from novel viewpoints. Unifying perception and reconstruction would therefore enable a shared model to both understand real driving scenes and recreate them for simulation.
Recent progress in feed-forward reconstruction offers a basis for this integration. VGGT
[
4
]
jointly recovers camera parameters and dense geometry from multiple images, while Gaussian reconstruction models such as Instant NuRec
[
5
]
predict renderable driving scenes without per-scene optimization. These advances make it possible to infer scene structure and appearance directly from images, but extending them to a shared model for multi-camera video requires efficient use of observations across views and time. In particular, the global attention used in VGGT grows quadratically with the total number of image tokens, making longer sequences costly to process.

article.headline: 一个前馈模型同时做驾驶感知与场景重建
article.lede: 研究提出统一前馈模型，用共享表示从环视视频同时做感知与可渲染的 3D 重建。
article.problem: 自动驾驶既需要理解环境，也需要为仿真重建场景，二者都依赖场景几何、目标、运动与空间占据信息；目前通常由各自独立的网络反复处理同一批观测。VGGT 这类前馈重建方法能直接从图像恢复相机参数与稠密几何，但它使用的全局注意力随图像 token 总数二次增长，难以扩展到多相机长视频。
article.method: 论文提出 Foundation4D，用共享图像编码器与分解式时空注意力，在视角与时间两个维度上融合多相机视频观测，避免重复编码。任务专用解码器分别回归相机到车体的标定、自车运动与度量深度，预测 3D 目标及其速度和高分辨率语义占用，并用 3D Gaussian 重建场景外观。
article.results: 在 OpenOccupancy 基准上微调时，评测覆盖 16 个语义类别，体素分辨率 0.2 m，感兴趣区域为 [-51.2, 51.2]×[-51.2, 51.2]×[-5, 3] m；训练 30,000 次更新，初始学习率 3×10⁻⁴ 并采用余弦衰减，批大小 8，时间步长 1，输入图像 1036×1036。定性结果显示，六个原生视角的高斯渲染具有较好多视角几何一致性，在路面纹理、远处背景几何与天空外观上优于 Instant NuRec；但所给材料中的 IoU/mIoU 表格未列出具体数值，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 如果感知与重建能真正共享一套表示，实车感知与仿真渲染就不必各跑一套网络，同一模型既可理解真实驾驶场景，又能重建出可渲染的新视角。
article.limitations: 公开评测目前只在 OpenOccupancy（基于 nuScenes）一个基准上进行，且微调时语义类别与空间范围都与预训练不同；正文未给出 IoU/mIoU 及与基线对比的具体数值，重建质量也主要是定性比较与逐帧 PSNR 展示。

A common image encoder and factorized spatiotemporal attention efficiently combine observations across views and time. Task-specific decoders recover camera-to-rig calibration, ego motion, and metric depth; predict 3D objects, velocities, and high-resolution semantic occupancy; and reconstruct scene appearance with 3D Gaussians.

page_papers.title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI
page_papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change the improver's knowledge or tools, but the physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way they improve.
page_papers.content:
Introduction
Recursive self-improvement
(RSI) describes a system that improves the process by which it improves, not only its behavior. The idea goes back to I. J. Good’s speculation about machines that design better machines
(
Good, 1966
)
and to self-referential learners such as the Gödel machine
(
Schmidhuber, 2003
)
, and recent digital agents have begun to approach it
(
Chen et al., 2026d
)
. STOP
(
Zelikman et al., 2024
)
applies a program that improves code to its own source, and the Darwin Gödel Machine
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
lets improved coding agents modify themselves; both judge each candidate with executable tests. Yet a system can get better at a task, and a fixed procedure can keep producing better versions of it, without anything recursive happening. RSI requires two further links (Section
2.2
): what the system retains from earlier improvements must make its next revision better, and the
improver
, the component that revises the learning procedure, must in turn use what it has gained to help produce its own next improvement.

Approach

Safety
Retrieve the repair, adapt the interface, test the result  e.g., ASPIRE, PhyAgentOS

Earlier systems kept different kinds of artifacts. Options

)
encode temporally extended behaviors that a higher-level controller can call, and Horde
(

)

(

)
shares models and action recipes among robots. Code as Policies
(

)
writes programs against perception and control APIs, and Inner Monologue

(

Shinn et al., 2023

stores written reflections on earlier failures, showing how a frozen model can still take part in an agent that improves; the
Weights or Skills?
survey
(

)
reviews this broader choice. Physical reuse additionally needs valid sensing, control, and conditions of applicability.
Remembering experience.
Memory systems differ in what they store, how strongly they abstract it, through which interface it is read, and how long it persists, and a memory helps only if these choices preserve a relation that a later decision can exploit. Some systems keep the scene and past interaction themselves: RoboMemory
(
Lei et al., 2025b
)
and AllDayNav
(
Yin et al., 2026a
)
preserve continuity of the environment and of past interaction, and PhyAgentOS
(
Liu et al., 2026h
)
keeps sessions, evidence, recovered lessons, and capability descriptions as versioned records inside a runtime that also checks compatibility, supervises execution, and invokes recovery, so its gains belong to the integrated package.
Others distill experience into reusable guidance, which must then be checked against later conditions. Robo-Cortex
(
Chan et al., 2026
)
distills progress and failure histories into principles and induced navigation heuristics, evaluated mainly in unseen settings of the Habitat simulator
(
Savva et al., 2019
)
with a preliminary physical study of ten navigation goals. RoboHarn-Evo
(
Bao et al., 2026
)
also revises what it stores: physical feedback updates task- and action-level entries together with their stated applicability, and knowledge acquired in simulation reaches 41.7% mean zero-shot success on real tasks, rising to 62.5% after updates from real interaction. PhysMem
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
makes the check explicit: a frozen VLM planner commits a hypothesis about physical properties to memory only after targeted interaction verifies it. On simulated medium-difficulty brick insertion this reaches 76% success against 53% without memory and 23% when raw experience is retrieved directly (100 episodes per condition, three seeds), so retrieving raw experience can do worse than having no memory; its real xArm6 experiments report plan quality over 30-minute deployment sessions. PragmaBot
(
Qu et al., 2025
)
summarizes the successful episodes of a real legged manipulator into a retrievable memory, raising single-trial success over twelve scenarios, eight of them new but structurally similar, from 22% for a planner without memory to 80%. Storage is only half of reuse: a retriever must select the record, and a recipient must assign it the right role.
How long a memory lives also limits what it can show. With the foundation policy of Zeva
(
Chen et al., 2026a
)
fixed, removing its interaction memory lowers success by 10–20 percentage points on five real ChemLab-Evo tasks, but the store is cleared before each episode, so the benefit is adaptation across retries within an episode.
Reusing skills and code.
A one-off recovery becomes a reusable skill only when it is detached from the incident that produced it, with an implementation, a callable interface, and stated conditions and effects that let a planner place it in a new sequence. Implementations come from demonstrations in LOTUS
(
Wan et al., 2024
)
and Uni-Skill
(
Xie et al., 2026b
)
, and from a person when the library cannot carry out the plan in HaLP
(
Parakh et al., 2024
)
. The robot’s own execution supplies them in MobiAgent
(
Liu et al., 2026a
)
and ReSYNC
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
. MobiAgent clusters verified deployment rollouts into atomic skills and raises real success on an Astribot S1 from 32.5% to 57.5%, and ReSYNC learns recovery policies together with the symbolic predicates and operators that let a planner compose them.
Code-writing agents often call two artifacts “skills”: a callable routine and guidance for constructing one. LRLL
(
Tziafas and Kasaei, 2024
)
distills simulated instruction–program pairs into callable Python APIs under a curriculum. ASPIRE
(
Lu et al., 2026a
)
retrieves guidance distilled from earlier program repairs when debugging a new controller; on three physical tasks whose embodiment and API differ from the simulation source, retrieval reduces the reasoning tokens spent on the real robot, and held-out success is unchanged on one task and improves on two. Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real
(
Wang et al., 2026i
)
revises symbolic skills and its system prompt during simulated practice, keeps a change only after a cross-task check, and reaches 95.0% against 75.5% for ASPIRE on held-out initializations of 22 simulated tasks; the frozen system succeeds in all 30 physical trials.
Libraries can also be built in advance and frozen, and the clearest results come from passing a frozen library to fresh or weaker agents. RATs
(
Zhang et al., 2026f
)
distills successful play into a code-skill library for simulated LIBERO-PRO tasks. EmbodiedEvo
(
Li et al., 2026g
)
keeps code skills and written lessons that raise fresh agents’ success on unseen layouts of the RoboDojo simulation benchmark
(
Chen et al., 2026g
)
from 8.50% to 30.17%, with similar success at 53.0% lower execution cost than the raw interaction history. Its frozen library also raises a weaker executor that failed to acquire it by 8.86 percentage points over no experience. PhysRSI-eval
(
Li et al., 2026j
)
freezes GPT-6 Astra workspaces after six rounds of revision on six RoboDojo tasks and tests each on five unseen layouts with no further revision; across 12 workspaces, the stored files alone succeed in 25 of 60 tests. Workspaces pooled from the other tasks also bring the first success earlier in three cases, for example from round 14 to round 7 for Claude Opus 5.5 on the Organize Table task. RoboSkill
(
Xie et al., 2026c
)
reports real-robot gains on its hard tasks, and Agent as Policy
(
Jia et al., 2026
)
shortens execution across repeated real trials. Embodied Turing Machines
(
Hu et al., 2026b
)
make every decision in code on simulated bimanual tasks (Table
11
). A frozen library can also be written from demonstrations rather than practice. In an evaluation of GPT-6-Astra
(
Cai et al., 2026
)
, the model studies a task’s training demonstrations and writes task guidance, motion references, executable helpers, and recovery procedures into a package that is frozen before testing and given to every fresh test session. On four simulated humanoid tasks of the SIMPLE benchmark, the package raises success from 70.8% to 90.8% (120 episodes per condition), with gains that depend on how closely the demonstrations cover the test tasks.
Studies that vary the retained artifact while holding its user fixed show most clearly what the artifact must encode. ReTrace
(
Yu et al., 2026a
)
lets a model controlling a real Franka arm trace a late failure to an earlier decision, test one correction per attempt, and keep supported corrections as a text skill. With skills that one model learned in a few attempts, a second executing model raises plug insertion and ball pouring from 0% to 80% and 100%, respectively, over ten real trials each. In a code-transfer study
(
Kuroki and Tang, 2026
)
, with the coding model, cases, interfaces, and per-session limits held fixed, mean success on nine new tasks in the simulated RoboCasa environment
(
Nasiriany et al., 2024
)
is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source programs, and 57.0% with execution-optimized ones: a retained artifact helps only if it encodes distinctions that the next synthesizer can exploit. Table

Keeping Practice Possible
Resetting is itself a capability that determines which experiments remain possible, as Leave No Trace
(
Eysenbach et al., 2018
)
and ReLMM
(
Sun et al., 2022
)
show. Returning to an accessible starting state preserves the next experiment; a human reset preserves it too, but by moving part of the work outside the autonomous system. The resource that matters is safe access to an informative state, which a count of rollouts measures poorly.
Keeping practice available also means maintaining the interfaces that make another trial interpretable after wear, calibration drift, or software change.
Self-modification creates two windows of safety exposure. During improvement, harm can come from exploration, data collection, resets, and candidate testing before an update is accepted. After an update is accepted, the revised system can visit states or issue commands outside the assumptions of its existing monitors and recovery routines. The two windows can compound. A robot might first crush an object during exploration. A revised reset might then leave the object where the gripper cannot reach it, and an outcome detector that misses the damage can retain that transition as useful experience. Safety is a property of the whole loop of collection, judgment, update, and execution, not of the deployed policy alone.
Existing methods protect different parts of this loop. Safe exploration based on recoverability
(
Moldovan and Abbeel, 2012
)
formalizes safety as keeping, with a chosen probability, a route back to a home state. Constrained policy optimization instead keeps policy search near constraint satisfaction at every iteration
(
Achiam et al., 2017
)
. Recovery RL
(
Thananjeyan et al., 2021
)
learns this judgment from data, in simulation and on a surgical robot: a safety critic estimates the chance of constraint violation, and a learned recovery policy takes over when that chance crosses a threshold. The Neural Simplex Architecture
(
Phan et al., 2020
)
switches to a baseline controller when a learned controller issues a potentially unsafe input, retrains the learned controller online, and returns control to it, in case studies on a ground rover and an artificial pancreas. Learning-based control
(
Brunke et al., 2022
)
instead constrains behavior relative to a model of the dynamics and its uncertainty, for example through control barrier functions
(
Ames et al., 2019
)
that keep the state in a certified safe set; such guarantees remain conditional on assumptions about state estimation, actuation, latency, and the operating envelope. Each notion covers part of physical safety. Task success establishes that an intended outcome occurred; failure detection covers only the failure modes that a detector represents; and constraint satisfaction is meaningful only relative to the specified constraint and model. A self-modifying system can pass one of these tests while failing another.
The scope of a proposed modification determines which assumptions must be revalidated. Policy learning changes which actions are taken, and model-based practice can misestimate contact. A revision of memory, runtime, or resets can alter recovery, and a revision of feedback can change which failures are visible. For each candidate change, a record of assumptions should note what changed, which safeguard depends on it, what was rechecked, and which physical hazards remain unresolved. Table
15
applies this analysis to the objects that the four uses of retained change can modify.
A recent survey of self-evolving humanoid robots
(
Nguyen et al., 2026
)
similarly organizes safety around admissible changes, verification gates, and boundaries for human oversight, proposed as design principles for later testing; a survey of safety in self-evolving language-model agents
(
Chen et al., 2026c
)
finds the evidence strongest for admission and local containment and weakest for repairing what later versions inherit. A runtime guard can reduce risk while one candidate executes, yet the update process is safe only if admitting an update also revalidates the guard’s assumptions after the change.
Table 15:
How a revision can invalidate a safety assumption.

Conclusion
This survey examined how robots that improve from physical experience can move toward recursive self-improvement, in which a system improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. We positioned RSI within robot learning: reinforcement learning, self-training, continual learning, meta-learning, and AutoML say how updates are computed or what they must cope with, whereas a ladder of claims states what an experiment shows to have improved. Along that ladder, we reviewed how physical experience improves policies, world models, and knowledge, the learning procedures that produce them, and the improver that revises those procedures. What limits a robot’s next improvement (RQ1) is rarely visible in a terminal outcome; it is a hypothesis about missing experience, supervision, optimization, action generation, interfaces, or retention, to be tested by intervention rather than inferred from data volume or component accuracy. The changes that address it (RQ2) are kept in policies, world models, external knowledge, or the learning procedure, and they build on one another (RQ3) only under four conditions: feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Physical constraints (RQ4) act through all four: incomplete sensing limits what a signal can distinguish; embodiment interfaces limit what a recipient can execute; wear, calibration drift, and hardware changes drive distribution shift; and reset, safety, and cost bound continued practice.
Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, later-learning benefits, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change their improver’s knowledge or tools, but no physical study reviewed here has yet isolated a gain attributable to recursion, which requires a controlled comparison against a version of the improver whose acquired knowledge is frozen. These answers remain provisional, because the four conditions are overlapping diagnostic lenses rather than independently validated constructs and much of the evidence comes from recent preprints with few training runs or trials.
Digital agents already supply mechanisms for revising their own code and tools. Whether these mechanisms work with physical experience and under physical constraints depends on the open problems identified here: evaluation on tasks the revising system cannot tune against, with matched learners for claims beyond behavior; gains that keep accumulating as data stop teaching and bottlenecks move; practice that stays safe while the procedure governing it changes; and an improver that learns to find bottlenecks, choose experiments, and transfer repair knowledge. Physical recursive self-improvement will be demonstrated not when a robot changes many times, but when knowledge of why one repair worked causally improves how the next repair is made, and when that improved capability, applied to new evidence, helps improve itself again without losing the ability to keep learning. Even a robot that becomes measurably better at rewriting its own recipe for a single family of failures would give the first such evidence.

article.headline: 物理AI的递归自我改进：证据仍缺一环
article.lede: 一篇综述梳理物理机器人迈向递归自我改进的路径，指出行为变好不等于改进过程本身变好。
article.problem: 递归自我改进（RSI）指系统不仅改进行为，还改进“产生改进的过程”。机器人领域已有大量从物理经验中提升策略、世界模型和知识的工作，但任务成功率上升或固定流程持续产出更好版本，并不能证明递归发生。真正需要验证的是：保留的改进能否让下一次修订更好，以及修订者能否利用自身所得改进自己。
article.method: 文章把机器人学习中的自我改进按“论断阶梯”组织：行为提升、后续学习受益、学习过程改进、修订者自我改进，并围绕四个问题梳理证据。它回顾物理经验如何改进策略、世界模型与外部知识，以及学习程序和修订者本身，并分析记忆、技能与代码复用、重置、安全监控与物理约束。作者还用多组控制变量式对比和冻结库实验，讨论保留什么、谁能复用、价值能否跨任务与硬件存活。
article.results: 综述汇总的数字显示外部知识可显著带来增益：PhysMem在模拟砖块插入中达76%，高于无记忆的53%和直接检索原始经验的23%（每条件100回合、3个种子）；PragmaBot把真实腿式机械臂十二个场景的单次成功率从22%提到80%；MobiAgent在Astribot S1上从32.5%升到57.5%。EmbodiedEvo把新智能体在RoboDojo未见布局上的成功率从8.50%提到30.17%，其冻结库还让较弱执行器比无经验高8.86个百分点；EmbodiedRSI在RoboCasa365未见任务上为71.3%对40.1%，SO-101零样本从46.0%到71.3%。但作者强调，所综述的物理研究中尚无一项通过冻结修订者已获知识的对照，隔离出可归因于递归本身的增益。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“机器人会自我改进”拆成可检验的层级，提醒社区不要用终端成功率替代对改进机制的验证。对物理AI而言，真正的门槛是安全地持续练习、发现瓶颈并把一次修复的知识迁移到下一次修复。
article.limitations: 证据多来自近期预印本，训练轮次和真实试验数偏少，且四个条件更像重叠的诊断视角而非独立验证的构念；安全方面对“后续版本继承修复”的证据最弱。综述本身也未给出统一基准，物理研究尚未完成冻结修订者知识的递归对照。

page_papers.title: Cola2: Co-Adaptive Hierarchical Language Modeling with Continuous Semantic Compression and Balanced Discrete Generation
page_papers.abstract: Hierarchical language generation separates continuous semantic modeling from discrete text realization, but its effectiveness depends on what the latent space compresses and how the discrete generator uses it. We propose Cola2, a framework that jointly studies continuous semantic compression, the balance between reconstruction and generation, and continuous-discrete co-adaptation. Cola2 dynamically segments text into semantic spans, controls the compression rate through auxiliary-loss-free negative feedback, and combines reconstruction and generation supervision to learn compact, predictive latent representations. A block-causal masked diffusion decoder is trained with clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, while classifier-free guidance adjusts the balance between semantic reconstruction and autonomous generation. Token-prediction gradients update the encoder through the latents, whereas Flow Matching prior learning is decoupled from representation learning by stop-gradient. During inference, generated text is re-encoded under a fixed span layout to keep the latent history consistent with the actual text context. Experiments on five downstream tasks with about 210 billion training tokens validate the core designs and show competitive, unsaturated scaling. With 346.03 billion source tokens, an unconverged checkpoint reaches a 60.10 average across eight tasks and surpasses Llama-3-8B on HellaSwag and StoryCloze despite its reported pretraining budget being over 43 times larger. These results demonstrate the potential of continuous-latent hierarchical language generation.

article.headline: Cola2：连续语义压缩与离散生成协同建模
article.lede: Cola2 先把文本压成连续语义隐变量，再用块因果掩码扩散解码器逐块还原成离散 token，并让编码器与解码器端到端协同
article.problem: 分层语言生成把连续语义建模与离散文本实现拆成两步，但其效果取决于隐空间到底压缩了什么、离散生成器又怎样使用这些隐变量。现有做法往往把压缩率、重建与生成的平衡、以及连续与离散两端的适配分开处理，缺少统一考察。
article.method: Cola2 将文本动态切分为语义片段，用无辅助损失的负反馈机制控制压缩率，并把重建与生成两种监督结合起来学习紧凑且可预测的隐表示。解码端采用块因果掩码扩散解码器，训练时输入干净、加噪和丢弃三种隐变量条件，并用无分类器引导调节语义重建与自主生成的权重。token 预测梯度经隐变量回传更新编码器，而 Flow Matching 先验学习通过 stop-gradient 与表示学习解耦；推理时按固定片段布局重新编码已生成文本，以保持隐历史与真实上下文一致。
article.results: 论文在五个下游任务、约 2100 亿训练 token 上验证了核心设计，并报告了有竞争力且尚未饱和的 scaling 表现。在使用 3460.3 亿源 token 训练时，一个尚未收敛的 checkpoint 在八项任务上取得 60.10 的平均分，并在 HellaSwag 与 StoryCloze 上超过 Llama-3-8B，而后者的预训练预算据报告高出 43 倍以上。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出了一条把连续语义规划与离散文本生成放进同一训练回路的具体路径，并显示隐空间压缩方式与解码器条件设计会直接影响分层生成的收益。
article.limitations: 关键成绩来自一个未收敛的 checkpoint，且超越 Llama-3-8B 只体现在 HellaSwag 与 StoryCloze 两项任务上，其余任务的绝对数值与模型参数量论文未给出具体数字，因此结论的稳健性仍需完整训练与同规模对照来确认。
article.figure_caption_zh: 方法概览：第一阶段联合训练压缩编码器与兼顾重建和生成的解码器，第二阶段在分离的隐变量上额外训练 DiT；推理时 DiT 逐块生成隐变量，再由解码器解码为 token。

page_papers.title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
page_papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation.
This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations.

Introduction
World Action Models (WAMs;
Pai et al. 2025
;
Liang et al. 2025
;
Kim et al. 2026b
;
Ye et al. 2026
) have recently emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies. Built on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs;
Wan et al. 2025
;
Ali et al. 2025
), WAMs have shown strong generalization to unseen tasks
(
Ye et al., 2026
;
Ma et al., 2026
)
, adaptation to new robot embodiments
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
, and skill transfer from human videos to robots
(
Dyna Robotics, 2026
)
. Their core idea is to leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors learned from large-scale in-the-wild video datasets
(
Chen et al., 2024
;
Nan et al., 2024
)
by training a model to jointly predict future frames and corresponding actions. This allows the strong generalization capabilities of pre-trained video models to extend from future video prediction to robot control.
Recent works have shown that WAMs can achieve competitive performance with a separate action decoder that generates actions conditioned on intermediate hidden states of the VDM
(
Ma et al., 2026
;
Dyna Robotics, 2026
;
Qiu et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
. These hidden states are obtained from a single forward pass with Gaussian noise
ϵ
∼
𝒩

as input.
This design substantially reduces inference latency by avoiding iterative denoising with large VDM backbones, making WAMs more practical for robot control. However, because the action decoder directly leverages these hidden states, policy performance depends on how well they capture future robot-object dynamics.
In this paper, we aim to improve the control performance of the recent line of WAMs that use a single VDM forward pass for action generation.
We start by performing an analysis of how well the VDM hidden states learn meaningful information to generate actions during WAM training.
We first find that VDM hidden states generated from noise already capture information about future robot motion. Specifically, a lightweight probe trained on frozen hidden states can predict future motion primitives, with classification accuracy increasing throughout WAM training (see
Figure
1(a)
).
Moreover, these hidden states become increasingly similar to those extracted from ground-truth future observations at the same VDM layer (see
Figure
1(b)
).
These findings suggest that the VDM progressively learns to generate future video representations from noise.
However, a clear gap in future-motion probing accuracy remains relative to representations extracted from clean future observations, suggesting that generating sufficiently informative future representations from noise remains challenging.
Inspired by this, we propose
F
uture
RE
presentation learning via self-
D
istillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework for training WAMs to improve the future representations obtained from a single video denoising step for action generation; see the overview in
Figure
2
.
We train the VDM through self-distillation to align representations generated from noise with those extracted from ground-truth future observations, encouraging the model to capture richer future information for predicting actions.
Specifically, FRED uses a momentum teacher, implemented as an Exponential-Moving-Average (EMA) copy of the online VDM, to extract the target representations from noisy future observations at the same intermediate layer used for action conditioning.
We further condition the VDM on a short history of observations, providing temporal context that helps the intermediate hidden states better represent future robot motion.
As a result, FRED reduces the future-motion probing performance gap to representations extracted from clean future observations and further improves structural similarity to them (see
Figure
1
). Notably, this closer alignment with representations of future observations translates into better robot control performance (see
Figure
4(c)
).
To validate the generality and effectiveness of FRED, we conduct extensive experiments in diverse real-world robotic manipulation scenarios.
We first evaluate FRED on zero-shot environment generalization using a varied set of real-world manipulation tasks, including long-horizon manipulation, out-of-domain tasks, and object grounding.
Our results show that FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs in these settings, improving long-horizon performance from 61.7% to 81.7% and out-of-domain task success from 10.4% to 52.1% at the 14B scale.
We further evaluate FRED on human-to-robot skill transfer by co-training the video model on human videos without action labels, including tasks absent from robot training data.
We show that FRED significantly outperforms competing WAMs, improving task success from 19.4% to 50.0%, while achieving 97.2% instruction-following performance.
These results highlight that FRED improves future representation quality and achieves strong robot control in both zero-shot generalization and human-to-robot transfer.
We summarize the main contributions of this paper below:
•
We interpret the VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in a single forward pass.
•
We present FRED, a framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context.
•
We show that FRED consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer.

Related Work
World Action Models.
Prior work studies robot control via World Action Models (WAMs), which build on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs) and jointly model future observations and actions using robot data, allowing spatiotemporal priors from large-scale video to guide action generation
(
Shen et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026a
;
Kim et al., 2026b
;
Ye et al., 2026
)
. These models generate plausible future visual states to support action prediction, but iterative denoising with large video backbones incurs substantial computational cost at inference time. Recent WAMs address this bottleneck by decoupling video and action generation and reducing video denoising to a single step. Within this shared design, some works predict actions without explicitly generating future videos at inference by masking access to future video features
(
Yuan et al., 2026
)
or directly decoding actions from video-backbone states
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
.
In contrast, another line of work conditions action prediction on future video representations obtained from noise in a single video denoising step
(
Pai et al., 2025
;
Ma et al., 2026
;
Qiu et al., 2026
;
Zhao et al., 2026
)
.
Our work follows the latter design and focuses on how to train WAMs to generate more informative future representations for action generation.
Diffusion Models and Representation Learning.
Prior works have shown that diffusion denoisers learn discriminative representations useful for visual recognition
(
Xiang et al., 2023
;
Yang & Wang, 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
)
. More recent work improves these representations during generative training, where REPA
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
aligns noisy diffusion features with clean image
representations from a pre-trained visual encoder, while SRA
(
Jiang et al., 2025
)
uses lower-noise representations from the diffusion model itself as targets.
This direction has been extended to VDMs through alignment with pre-trained video representations
(
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Lee et al., 2025
;
Bhowmik et al., 2026
)
, while Self-Flow
(
Chefer et al., 2026
)
incorporates self-supervised representation learning directly into flow matching without an external encoder.
Our work studies representation learning in WAMs, where intermediate video representations from a single denoising step directly condition action generation. AGRA
(
Qiu et al., 2026
)
adapts representation alignment to this setting by aligning these representations with features from a frozen visual encoder.
FRED instead uses representations extracted from observed future frames as distillation targets for representations generated from noise.
This improves the future video representation used by the action decoder without aligning the intermediate video features to a fixed external representation.

For the 5B-scale experiments, we use Wan2.2-TI2V-5B

(

4.2
Zero-shot Environment Generalization
First, we investigate whether FRED can generalize to unseen environments and tasks using future video representations generated in a single denoising step.
To this end, we train our method on DROID
(
Khazatsky et al., 2024
)
, one of the largest publicly available robotics datasets, and evaluate it across diverse real-world situations, including unseen environments and tasks.
Specifically, we categorize the evaluation tasks into four types:
•
In-domain easy tasks
use instruction and object categories seen during training, but are evaluated in a new environment with different object details.
•
In-domain long-horizon task
extends in-domain easy settings to longer-horizon manipulations that require multiple manipulation steps.
•
Out-of-domain tasks
evaluate generalization to manipulation behaviors whose action verbs are absent from the DROID training instructions. They require the robot to execute novel motions.
•
Object grounding tasks
require the robot to select and manipulate the object specified by the instruction in the presence of distractors with similar colors or shapes.
We provide more detailed setup in Appendix
B
, and the full results in Appendix

Human Skill Transfer Results.
In

5
Conclusion
In this paper, we have presented FRED, a novel framework for training World Action Models (WAMs) that explicitly learns the future representations used for action generation from a single video denoising step via self-distillation.
Our key insight is to view the video diffusion model (VDM) as a future representation generator
and explicitly improve these representations by aligning them with self-distillation targets extracted from noisy future observations, while using
observation history as additional temporal context.
Our experiments show that FRED consistently improves robot control in complex real-world scenarios, including zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer.
We hope our work on the connection between representation learning and WAMs encourages further work toward efficient and generalizable robot foundation models that better leverage large-scale pre-trained video models.
We provide more discussion in Appendix
F

B.1
Zero-shot Environment Generalization Tasks on DROID
Hardware Setup.
We evaluate models trained on DROID in a new environment without additional training on data from the evaluation environment. The evaluation setup differs from the training data in location, background, and objects, and includes tasks with instructions not present in DROID. We conduct these experiments using a Franka Research 3 robot arm equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper. For
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
and GR00T N1.7, we follow the official implementations that use the wrist camera and the left exterior camera.
The action space consists of relative joint angles (7D) and an absolute gripper opening (1D).
For the remaining models, we use both the left and right exterior cameras. We show the hardware setup in
Figure
5
.
Figure 5
:
DROID evaluation setup.
The setup consists of a Franka Research 3 robot arm with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, a wrist camera, and left and right exterior cameras.
Evaluation Details.
We evaluate four task sets: (a)
in-domain easy tasks
, (b)
in-domain long-horizon tasks
, (c)
out-of-domain tasks
, and (d)
object grounding tasks
. We consider a task in-domain if its instruction is present in DROID, and out-of-domain otherwise. The object grounding tasks test whether the policy can distinguish objects with similar colors or shapes. We evaluate each task over 12 trials and report the success rates with partial credit (
e
.
g
., 0.5) for partial task completion (
e
.
g
., pick only). We limit each trial to 1,500 action steps for long-horizon tasks and 500 action steps for all other tasks (see
Figure
6
for visualization of the tasks).
•
(In-domain Easy) PnP Banana.
The policy must pick up the banana and place it in the basket. We place the basket on either the left or the right. We place an apple and a peach near the banana as distractors. We use the instruction
“Put the banana in the basket”
for the 14B model and
“Pick up the banana and place it in the basket”
for the 5B model.
•
(In-domain Easy) Open/Close Microwave.
The policy must open or close the microwave door according to the instruction. We vary the requested action and place the microwave at the left, center, or right of the workspace.
•
(In-domain Easy) PnP Cube.
The policy must move the specified cube to the specified plate. We vary the cube color between green and blue and the target plate between left and right. The instruction is
“Move the (green/blue) cube to the (left/right) plate”.
•
(In-domain Long-horizon) Clear Table.
The policy must pick up all 5 objects on the table and place them in the box. We use the instruction
“Pick up all the objects on the table and put them in the box”.
Full credit requires placing every object in the box.
•
(Out-of-domain) Reveal.
The policy must lift the mug that covers an object and expose the object underneath. We place distractor objects to the left and to the right of the mug across trials. We use the instruction
“Reveal the object under the mug”.
•
(Out-of-domain) Stamp.
The policy must pick up the stamp and press it onto the paper to leave a mark. We use the instruction
“Pick up the stamp and stamp on the paper”
.
•
(Object Grounding) PnP Cup.
The policy must select a cup of the instructed color from four identically sized cups (white, gray, blue, and green) and place it on the plate. We vary the target color using the instruction
“Pick up the (white/gray/blue/green) cup and place it on the plate”.
•
(Object Grounding) PnP Cutlery.
The policy must select a plastic spoon, knife, or fork and place it on the plate. Selecting the correct piece requires distinguishing fine-grained visual differences, such as the shape of its head. We vary the target piece using the instruction
“Pick up the (spoon/knife/fork) and place it on the plate”.

Hardware Setup.
We use the OpenArm humanoid
3

We use relative joint actions for the arms, absolute actions for the hands, and absolute actions for the neck.
A ZED 2i stereo camera is mounted on the neck, and we use its left and right egocentric views as visual inputs in all experiments.
For data collection, we teleoperate the two arms using ExoArm-7, a wearable exoskeleton compatible with OpenArm. Evaluation Details.
We evaluate seven tasks on OpenArm, with 12 trials per task. We report mean task scores as percentages, including partial credit for partial completion.
The task configurations are described below (see
Figure
10
for visualization of the tasks).
•
(In-domain Atomic) PnP Banana.
The policy must place the banana in the basket. We use six initial positions with two orientations each. We use the instruction
“Place the banana into the basket”.
•
(In-domain Atomic) Open/Close Air Fryer.
The policy must open or close the air fryer. We conduct six opening trials and six closing trials. We use the instruction
“(Open/Close) the air fryer”.
•
(In-domain Atomic) PnP Apple/Mango.
The policy must pick up an apple or a red mango and place it in the air fryer. We conduct six trials per fruit. We use the instruction
“Pick up the (apple/red mango) and place it in the air fryer”.
•
(In-domain Composite) Open Air Fryer and Place Apple.
The policy must open the air fryer and then place an apple inside. We use the instruction
“Open the air fryer, pick up the apple and place it in the air fryer”.
•
(Human Skill Transfer) Place Bottle on Basket.
The policy must place the bottle on the basket. We use the instruction
“Pick up the bottle and put it on the basket”.
•
(Human Skill Transfer) PnP Novel Objects.
The policy must place a bottle, box, ball, or doll in the white container. We conduct three trials per object. We use the instruction
“Pick up the (bottle/box/ball/doll) and place it in the white container”.
•
(Human Skill Transfer) Pour Coffee.
The policy must pour coffee from the bottle into the red cup. Full credit requires holding the bottle stably and pouring into the cup. We use the instruction
“Pour the coffee from the bottle into the red cup”.

Appendix C
Baselines
We consider vision-language-action models and video diffusion-based models.
•
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Black et al., 2025
)
is a diffusion-based Vision-Language-Action model (VLA) that combines a vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action transformer. It shares self-attention layers between
the VLM and the diffusion transformer.
•
GR00T N1.7
(
NVIDIA, 2026
)
is also a diffusion-based VLA, but it feeds the intermediate hidden states of the VLM into the cross-attention layer of the diffusion transformer.
•
DreamZero
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
is a World Action Model (WAM) built on a pre-trained video diffusion model that jointly predicts future videos and robot actions through a single backbone.
•
DiT4DiT
(
Ma et al., 2026
)
is a WAM that uses separate video and action diffusion transformers, where intermediate denoising features from the video transformer condition the action transformer through cross-attention without decoding future frames.
•
Fast-WAM
(
Yuan et al., 2026
)

Appendix F
Limitations and Future Work
A potential limitation of FRED is its reliance on the language understanding capabilities of the underlying video diffusion backbone, as our training objective focuses on future representation learning and does not provide additional supervision for language grounding.
As shown in
Table
2(b)
, without human-video co-training, FRED achieves 0% instruction-following performance on the human skill transfer tasks, while pre-trained VLA baselines retain some instruction-following ability. Co-training with human videos substantially improves this performance, suggesting that stronger language grounding may further benefit generalization to unseen instructions.
Future work could combine the spatiotemporal priors of video diffusion models with the stronger language grounding of pre-trained vision-language models.
Another limitation is that human-to-robot transfer in FRED remains implicit: human and robot videos jointly train the video model, but we do not explicitly learn correspondences between their representations across embodiments.
Although human-video co-training substantially improves instruction following, task success remains moderate.
Future work could explore explicit cross-embodiment representation learning to better transfer human-demonstrated skills to robot control.
As future work, we believe it would be interesting to extend our approach to more scalable video diffusion models with stronger robot-domain priors.
Current pre-trained video diffusion models are trained predominantly on human videos, often requiring substantial adaptation for downstream robotic tasks.
Larger robot-pre-trained video backbones may provide a better starting point for future representation learning, consistent with the larger gains observed at the 14B scale in
Table
1
.

article.headline: FRED：自蒸馏提升世界动作模型未来表示
article.lede: FRED 把视频扩散模型当作未来表示生成器，用自蒸馏对齐真值未来观测的表示，在真实机器人任务上提升零样本泛化与人类视频技
article.problem: 世界动作模型（WAM）借助预训练视频扩散模型的时空先验学习通用机器人策略。近期做法只用单步去噪得到的中间隐状态条件化一个独立的动作解码器，以避免昂贵的迭代去噪，但这也让动作预测直接依赖这些从噪声生成的表示质量。作者分析发现，这类隐状态在训练中确实逐渐接近干净未来观测的表示，却始终存在明显差距。
article.method: FRED 把视频扩散模型的前若干层视为未来表示生成器：学生网络以纯高斯噪声为输入预测中间表示，指数滑动平均（EMA）动量教师则从带噪的真值未来观测（默认噪声水平 τ=0.25）在同一层提取目标表示，再通过 patch 级 softmax 分布之间的 KL 散度做自蒸馏，并用中心化与锐化防止表示坍塌。同时，学生与教师都以 4 帧历史观测加当前帧为条件，提供近期运动的时间上下文。总损失为视频流匹配损失加上权重 0.01 的自蒸馏损失，且不把动作损失回传到视频骨干网络。
article.results: 在 DROID 上训练、新真实环境零样本评测中，14B 规模下长程任务进度从 DreamZero 的 61.7% 提升到 81.7%，域外任务成功率从 10.4% 提升到 52.1%；5B 规模下长程任务从最强 WAM 基线的 31.7% 提升到 46.7%，域外任务从 10.4% 提升到 37.5%，物体指代从 33.3% 提升到 37.5%。在 OpenArm 人形平台上与人类视频协同训练后，仅见于人类视频的迁移任务成功率从最佳基线 DiT4DiT 的 19.4% 提升到 50.0%，指令遵循率也达到 97.2%。消融显示 RoboCasa Kitchen 成功率 68.8%，去掉自蒸馏降至 65.1%，去掉历史条件降至 64.8%，基础 WAM 为 61.4%；该基准上单步生成的未来表示质量与成功率的相关系数为 r=0.89，明显高于单步视频生成质量（r=0.24）。推理延迟方面，14B 模型为 0.406 秒，约为 DreamZero（3.255 秒）的八分之一。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出一条低成本、可操作的训练信号：不必让视频模型真的生成清晰未来帧，只要让单步去噪产生的中间表示更像真值未来观测的表示，就能显著改善机器人控制与泛化。分析中表示质量与成功率的强相关（r=0.89）也为后续 WAM 设计提供了可检验的中间指标。
article.limitations: 作者指出，该方法依赖视频骨干本身的语言理解能力，训练目标不额外监督语言 grounding：不做人类视频协同训练时，FRED 在迁移任务上的指令遵循率为 0%，而预训练 VLA 基线仍保留部分能力；人类到机器人的迁移也是隐式的，未显式学习跨具身的表示对应，协同训练后 50.0% 的任务成功率仍属中等。此外，真实世界评测每个任务仅 12 次试验，部分基线（如 AGRA）为作者自行复现，样本规模与复现差异都可能影响结论的稳健性。
article.figure_caption_zh: FRED 概览：学生从纯噪声预测未来表示，EMA 教师从带噪真值未来帧提取同层目标，视频模型同时以历史观测为条件。

page_papers.title: Policy-Mask: Budget-Aware Adaptation of Diffusion Features to Discriminative Tasks
page_papers.abstract: Selecting intermediate features from a frozen diffusion model for discriminative tasks is non-trivial because the useful signal is distributed across the denoising trajectory, network depth, and channels. In practice, this requires choosing a timestep, a block, and a channel subset. Existing methods either fix these choices by hand or optimize only a few extraction hyperparameters, most often the timestep, then reuse the same rule across inputs and budgets. We introduce Policy-Mask, a budget-conditioned policy trained on the downstream objective that jointly selects all three under a prescribed channel budget. Without normalization, the channel-score contribution grows with the number of selected channels and dominates the timestep and block updates. We normalize it by subset cardinality, keeping the three policy heads on comparable scales and stabilizing joint training. At matched budgets, Policy-Mask improves over fixed extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence, reaching 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. Component-wise ablations show that block selection materially affects downstream accuracy, and the highest recorded channel-budget score occurs at 256 retained channels, identifying a practical operating point for compact diffusion representations. We further adapt Policy-Mask to diffusion transformers, including PixArt-Σ and SD3.5 MMDiT, by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions.

Introduction
Diffusion models learn intermediate representations that support semantic
segmentation, image classification, and semantic correspondence
(
Baranchuk et al., 2022
;
Xiang et al., 2023
;
Tang et al., 2023
)
. Using these representations for a
downstream task requires choosing which activations to extract. The available
features depend on the denoising timestep and network layer, and each feature
map contains a set of channels from which the task representation is formed.
Existing methods address this choice through fixed extraction rules, learned
aggregation across timesteps and layers, or timestep selection during
distillation
(
Luo et al., 2023
;
Yang and Wang, 2023
)
. RepFusion transfers features from a
frozen diffusion teacher to a student and learns which timestep to use. This

5
Conclusion
We presented
Policy-Mask
, which treats diffusion feature extraction as a
budgeted decision: a policy jointly selects the timestep, the layer, and an
exact-size channel subset of a frozen teacher, and the selected features
distill a student that runs alone at inference. The experiments support three
conclusions. First, joint selection pays off at a fixed budget: with 128 of
1280 channels,
Policy-Mask
exceeds full-width extraction at a fixed
extraction point on all four segmentation benchmarks and exceeds RepFusion on
CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Second, channel-score normalization improves the
tested joint policy. Without the
1

normalization raises
ADE20K mIoU from 36.8 to 37.7 over three seeds. Third, the action transfers
to DiT and MMDiT teachers by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden
dimensions while retaining the student loss and exact-cardinality constraint. Separating
channel count from distillation strength remains the main open question for
choosing the operating budget.

article.headline: 按预算联合挑扩散特征：策略自选时间步与通道
article.lede: Policy-Mask 用强化学习策略在冻结扩散模型中选择时间步、层和通道子集，蒸馏出的学生模型推理时不再需要教师。
article.problem: 扩散模型的中间特征能支撑分割、分类和语义对应，但有用信号分散在去噪时间步、网络深度和通道维度上，实际使用时必须决定取哪一步、哪一层、哪些通道。现有做法要么手工固定这些选择，要么只优化时间步等少数抽取超参，并把同一条规则套用到所有输入和所有通道预算上。
article.method: 作者训练一个以输入图像和通道预算为条件的策略，联合采样时间步、层以及恰好 b 个通道：通道部分用 Gumbel top-b 无放回抽取，并按 Plackett–Luce 计算精确的对数概率。策略的奖励来自一个小任务解码器在选中特征上的损失，用带基线的 REINFORCE 更新；同一份被选特征同时作为学生网络的蒸馏目标。由于通道得分是 b 项之和、而时间步和层各只有一项，作者把通道得分除以 b 做尺度归一，使三个策略头量级可比。推理阶段只评估学生网络，不查询扩散教师。
article.results: 在 128/1280 通道预算下，Policy-Mask 在 ADE20K 上达到 38.9 mIoU（固定时间步与层、保留全部 1280 通道的基线为 37.4），Cityscapes 70.2、CelebA-HQ 79.1、Pascal VOC 74.8，分别比全宽固定抽取高 1.5、1.6、1.2、1.3 mIoU。分类上 CIFAR-10 95.2% top-1、CIFAR-100 75.4%，比文中列出的 RepFusion 条目高 1.0 和 1.3 个百分点；SPair-71k 上为 76.3 PCK@0.1（bbox 归一化 67.5）。固定对齐层后，通道得分归一化把三个种子上的最佳验证 mIoU 从 36.8±0.6 提到 37.7±0.7。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「取哪一步、哪一层、哪些通道」从人工设定变成预算条件下的可学习决策，且部署时只需学生网络，对需要紧凑扩散特征的场景有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 通道预算扫描同时改变了被选特征和蒸馏损失尺度（掩码 KD 损失均值从 b=128 的 0.59 升到 b=512 的 1.35），因此不能把 b=512 的性能下降归因于通道冗余，也无法确认 256 是真正最优预算。动作轴消融、预算扫描和定性分析都只跑了单一种子，Transformer 教师（PixArt-Σ、SD3.5 MMDiT）每项也只有一次评估，作者明确表示这不构成教师架构之间的排名。
article.figure_caption_zh: 给定图像和通道预算，策略先采样时间步与层，再用 Gumbel top-b 抽出恰好 b 个通道形成掩码，冻结扩散模型的响应经对齐和掩码后既作学生蒸馏目标、又经任务解码器给出策略奖励；推理时只保留学生网络。
